Adversarial interoperability is a team sport (permalink) Enshittification is particularly galling because (in theory, at least), digital technology should be really hard to enshittify. That's because the only digital computer we know how to build is the "Turing-complete, universal von Neumann machine," which is to say, a calculating engine capable of computing every valid program. In some deep, important, foundational sense, every computer is the same as every other computer. Sure, they vary in terms of speed, storage and RAM, but given enough time and electricity, every computer can run every program. This has profound implications for enshittification. Say a tech boss takes away a feature you value (as when Sonos pushed an update that removed nearly all the functionality from its "smart" speakers), or adds a feature you hate (like when Chamberlain blocked third-party apps from controlling its garage doors so it could force its customers to view seven ads before they could open or close their garages). At that point, a programmer can write an "interoperable" program that restores the good feature or blocks the bad one. This program can be costlessly and instantaneously distributed to every affected technology user, and those users will likely pay something for it. After all, enshittification is a way to shift value away from technology users to tech companies, which makes the case for you paying for disenshittification technology that wrestles that value back. All of that means that, in a state of nature, companies that are contemplating enshittification need to worry that their greed will tempt new companies to enter the market and poach their customers and suppliers. This alone might be enough to frighten companies off from enshittificatory gambits, and if companies press ahead regardless, then they open market opportunities for better companies that can costlessly, instantaneously usurp the original manufacturer's relationship with their entire affected customer base. That's how it should work. But in 1998, Bill Clinton signed the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, and Section 1201 of the DMCA establishes a felony (punishable by a five-year prison sentence and a $500,000 fine) for reverse-engineering and modifying technology without the manufacturer's permission. Then, the US Trade Rep spent the next 25 years making sure that every US trading partner had an identical (or even worse!) "anticircumvention" law: https://pluralistic.net/2025/05/26/babyish-radical-extremists/#cancon The result is a grotesquely asymmetrical digital world, in which companies are free to use the flexibility of digital computers to downgrade or brick your digital devices, but where you commit a crime if you avail yourself of a countermeasure to get more out of something you own. This is the core technological factor at play in enshittification. Enter AI. Thanks to vibe-coding, everyday people are rolling their own software for their devices and building the tools to shatter the digital locks that manufacturers use to block disenshittification. An excellent article by 404 Media's Jason Koebler runs down some of these hacks, including drop-in replacements for smart TV software that blocks the endless ads and surveillance that have made TVs all but unusable: https://www.404media.co/reverse-engineer-anything-is-the-new-wild-west-of-ai/ These AI tools mix several techniques to disenshittify users' devices. One major component is automating the installation of existing alternative firmware for these devices that have been (possibly illegally) created by hobbyists and uploaded to various code repositories. Installing these alternative OSes is typically a gnarly task, requiring the user to do a lot of complex, fiddly, highly technical work to bypass their devices' digital locks. In a world without anticircumvention law, a company that sold alternative OSes could hire a ton of programmers and UX developers to smooth over this process, but this is beyond the reach of a typical hobbyist or even a community of hobbyists, especially if they must operate in the shadows, under the threat of civil and criminal liability. There's a useful analogy here to the trajectory of desktop versions of GNU/Linux. The first time I tried to install Linux (on an original iMac, in the late 1990s), the installation process included a multi-week post-installation wrangle that saw me (often unsuccessfully) compiling key modules from source code and then painstakingly configuring them to get the computer's graphics and I/O working reliably. Fast forward 30+ years and installing Linux is trivial, thanks to highly capitalized companies like Canonical (makers of Ubuntu, the flavor of Linux I've used for nearly 20 years now). Installing Ubuntu today merely requires that you download the OS to a thumbdrive, reboot your computer using the drive as a startup disk, and click "install." Canonical's installer automatically hunts down the correct software for your hardware and configures it. Canonical writes and contributes to a lot of parts of the Linux OS, but the most important work it does is the fiddly, painstaking, labor- and capital-intensive work of perfecting that installer so it Just Works. Much of what a vibe-coded jailbreaking tool does is stand in for Canonical, but for hobbyist OSes for smart TVs and speakers and many other devices. These LLMs patiently research every weird error and peccadillo and parse through message boards and logfiles detailing other hobbyists' struggles to get the code working and methodically apply and adapt those solutions until your device Just Works. Some of these vibe-coded interop tools go farther than that. According to Koebler's coverage, some device owners had their coding assistants scratch-build entirely new, heavily customized OSes for their devices, complete with bypasses that allow this new code to be installed despite the manufacturer's countermeasures which are designed to prevent this. Delightfully, many of these users have created software that revives their bricked, discontinued devices. This poses the possibility of a world in which manufacturers no longer have the last word in your use of your own property: the mere fact that the manufacturer lost interest in a device and killswitched it does not mean that you must consign that valuable device to a landfill to become immortal, toxic e-waste. All of this is good news. Some of the most sophisticated jailbreaking tools (such as those on the super viral "Reverse Engineer Anything" Github page) run locally, on your own computer, without invoking the "frontier models" that the big, awful AI companies have created: https://github.com/morluto/rea This is good even if you're just modifying your own devices to get them to more closely conform to your own use-case. LLMs are genuinely good at coming up with the abstruse and obscure configuration lines and other incantations to get your technology working. Recently, I used a local model to fine-tune the power-management on my new laptop in ways that go beyond the options that are exposed through user-friendly graphic interfaces. The LLM spat out a grub "GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT" line that (again) Just Worked. The last time I had to do this, I spent days painstakingly trouble-shooting options by trial-and-error. Using a chatbot to fill in the gaps left by decisions about which configuration options to place within reach of regular users and which to reserve for power-users has made my computer much more useful to me for the things I want to do, like writing and making collages. The reality is that it's just not practical for technology developers to turn every conceivable function of your computer into a simple-to-use, accessible tool. A large part of technology design is about leaving things out (or, as my favorite Eno Oblique Strategy goes, "Be the first person to not do something that no one else has ever thought of not doing before"). No matter how thoughtful and diligent a technology designer is, they will never fully anticipate the needs and exigencies of their users. That's why the motto of the disability rights movement is "Nothing about us without us." The users of technology know more about their use-cases than can ever be captured through a requirements gathering exercise and user testing. One of the best and proudest legacies of technology is the lineage of "user-friendly" programming tools that let nontechnical people design their own applications that exactly met their needs, from Hypercard to Visual Basic to Scratch, a lineage that vibe-coding tools are arguably part of: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/25/other-people/#right-there But these tools are not perfect (nothing is). For all that Hypercard lets you do many things that would otherwise require a skilled programmer, it was also always limited relative to, say, writing MacOS code in Objective C. Your Hypercard program might do exactly what you needed it to, but slowly, and sometimes unreliably, and with serious limitations, such as a relatively low ceiling for the number of records you could add to a database. Vibe-coded personal apps aren't necessarily subject to these limitations, but they come with some significant risks. Vibe-code can have serious security vulnerabilities that expose the user to things like identity theft or sextortion. It's conceivable that a vibe-coded garage-door opener app might make it possible for attackers to open your garage door when you're not home (or worse, when you are!). Depending on your risk-tolerance and expertise, these might be acceptable prices, or they might be too high. But it's important to clearly identify the problem here: if the alternative OS you install on your smart TV exposes you to privacy-invading hack attacks, the problem is the defect in that software. The problem isn't that you had the temerity to rip out the manufacturer's own software and replace it with code of your choosing. You bought that TV, it's yours, and you don't owe the manufacturer an obligation to expose yourself to its own, built-in, intentional surveillance and invasive ads. Here's a parallel: you have the right to put any shoelaces in your running shoes. Sure, Nike might prefer you to lace up your Jordans with its expensive OEM laces, but that's Nike's problem, not yours. Now, Nike might argue that by using no-name laces, you run the risk of having a lace break while you're running, which could also break your ankle. That's certainly a possibility: shoelaces do break, and Nike might be justifiably proud of the quality of its laces. But if your generic laces snap (and so does your ankle), the problem is that the shoelaces you chose were defective. The problem is not that you chose someone else's laces. Your stuff is yours. You can put anyone's milk on your cereal, not just the milk that Kellogg's endorses. If the milk you choose is sour and you have to pour your cereal down the toilet, that's too bad, but it doesn't mean that Kellogg's should have the right to shame you for having the temerity to choose the milk you preferred, and it certainly doesn't militate for DMCA-style enforcement to coerce you into using Kellogg's official milk in the name of protecting you from food wastage. I raise this because there's a live debate over this subject, which is well represented in the latest 404 Media podcast: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UbG1qwxMtU0 In the podcast, Koebler and his 404 co-founder Joseph Cox express misgivings about various possible uses of "slop interop." Koebler discusses the fact that John Deere sells the same physical tractor at many different price-points, depending on which software a farmer chooses, and raises the possibility that a farmer might vibe-code software that replicates the high-end functionality without paying for it. Koebler discusses two possible downsides to this: first, that the vibe-coded software might be defective and expose the farmer to risk; and second, a question about whether it's fair or just for a farmer to get those additional functions of their tractor without paying for them. I think the first objection is entirely legitimate. The software you run on your expensive tractor should be secure, both for your own benefit and for the security of our food supply. That's actually a pretty good reason to ditch John Deere's own software, which is very insecure: https://pluralistic.net/2022/05/08/about-those-kill-switched-ukrainian-tractors/ But I think the second question – whether it's legit to get this functionality without paying John Deere for it – is spurious. Sure, if John Deere provides you with that functionality, then they can send you the bill for it. But if you provide yourself with that functionality, using software you procured independently of John Deere, then John Deere has no right to get paid for it, and they certainly shouldn't have the right to stop you. That tractor is yours. The fact that John Deere manufactured it is irrelevant. If you pay a contractor to build a house for you and later on pay a different contractor to add another bathroom to it, you don't owe the first contractor anything. It's your house (and if that bathroom has a leaky toilet, that's a matter between you and the second contractor, and not a reason to force you to only use your original contractor). The law defines a narrow slice of functions that manufacturers get to control: those ideas that a patent examiner deems "novel, useful and nonobvious." It's legit (and good) for commercial operators to copy and improve the ideas of their rivals and competitors. It's why skilled tradespeople cluster together in the same geographic area. Take Clerkenwell, the neighborhood in London where precision machining was invented by the jewelers and machinists who clustered there during the Longitude rewards. The reason all those competitors sought such close promixity to one another was because they wanted to copy the new techniques their rivals were developing (even if that meant that their rivals would be able to copy them): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude_rewards If you're old enough to remember the advent of spreadsheets and the rollout of Visicalc, Lotus 1-2-3 and Excel, you'll know that every time a software vendor invented a new spreadsheet feature, all the other ones immediately copied it. This wasn't bad for spreadsheets: it was good for spreadsheets, just as copying your competitors was good for precision machining in Clerkenwell. Everything from GNU/Linux (a feature-for-feature clone of AT&T Unix) to SAMBA (a plug-compatible clone of Microsoft's SMB) to iWork (file-compatible, feature compatible clones of MS Office's apps) came about through this "adversarial interoperability." What's more, the heyday of this kind of adversarial interop was also the heyday of disenshittification, the era in which any anti-feature installed by your existing vendor could be countered by a disenshittifying patch from a new one: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2019/06/adversarial-interoperability-reviving-elegant-weapon-more-civilized-age-slay The question of whether vibe-coded software is any good is separate from the question of whether it's good to replace the software in your devices, even if you replace it with software that has features that the manufacturer would normally charge a premium for. You are under no obligation to arrange your commercial affairs to the financial benefit of manufacturers, and anyone who claims to be surprised that someone they sold a device to used it to benefit themselves at the manufacturer's expenses is either disingenuous…or unserious. You bought it, it's yours. But just as this vibe-coded adversarial interop has drawn both valid and spurious criticism, it's also drawn excitement that is partially justified and partially overblown. When it comes to reviving bricked devices or rooting out the surveillance and ads from your smart TV, vibe-coded interop tools are genuinely exciting. These are the kinds of enshittification that can truly be remediated with individual jailbreaks. But the real, meaty examples of enshittification can't be addressed on an individual level – they require systemic fixes. If you jailbreak your iPhone so that it can use alternative app stores, that fact is not sufficient to cause those alternative app stores to come into existence. If we want to stop Apple from levying a $100b "app tax" on the digital economy, it's not enough for individuals to vibe-code their own iPhone patches. We need to repeal the law that bans jailbreaking iPhones, so that a would-be alternative app store can raise capital and pay programmers and tech support staff and salespeople to assemble rival catalogs of software and help customers figure out how to get up their phones to use it. The same goes for jailbreaking your printer so it accepts generic ink. Sure, this may work for you if you're up for refilling your own cartridges, and I'm sure that you can find someone on Alibaba who will sell you ink by the gallon. But the mere fact that a few users have secretly and privately jailbroken their inkjets won't conjure up a generic inkjet cartridge manufacturing sector. For that to happen, we need to make jailbreaking printers legal, not just possible. Indeed, if we want to improve the quality of all that jailbreaking code the chatbots are writing and circulating, we need to be able to put those jailbreaks in public repositories for public inspection and public critique. It's possible for some of the code produced by an LLM to be slop, and for other code to be fine, and for yet a third tranche of code to be remediable slop that can be made robust and reliable through auditing and refactoring. You can't figure out which is which if you have to keep that vibe code a secret on pain of a long prison-sentence. I think there's good cause to be excited at the prospect of getting your devices working better, or just working at all. I think that even if the code stops working after a while, that's still fine – either you got more use out of your device than you would have without the new code, or maybe you just make more code that runs for a while for you, and then you do it again. These individual improvements to your devices and technology are worth celebrating. But they are no substitute for systemic intervention. If we're going to have a new, good internet, a post-American internet that truly disenshittifies America's defective tech exports and replaces them with robust, transparent digital public goods, we need to make reverse-engineering legal again. No Need for Retirement When Utopia Is Around the Corner

2026-10-21

I’ve mentioned before my interest in the history and development of nuclear weapons.

Currently, I’m reading The Doomsday Machine: Confessions of a Nuclear War Planner by Daniel Ellsberg (of Pentagon Papers renown).

In the first chapter, Ellsberg talks about his time working at the RAND Corporation during the missile gap years when the U.S. thought it was falling behind the Soviet Union in nuclear capabilities.

Many of his descriptions sound strikingly similar to the rhetoric coming out of places like Anthropic. For example, note the religious overtones of working at a corporation:

I loved RAND, where I ended up spending ten years [...] Much, I imagined, like members of a religious order would, I shared with my colleagues a sense of brotherhood, living and working with others for a transcendent cause.

They were insiders: burdened with the responsibility of knowledge others did not possess.

precisely in my early missile-gap years at RAND and as a consultant in Washington, there was our sense of mission, the burden of believing we knew more about the dangers ahead, and what might be done about them, than did the generals in the Pentagon or SAC, or Congress or the public, or even the president. It was an enlivening burden.

And what was their “enlivening burden”? Saving the world:

[My colleagues] shared a feeling—soon transmitted to me—that we were in the most literal sense working to save the world.

What really stood out was this part, where Ellsberg describes how he and his colleagues truly believed the end was nigh:

From the Air Force intelligence estimates I was newly privy to, and the dark view of the Soviets, which my colleagues shared with the whole national security community, I couldn't believe that the world would long escape nuclear holocaust. Alain Enthoven and I were the youngest members of the department. Neither of us joined the extremely generous retirement plan RAND offered. Neither of us believed, in our late twenties, we had a chance of collecting on it.

This reminds me of the report that AI researchers have taken up smoking as a way to signal their belief that AI will cure cancer before smoking kills them.

At this point, I wouldn’t be surprised to hear a lab like Anthropic announce they’re discontinuing all employer-sponsored retirement benefits. It’d be a small sacrifice on behalf of the employees to demonstrate their faith that universal high income is just around the corner. (The corporate cost savings would just be a nice bonus.)

Pluralistic: The death of history's most successful publisher (20 Oct 2026)

2026-10-20, updated: 2026-10-23

Today's links The death of history's most successful publisher: Google has a scorching case of "main character syndrome." Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Civil War x 4,400 ceramic cats; Okaysellers; Frankenstein hat; Clockwork Fagin; Tracking trackers; "Fever Beach." Upcoming appearances: Victoria, Vancouver, Ottawa, Vienna, Kilkenny, Couretnay, Vancouver, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. The death of history's most successful publisher (permalink) I published my first story in 1988, when I was 17 years old. Today, at 55, I've published more than 30 books, with three more coming in the next year or so. In the intervening years, I've spent a lot of time thinking and talking about publishing. I've had plenty of opportunity to reflect on publishing: I've been a bookseller and worked in libraries, I wrote a column for Publishers Weekly, self-published a few books of my own, published the first-ever book licensed under Creative Commons, and broke several Kickstarter records for audiobook projects. But most of all, I've worked with publishing professionals: publicists, marketing directors, operations people, copyeditors, and, above all, editors. My first novel editor was the magnificent Patrick Nielsen Hayden, who supported my publishing career from the very start, donating to help send me to the Clarion science fiction writers' workshop and inviting me to come read slush at Tor Books whenever I was in New York. Patrick didn't teach me everything I know about publishing, but he sure taught me a lot about publishing, and hardly a day goes by without my having cause to reflect on one of our many discussions over our decades-long professional and personal association. Out of all the things I learned about publishing from Patrick, one truth stands out above all: publishing is "the act of making something public." Publishing may or may not involve editing, layout, printing, binding, marketing or other activities that we associate with publishing houses, but publishing always involves identifying a work, identifying an audience, and finding ways to connect that work to that audience. This definition does a lot of useful work. For one thing, it locates publishing as part of the hard problem of human society, namely, "getting people to care about something that matters to you." Beyond publishing, this is the crux of politics, religion and commerce: https://pluralistic.net/2021/07/04/self-publishing/ For another, this definition lets us understand that (for most of its existence) Google was the most successful publisher in human history. No other institution of any kind connected more works with more audiences. Lots of people have heard of Google's wildly unsuccessful motto "Don't be evil," but far fewer are familiar with Google's wildly successful mission statement, "organize the world's information and make it universally accessible and useful." But all of that is in the past tense. With its AI projects – AI summaries, the Gemini chatbot – Google has abandoned the practice of "connecting works with audiences." Today, Google's function is to plunder all the works on the internet and chop them up and arrange them in an unimaginably vast, multidimensional array for the explicit purpose of preventing audiences from connecting with those works. For most of its history, Google operated in a virtuous cycle with publishers whereby they allowed Google to crawl their sites and Google located audiences and connected them with the pages on those sites. Today, that cycle has turned vicious, with Google acting as a parasite that extracts value from the web's publishers and offers nothing in return. This is entirely in keeping with the enshittification hypothesis: that once a platform is liberated from the disciplining forces of competition, regulation, labor and interoperability, it will squeeze its suppliers and users and harvest all the value for itself: https://pluralistic.net/2023/01/21/potemkin-ai/#hey-guys But AI represents a new phase in enshittification. Google has assayed enshittificatory gambits in the past, like deliberately worsening its search results in order to force you to search repeatedly, which gave the company more chances to show you ads: https://pluralistic.net/2024/04/24/naming-names/#prabhakar-raghavan But as sleazy as those gambits were, they were profitable. In some important sense, they were sustainable. Assuming Google could carry on indefinitely scamming its users in this way, they'd continue to bring in more cash than they spent, and continue to be the world's most successful publisher, connecting works and audiences (albeit in a deliberately degraded way). Contrast this with AI, the money-losingest endeavor in the history of human civilization. Google is losing hundreds of billions of dollars on AI. The more AI Google does, the worse the company's financial footing becomes. If Google does this for long enough, it may cease to exist altogether. This collapse can only be prolonged by Google's ongoing extraction of value from web publishers, who no longer have their works connected with audiences via Google search results. Instead, Google usurps those audiences, shows them as many ads as it can, and still loses money in the bargain. In Tim Wu's Age of Extraction, Wu lays out a thesis about how intermediaries – middlemen who perform a useful function connecting different groups, firms and individuals – are prone to developing "main character syndrome," abandoning their role as facilitators for others and abusing their position to make themselves the prime beneficiary of the transactions they facilitate: https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/691177/the-age-of-extraction-by-tim-wu/ Google has a scorching case of main character syndrome, and nowhere is that more obvious than in its AI-fueled transformation into web-scale parasite. The fact that this gambit might well destroy Google and the publishers the company once served – rather than merely enshittifying search with worse results and more ads – makes the whole thing look more like a Mafia bust-out than the enshittification of the first half of the 2020s: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bust_Out It's certainly an ignominious end for history's most successful publisher (as was). via The Browser

The Underpants Gnomes' Step 2

2026-10-20, updated: 2026-10-25

Source Barry Ritholtz posted this up-and-right chart, which is a classic of exponential extrapolation. Given the difficulty, delays, and cost of bringing the current generation of data center projects on-line, highlighted by Oracle's "force majeure" on a 2.5GW project which is clearly not going to be complete next year, the idea that 4-5GW projects will be up and running in 2029 seems optimistic.

Below the fold I apply some skepticism, because this is starting to look like the classic South Park episode Gnomes:

The episode is also known for the nonsensical business plan that the gnomes of the title devise, whose three steps consist of:

  1. Collect underpants
  2. ?
  3. Profit

which later became a common meme used to mock poorly-thought-out business and political strategies.

Ritholtz' graph came from a report from David Crawford et al of Bain entitled New Innovation Is Required to Fund AI’s $6 Trillion Buildout which projects that:

By 2031, annual spending on AI infrastructure could reach $1.5 trillion, including new data center infrastructure and compute capacity as well as ongoing upgrades to the installed base of GPUs, memory, and networking equipment.

If we assume that capital expenditures amount to about 25% of industry revenue (an ambitious but reasonable percentage based on trends among cloud providers), sustaining this level of investment would require an AI market approaching $6 trillion annually.

...

Together, the consumer and enterprise AI market could total between $1.2 trillion and $1.8 trillion, leaving about $4.2 trillion of new revenue to reach the $6 trillion market that we estimate will be necessary to fund the buildout (see Figure 2).

That revenue must come from new sources of economic value.

Note that when they say "about" $4.2T they really mean "at least" $4.2T — it could be $4.8T. Their ideas on where "about" $4.2T of new revenue to pay for data centers would come from are laughable. For example, they suggest that autonomous vehicles would supply 10% of it but don't notice that the AI for the vehicles wouldn't be in a data center, it would be in the vehicle.

They conclude:

The economics required to generate ROI from AI infrastructure are demanding trillions in new revenue, not just cost savings.

The industry needs a wave of application innovation comparable with what mobile and cloud unlocked, not just productivity gains on existing workflows.

Source But we're not even getting the "productivity gains on existing workflows". Gary Marcus' It remains “very difficult [to find] actual, materially measurable financial impacts” from spending on AI, per new study reported that:

In an emailed newsletter, Laura Bratton at The Information has reported on a new study

The study was from the Wharton School:

Jeremy Korst, one of the Wharton study's authors, said it was "very difficult" to find "actual, materially measurable financial impacts" from AI spending.

Marcus commented:

Anybody remember back in early 2023, when people imagined that ChatGPT was going to 10x every employee’s productivity and radically boost the GDP’s of entire countries?

So far, there’s zero evidence of anything like that happening at scale.

Source Kyle Orland reports that AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software:

A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”

...

For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies.

In Character.ai's Bankruptcy Documents Show the Economics of AI Don't Work Jason Koebler provides evidence that not even enshittification can get the gnomes step 2 to work for AI applications companies:

The company spent $56.1 million on compute costs between January and August of 2026 alone and as of August was losing “approximately $8-9 million per month,” which it said was a massive improvement over the previous year. The company spent $19.7 million on employee salaries and benefits during that same eight-month time period and that a lot of employees quit because they “began questioning Character’s long-term viability,” according to the company.

Character said that its finances had improved to only be losing $8-9 million per month by taking “significant actions to reduce operational costs and improve revenues” by spending less on compute by simplifying its AI model, laying off staff, and injecting ads into its chats.

Source The original neocloud is showing that the gnomes step 2 isn't working for data centers either, as Rachel Graf and Katherine Schwartz reported in CoreWeave’s Bonds Turn Distressed, Drawing ‘Yikes’ From Musk:

The AI cloud-computing provider’s unsecured debt due in 2032 traded below 80 cents on the dollar on Wednesday, according to Trace pricing data. That’s widely considered the threshold for when a borrower is financially strained.

At that price, the bonds yield more than 15% — a figure noted by Palihapitiya that led Musk to respond “yikes” on his social media platform.

In CoreWeave’s bonds scream financial distress, Toby Nangle looks at the cost of insuring against Coreweave defaulting:

someone wanting to buy $10mn of protection against a CoreWeave default needs to pay $1.95mn on day one, then an additional $125k each quarter.

That is rather expensive. Oracle's debt for the "force majeure" data center is trading at 84 cents; this isn't just about Coreweave.

Fundamentally, finding a working step 2 depends upon finding applications for LLMs that increase productivity significantly more than their cost. This would generate profits for the application vendors above the costs they have to pay the data centers, which might increase revenue more than enough to cover the power, depreciation and debt service. It looks like step 2 remains elusive.

via LitHub

2026-10-20 People who hate to write

2026-10-20

2026-10-20 People who hate to write

Why do people like chat bots to write for them? My personal opinion is that this is an extension of learning to write in school. Adults keep telling you what you did wrong. Orthography! Grammar! Messaging! It’s all wrong. And you learn to hate to write. So you only write when it’s necessary, and it’s only necessary when things are important: A cover letter, a job application, a flat you want to rent, a CV you send along – and the rejections keep piling up. If you don’t write for the love of writing, then writing is a chore and an endless test with the world out there to judge you and reject you. And here comes the machine that writes for you! People read what it wrote and nod their head and say to themselves, if only I could have written it that well! So convincing! Such vocabulary. Such fluency! Such elegance. I wish I had written this. This is what I wanted to write. Send.

I don’t see a way out, here. Before AI, people were looking for example letters to adapt online as well. Now they’re using the chat bot for the same thing.

People who love to write might think, ah, but what hurts is when people write notes to their family using the chat bot! And when I look around, I see plenty of people sending me voice messages. Everybody writes instant messages instead of writing long love letters. To focus on the few that write their love letters using a chatbot is to be irate at the smallest minority: The ones who don’t like to write, feel that the must write and have no other option. If they could have sent a voice memo, they would have. If they could have made a phone call, they would have.

Every misplaced use of AI, I feel, is a need that we failed to address before the advent of AI. Now we’re using the terrible hammer for all these problems that remain unresolved. If you love to write and wish for more people to write in their own voice, we need to figure out how teach people how to love to write. Or we need to learn how to live in a world were fewer people have to write. And as long as this tension is not resolved, the chat bots will do the writing people hate.

Anyway, these thoughts prompted by @Remittancegirl writing:

… it is very easy to feel like one’s voice isn’t heard and doesn’t matter. In that case, what does it matter if one’s voice is being usurped.

I think that’s at the heart of it, yes.

#AI

Americans Feel Awful About the Economy

2026-10-20

The Consumer Sentiment Index has tracked how Americans experience the U.S. economy through bouts of runaway inflation, a mortgage crisis, stock market bubbles, and six recessions. And yet the scores right now are lower than at any of those moments. After nearly 50 years of tracking by the University of Michigan, Consumer Sentiment has broken through the basement. Beneath the five index questions are some clues as to why: Since 2008, the number of people who say the government is doing a poor job has grown from about a third to about three-quarters. This dissatisfaction has been a slow burn — and it’s also evidence that Americans are ready for bold, non-incremental economic change.

2026-10-14 Showing a directory tree in Oddμ

2026-10-20

2026-10-14 Showing a directory tree in Oddμ

I was wondering about offering people a way to leave Obsidian. Obsidian is, according to Wikipedia, “a proprietary personal knowledge base and note-taking application that operates on Markdown files.” And Oddμ “helps you run a minimal wiki, blog, digital garden, memex or Zettelkasten … with Markdown files” – so we’re all set, right?

Not quite. For one, Oddμ follows a few conventions: If you visit a directory, you’re redirected to the index page. If that page does not exist, you’re redirected to the edit action for the index page. You never get an overview of where all the other pages are, no sidebar to show all the pages. I wanted to fix this.

The way to add interesting things to Oddμ is by writing code that gets called by the templates used. When looking at a page, the “view.html” template is used. The data it gets is a Page. When you read the oddmu-templates(5) man page, you’ll see what you do with it. It’s “attributes” are either fields of the Page structure, or functions. I wrote a new function called Tree which produces a linked list representing the directory, and some CSS to make it look like a directory tree as you might get it from tree(1).

SkipHomeChangesEditAddDiffZipUploadSearch:Go

. Vault

  • Oddμ: A minimal wiki
  • Welcome to Oddμ
  • themes
    • chat
      • 2026-04-28
      • 2026-04-28
      • Home
    • Themes
    • vault
      • 👉 Home

Home

The vault theme is for medium size wikis: between twenty and two hundred pages, perhaps. It shows a tree of all the existing pages in a sidebar. It’s good to have an overview over the directory structure and not having to write index pages everywhere.

(If you’ve read enough, go back up to themes.)

Comments? Send mail to Your Name you@example.org

The Tree data structure is a link and possibly children for the link. The problem is, of course, that a directory is not really a page. What the code does, in this situation, is it links to the index page of the directory and gives it the name of the directory.

At the end of the list above, for example, “vault” is a link with the name “index” and the title “vault” and it’s only child is a link with the name “index” and the title “Home”. Both link, in fact, to the same page. I know it’s confusing but it looks pretty intuitive until you start clicking on directory names.

type Link struct {
	Title string
	URL   string
}

type Tree struct {
	Link
	Here bool
	Children []*Tree
}

The recursive nav template to produce the HTML, reformatted for readability, is shown below. Here is what it does:

  • if there is a link (the root node has no URL to link to) and if this is the link to the current page you’re looking at, use an emoji and the title, but don’t link to it;
  • otherwise link to the page and use its title for the link text (not the file name);
  • if it has children, start a new list and call the nav template for every link (start at the top);
  • if there is no link (that is we’re at the root node), skip it, start a new list and call the nav template for every link (start at the top).
<nav>
  <p>. Vault
{{block "nav" .Tree}}
  {{if .URL}}
    <li>
      {{if .Here}}
        👉 {{.Title}}
      {{else}}
        <a href="{{.URL}}">{{.Title}}</a>
      {{end}}
      {{if .Children}}
        <ul class="tree">
          {{range .Children}}
            {{template "nav" .}}
          {{end}}
        </ul>
      {{end}}
    {{else}}
      <ul class="tree">
        {{range .Children}}
          {{template "nav" .}}
        {{end}}
      </ul>
    {{end}}
  {{end}}
</nav>

The CSS to generate the nice lines is shown next.

  • navigation ( nav) and page content ( main) are both in a div with flex display, putting them next to each other;
  • the navigation gets a minimum width as well as padding, border and margin on the right;
  • the list marker is not shown but there is an indent of 2ex;
  • instead, the invisible pseudo-element before the list item (except for the top ones) get a border to the left and at the bottom (an L shape) but it’s bottom is half a letter from the bottom (in the middle) and it’s top is 50 lines up (this will fail for very long lists), and the overflow is hidden so you can’t see the very, very long stem of the L (giving us the nice corner ┗ ) stretching up.

The CSS is a wonderful idea I got from StackOverflow.

div { display: flex }
nav { padding-right: 1ch; margin-right: 1ch; border-right: 1px solid #eee; font-size: small }
nav { min-width: 20ch }
nav p { margin-bottom: 0 }
ul.tree { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding-left: 2ex; overflow: hidden; }
ul.tree li { position: relative; }
ul.tree:not(.top-level) li::before {
  content: '';
  position: absolute;
  border-left: 2px solid #888;
  border-bottom: 2px solid #888;
  right: calc(100% + .25ex);
  top: -5000%; /* 50 lines of skipping upwards */
  width: 1ex;
  bottom: calc(100% - 0.5rem);
}

#Oddμ #CSS

2026-10-20. For an example of why this doesn’t scale, take a look at this page, where you’ll see the “vault” theme applied to this blog, with thousands of pages at the top level. It just doesn’t work. You need something to open and close, like a hierarchy of DETAILS and SUMMARY elements; or some sort of solution that shows the immediate siblings, children, and a trail of ancestors. This would be possible, since I have implemented the functions, but I haven’t actually tried it. Let me know if you have a better idea.

Anyway -- I figured out what I want to do. I want to go back to the point where CSS and JavaScript were added to the web. Everything is a document. It's a writer's web. The reader owns the look of the pages. The writer has no say in colors, or arrangements, it's just writing. No character limits. Simple styling. Full fidelity text. Reading and writing, and then the developers can come up with a million different ways to read, and everyone gets to use their favorite editor, always, and store all their writing where they live, and let everyone read it where ever they read. Any structure they can think of, but all the rendering code is with the reader. I think we can take what we've learned since the web got corporatized, and bring it back to the basic platform we had then. And btw, no HTML, just Markdown. :-)

2026-10-19 Wives – Ten Years After (1985), Do the Right Thing (1989)

2026-10-19

2026-10-19 Wives – Ten Years After (1985), Do the Right Thing (1989)

I started feeling better after spending most of Saturday in bed and on the couch. So we went to the cinema again! The first movie we saw at the Filmpodium and then we had to rush to Xenix – and it was worth it!

Wives – Ten Years After (1985) was weird. For the longest time we didn’t get what was going on. What was this party? What’s this business about having children? Being divorced? Being a chimney sweep? Drinking all that alcohol? The sex? Slowly I started to understand. There is no plot with reprises of things mentioned before, rather a growing understanding of what life is like for these women, how they cope, how they react, how it changes them. It wasn’t easy for us to identify with the women. A lot of things didn’t seem to being well for the women. I guess writing about movies ends up being the same as writing about myself and a movie about midlife crisis and failed relationships and drinking in great quantities is – at least for now – outside of my experience. I hope things stay that way. The women in this movie start out unhappy about different aspects of their relationships and living through it, their situation improves a little bit. Not perfect, but better. We still left the cinema confused.

Do the Right Thing (1989) was strange. It started out as a kind of Sesame Street, oddball characters living somewhere in New York. I don’t know New York or its neighbourhoods, so to me it all seemed like comic characters. Everybody has a role and they play it over the top. There’s a racist and a slacker and a drunkard and a sexy lady and an old lady and a radio DJ and on and on. There is conflict and shouting and swearing, insults and laughter and loving and caring. It was fun! There is the guy who is unhappy about there only being pictures of white people in the pizzeria even though it stands in black neighbourhood and all the clients are black. There is a weirdo who likes to carry around a huge stereo turned up to eleven. The situation boils up and then it calms down. And then, at the end, a few things come together. It’s late at night, the guy with the boom box shows up, the guy complaining about the pictures shows up, insults are traded, and suddenly the stereo gets trashed, a fist fight breaks out, the pizzaiolo nearly dies, the cops show up and then the guy with the radio gets killed by the cops. Fuckers! And then the cops leave and the neighbourhood starts rioting and the pizza parlour burns down. More cops, firefighters, everything. What a mess. The next morning, some people are staring at the ruins, others are walking by, just another day. And then two quotations are shown:

“Violence as a way of achieving racial justice is both impractical and immoral. It is impractical because it is a descending spiral ending in destruction for all. The old law of an eye for an eye leaves everybody blind. It is immoral because it seeks to humiliate the opponent rather than win his understanding; it seeks to annihilate rather than to convert. Violence is immoral because it thrives on hatred rather than love. It destroys community and makes brotherhood impossible. It leaves society in monologue rather than dialogue. Violence ends by destroying itself. It creates bitterness in the survivors and brutality in the destroyers.” – Martin Luther King, Jr.

“I think there are plenty of good people in America, but there are also plenty of bad people in America and the bad ones are the ones who seem to have all the power and be in these positions to block things that you and I need. Because this is the situation, you and I have to preserve the right to do what is necessary to bring an end to that situation, and it doesn’t mean that I advocate violence, but at the same time I am not against using violence in self-defense. I don’t even call it violence when it’s self- defense, I call it intelligence.” – Malcolm X

The End.

What a great movie. My only sadness is that the message is a important today as it was in 1989. Cops killing black people with impunity. And yet, violence is not the answer. So hard. And when will white people stop being racist? There are racists everywhere but I see mostly white racist.

The Wikipedia page says that at the 2021 Cannes Film Festival award ceremony, Spike Lee said: “You would think and hope that 30-something motherfucking years later that Black people would have stopped being hunted down like animals.”

Word.

2026-10-17 Some Came Running (1958), Blue Moon (2025), if.... (1968)

2026-10-19

2026-10-17 Some Came Running (1958), Blue Moon (2025), if…. (1968)

On IRC, Benjamin Wil mentioned how he had spent a week at a movie festival and I remembered going to the movies a lot. I near a few cinemas until 2007, moved a bit further away in 2014, and then Covid hit in 2020, and somewhere along the way I just stopped. But this short exchange energised me and I got the programs of Filmpodium and Xenix and signed up for newsletters and the club, talked to Claudia and we got excited and we went to see three movies! And now I have the cold. I suspect, this is not unrelated. Damn.

Some Came Running is from 1958 starring Frank Sinatra playing veteran who returns to his hometown, clearly an alcoholic, followed by a girl played by Shirley MacLaine, who really is in love with him, but seems very superficial. He likes her when he’s drunk. As more and more towns people are introduced, we see that all of them have flaws. The veteran’s brother values money. His wife hates being humiliated by the veteran. Her daughter starts to rebel when she sees her father having an affair. The veteran meets a gamble who also drinks to much and has diabetes. The veteran wants to take revenge on his brother and needles him but it doesn’t go anywhere. He still likes and care for his niece. The gambler is out of control but still a nice guy. My impression was that this shows how all of us live lives that we cannot control, surrounded by people who all have their own problems, and how difficult it is to make the right choices.

This being movie is from the fifties and had a lot of scenes that I’d consider to be sexual harassment. You know the kind: a man behaving like no means yes, coming up too close for comfort, being unaware of how consent is given. I cringed a few times.

When we left the cinema, however, I was still moved. Life is a complex tapestry and the simple fact that there are so many people in it can be a source of joy.

Blue Moon is from 2025 featuring a man nearly fifty years old, played by Ethan Hawke, being an alcoholic in a middle-age crisis and in love with a beautiful 20 year old woman played by Margaret Qualley. Most of the movie is the man’s monologue, talking to the bar man, the piano man, his composer friend with whom he had a career of 25 years but now that career is over and his composer friend is working with somebody else, and as it turns out, of course the young woman likes to talk to experienced song writer but she doesn’t love him like he loves her, and one one level he knows and on some other level of course he is consumed. It was wonderful.

What left the strongest impression on me was this attempt at describing the burning fire of attraction a man feels for a beautiful woman, who likes the attention, who laughs and talks and moves, knowing how she is magnificent but not understanding the pain in the man’s heart. It reminded me a lot of our own relationship, where I loved to listen to my wife talk and knew exactly that she didn’t understand how the attraction was so strong it was hard to focus on the words and it made her laugh but it was also so alien. Our relationship worked out, we’re still together after over 34 years, so we basically lived through the good parts and this movie shows the terrible abyss of midlife crisis that we’ve been able to avoid so far. I just hope we make it to the end without.

if…. is from 1968 and shows the squalid, terrible elite boarding school life with all its power abuse going on. It was a nightmare. And all the time I thought, unbelievable, the entire elite of a country grew up like that and thinks this is what their children should have to go through, too. And I was thinking of that transphobic author who wrote stories about a magic boarding school who romanticises the whole experience. I was primed for a rebellion, but the movie takes a surreal turn and eventually the viewer is unsure of what actually happened and what was just imagination.

Oof. I’m just glad my school experience was nothing like that.

All in all, I am very happy with the movies I saw. And I want to see more of them. If I did not have a cold right now, we could have gone again, today. It was rainy all day. Perfect cinema day! In fact, with winter coming, a perfect cinema season might be upon me.

But also: I need to get the flu and Covid shots. Damn!

No More Icons In Every Menu By Default

2026-10-19

Have you heard the good news? I bemoaned the approach of putting an icon in every menu item by default which shipped with macOS Tahoe — but now it’s gone in Golden Gate!

John Gruber wrote about this reversion back in June, including the fact that Apple’s new Human Interface Guidelines specifically call out Tahoe’s approach to menus as an example of what not to do on macOS.

As the old saying goes, it takes a big man corporation to admit when they’re wrong.

As I mentioned in my original post, one of the arguments I had in my quiver against this practice was “Apple doesn’t do it”. But once Apple started putting icons in all their menus in Tahoe, I lost a persuasive point in my argument.

But now, I think I have an argument that’s even stronger than before!

It’s no longer: “Apple doesn’t put icons in their menus.”

It’s: “Apple tried putting icons in all their menus, and even they went back on it!”

They designed it, shipped it, lived with it for a year, then publicly changed their guidance on it. To me, that’s a lot more persuasive than simply saying, “Apple doesn’t do this.”

Choosing not to do something you’ve never done is one thing.

Choosing not to do something you’ve done is experience.

That’s the essence of life: learning by doing.

2026-10-19, updated: 2026-10-25

Recently I had the happy task of contributing to a forthcoming issue of the American Behavioral Scientist honoring my PhD advisor, Paul DiMaggio. The issue engages with different aspects of Paul’s very varied work in organizations, culture, institutional analysis, and other topics. My contribution, which you can read a draft of here, puts his most-cited paper, DiMaggio and Powell (1983), in the context of other highly-cited articles in sociology since the 1930s and tries to see what that can tell us. It tries to do that through the lens of the paper itself.

“ The Iron Cage Revisited” is one of the most successful articles in the history of sociology. Web of Science says it has accumulated over thirty-two thousand citations; Google Scholar puts the figure at over seventy-seven thousand. It is the most-cited paper ever published in the American Sociological Review, and the most-cited sociology paper written in the 1980s. Its core ideas—coercive, normative, and especially mimetic isomorphism—have traveled well beyond sociology, most notably into organization studies and management.

Sociology’s top-ten most-cited papers by decade

Here’s the main figure from my paper:

The top 10 most-cited Sociology papers from each decade, 1930s-2010s.

To make it, I took a cohort-based approach to the Web of Science citation data. That is, I divided the period from 1930 to 2019 into decades and, for each decade, found the ten sociology articles published in that decade that have the highest number of lifetime citations.1 Each label shows the journal the paper appeared in. American Sociological Review (ASR) articles are in blue. The American Journal of Sociology (AJS) is in gold. Everything else is in gray. Looking at the very top of the field this way, a few things jump out.

First, there is the sheer volume of citations accumulated by papers from the 1970s and 1980s. For example, Granovetter (1973) is “The Strength of Weak Ties”. It has over 24,000 lifetime citations. The most-cited paper from the 1930s, Merton’s “Social Structure and Anomie” (1938), has about 3,800 by comparison, despite a thirty-five-year head start. “The Iron Cage Revisited” has over 32,000. Papers from more recent decades are of course at a disadvantage simply because they’ve had less time to accumulate citations. But the advantage held by the 1970s and 1980s cohorts isn’t just a matter of time. These are the papers that benefited most from the postwar expansion of the university system, and from the subsequent growth of the citation base as more and more faculty began writing more and more papers.

Second, there’s the character of the papers themselves. Across the decades, most of the top-ten papers are either primarily theoretical or primarily methodological. They are not, for the most part, reports of findings from a particular empirical study. “The Strength of Weak Ties” does briefly sketch Granovetter’s dissertation research, but only schematically, as one illustration amongst several of the main theoretical argument. “The Iron Cage Revisited” is wholly a theory paper. So is Swidler (1986) on culture as a toolkit, West and Zimmerman (1987) on doing gender, and Collins (2015) on intersectionality. On the methods side, we have Freeman (1978) on network centrality, Bentler and Chou (1987) on structural equation models, Corbin and Strauss (1990) on grounded theory, Raftery (1995) on Bayesian model selection, Heckathorn (1997) on respondent-driven sampling, and more besides. The papers that become the most widely cited present either theories or tools. Specific findings, however important, tend not to reach this (admittedly rarefied) level of influence.

The third pattern is the one the paper is mostly about. In the 1930s, five of the top-ten papers appeared in AJS. (ASR’s first issue was in 1936 but it still managed to get two papers in the top ten from that decade.) In the 1940s and 1950s, ASR dominates, with seven of the top ten in each decade and AJS accounting for most of the rest. The 1960s look much the same: one paper from Social Problems (Glaser 1965 on the constant comparative method) and the rest from ASR or AJS. Beginning in the 1970s, though, things start to fragment, and the two flagship journals decline in prominence decade by decade. By the 2000s, just one of the ten most-cited papers comes from ASR, and none from AJS. By the 2010s, neither journal has a paper in the top ten at all. The journals that take their place—the Annual Review of Sociology, Gender & Society, Sociological Methods & Research, Social Networks, Sociological Theory—are specialist outlets or review journals, not competing general-interest journals like Social Forces. This is a complete reversal of the midcentury pattern.

“The Iron Cage Revisited” sits right at the hinge of this change. It’s a pure example of a once fairly common kind of article: a theoretically focused, self-consciously agenda-setting piece published in one of the discipline’s two leading generalist journals. It is also the high-water mark of that combination of form and outlet. Now, the raw counts in the figure favor the 1970s and 1980s. It’s natural to ask what happens if we express each paper’s citations relative to some denominator. One option is to express the citation counts as a percentage of that decade’s citation base: that is, the total number of citations, from anywhere and at any time, to all sociology articles published in that decade. Here is each decade’s most-cited paper expressed as a share of that total.

DecadeAuthorsTitleJournalShare1930sMertonSocial Structure and AnomieASR15.49%1940sMillsSituated Actions and Vocabularies of MotiveASR5.08%1950sSykes & MatzaTechniques of NeutralizationASR4.11%1960sGouldnerThe Norm of ReciprocityASR4.56%1970sGranovetterThe Strength of Weak TiesAJS4.63%1980sDiMaggio & PowellThe Iron Cage RevisitedASR3.32%1990sCorbin & StraussGrounded Theory ResearchZS0.68%2000sMcPherson, Smith-Lovin & CookBirds of a FeatherARS0.62%2010sCollinsIntersectionality’s Definitional DilemmasARS0.26%

Because the citation base grows sharply almost every decade, normalizing this way tends to favor older papers. Merton’s “Social Structure and Anomie” (1938) accounts for over fifteen percent of all citations to sociology papers from the 1930s. From the 1940s through the 1980s the top paper’s share sits in a band of roughly three to five percent. About one in every thirty citations to a sociology paper published in the 1980s is to “The Iron Cage Revisited.” Then, from the 1980s to the 1990s the top paper’s share drops by about an order of magnitude, while the citation base grows by about fifty percent. After that point it’s no longer possible for even the most-cited paper to command the kind of share available to the 1980s cohort.

Why did this happen?

So, from the 1920s to the 1970s, sociology’s most-cited papers were published in its two most important generalist journals. Now, ASR and AJS remain the most prestigious journals in the discipline, and publishing in them is still vitally important for establishing and consolidating a career. But, at least at the very top of the distribution, these journals no longer publish the discipline’s most-cited work. Impact has become decoupled from venue. Why?

It’s plausible to think that the shift is broadly institutional in character, and driven by the forces that DiMaggio and Powell identified. The postwar expansion of American higher education happened in two phases. First came the rapid growth of universities from the late 1940s to the end of the 1960s, bringing many more sociology departments, faculty positions, PhD programs, and journals. Then came the arrival of the students educated during that expansion into the ranks of the faculty themselves. This makes the 1970s and 1980s the era of what you might call “Boomer Sociology”, when the first postwar generation was coming into its own and the discipline reached its largest size.

At this point, there were far more academics writing far more papers, and many more places to publish them. But the most prestigious journals had been founded in earlier waves of institutionalization, and they didn’t much change their format, frequency, or the number of articles they published. As job markets tightened after the initial wave of expansion, the career payoff to publishing in a top journal rose. That changed the character of the gatekeeping role the flagships played. Journals became focal points for career competition.

Over time, ASR and AJS responded with—or gravitated toward; the particular mechanism doesn’t matter much here—a model that demanded more of the papers it published. They had to make a significant contribution on several fronts at once: a substantial empirical finding and an advance in either theory or methods, while at the same time still on a topic of interest to a wide swathe of the field. The idea of a “full package” paper became the expectation. This is a high bar! Run-of-the-mill findings couldn’t clear it. But neither, increasingly, could papers whose main contribution was a theory or a method. You can see this in the figure. After the 1980s there’s only one purely big-idea theory paper from ASR or AJS in the top ten (Emirbayer and Mische 1998’s “What Is Agency?”). The other flagship papers that make the list—Uzzi (1996) on embeddedness, Inglehart and Baker (2000) on modernization and cultural change, and Burt (2004) on structural holes and good ideas—are empirically focused studies with a strong theoretical idea attached. They are exemplars of the newer sort of ASR or AJS paper. But they are also the last papers on these lists to appear in either journal.

It’s tempting to see this as a recognizable case of normative and mimetic isomorphism. Professionalization is one of the main engines of organizational homogenization. In a field whose members are trained in similar programs, credentialed in similar ways, competing for a limited number of positions, and evaluated by somewhat vague but widely shared criteria, organizations and their outputs will tend to converge in form. Sociology’s relative lack of disciplinary consensus may have made this process more intense at the level of the elite journals in particular. (Sociology has always been the least disciplinary of the social sciences, with both the most internal disagreement on theory and methods and— relative to the other social sciences—the most representation of different positions across the field.) Editors were more likely to see themselves as setting and modeling standards for the whole field through peer review. Meanwhile, in departments, a flagship publication could act as a point of consensus amongst colleagues who otherwise disagreed strongly about theory and method. It’s hard to dismiss the value of an ASR or an AJS. (John Levi Martin has referred to this tendency as the Pax Wisconsana.)

Research literatures still principally prize good ideas and useful tools, however. People didn’t stop writing theory and methods papers, and they certainly didn’t stop citing them. It’s just that those papers stopped appearing in the flagships. Big-idea theory papers found homes in Theory and Society (for a while) or Sociological Theory. Methods contributions went to Sociological Methods & Research or Sociological Methodology. Papers developing concepts within subfields like gender, race, culture, or networks went to journals like Gender & Society or Social Networks. And the Annual Review of Sociology emerged as one of the most important venues for highly cited work in the 2000s and 2010s. Reviews have an obvious citation advantage, as they can absorb credit from the work they summarize, though the evidence on how much this matters is mixed.2 Moreover, the most-cited Annual Review pieces tend to frame a problem, set an agenda, or introduce an organizing concept. That is, they are often theory papers disguised as literature reviews.

The upshot is that the demographic expansion and steady professionalization of sociology transformed the expectations attached to people facing an often-uncertain job market. Conditions distinctive to the discipline may have increased the gatekeeping power of its flagship journals. The resulting standards were reinforced through PhD training, the job market, and the tenure process. As a result, the average quality of work in the flagships went up, papers in those journals became more similar to one another, and what ASR and AJS were likely to accept became decoupled from what, at the very highest end of the distribution, the field found most valuable to cite. Elite journals remained elite, but the character of their importance shifted along with the composition of their content. “The Iron Cage Revisited” both marks that shift and helps explain it.

  1. “Sociology articles” means articles published in any journal classified as “Sociology” in the Social Sciences Citation Index. Citation counts are cumulative across all Web of Science databases, so they include citations from any field. Data and code to reproduce the analysis are available on GitHub. ↩︎

  2. The worry goes back at least to Michael H. MacRoberts and Barbara R. MacRoberts, “Problems of Citation Analysis: A Critical Review,” Journal of the American Society for Information Science 40, no. 5 (1989): 342–349. For mixed evidence, see Christian Lachance, Steve Poirier, and Vincent Larivière, “The Kiss of Death? The Effect of Being Cited in a Review on Subsequent Citations,” Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology 65, no. 7 (2014): 1501–1505; and Ruben Miranda and Esther Garcia-Carpintero, “Overcitation and Overrepresentation of Review Papers in the Most Cited Papers,” Journal of Informetrics 12, no. 4 (2018): 1015–1030. ↩︎

Training AIs to Solve CAPTCHAs

2026-10-19

Interesting research:

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can solve visual CAPTCHAs without task-specific training, but the agents built on them approach every challenge from scratch. For such an agent, the hundredth instance of a familiar puzzle costs as much time and compute as the first. Specialized detectors invert the trade-off, answering in milliseconds but only for categories they were trained on. Neither improves with exposure. We study what changes when a solver improves with use. Our system pairs a fine-tuned YOLOv8 detector with an open-weight VLM behind a confidence-based router, and runs entirely from screenshots and operating-system input events, with no browser automation or DOM access. It reaches 85.4% overall and 84.2% macro accuracy across 16 classes, exceeding either component alone. Every answer VLM produces also serves as a training label, so the detector absorbs categories it was never trained for, typically after one or two encounters and without human annotation. The same loop also repairs it. A CAPTCHA operator can perturb images against the publicly released detector and drive its accuracy to 0%, but the perturbations leave VLM untouched, and its labels let the detector recover. Under a year-long simulated arms race in which the CAPTCHA operator re-crafts its perturbations each month, the solver recovers every round, and a cheap ~70%-accurate open-weight teacher hardens it as effectively as a perfect oracle. Visual CAPTCHA defenses that assume a failing bot stays failing therefore understate how quickly an adaptive solver returns...
