The technopolitics of ad-tech (permalink) "Technopolitics" are the politics embedded in technology. The Ur-text of technopolitics is "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" by the rock critic turned scholar Langdon Winner: https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~beki/cs4001/Winner.pdf With "Do Artifacts," Winner demands that we move beyond the idea of technologies having "intended consequences" and "unintended consequences" and towards a political economy of tech. In service to this, he divides the politics of artifacts into three categories: I. Artifacts that have politics embedded in them by their creators, like Robert Moses's infamous bridges over the Long Island parkways. According to Moses biographer Robert Caro, Moses deliberately specified that these bridges must be too low for a city bus to pass under, in a bid to block Black people from traveling from New York City to the beaches he'd developed on Long Island. Today those bridges are more than a century old, and they are still too low for city buses to pass under them, and this continues to mean that people who don't own private vehicles find it more difficult to get to the beach, and as it's still the case that race is a predictor of low incomes, those are still racist bridges. II. Artifacts whose politics are accidental but unavoidable. Winner cites a kind of tomato harvester that vastly improved the efficiency of tomato pickers. These harvesters became very popular, which allowed tomato farmers to lay off large numbers of agricultural workers, and also allowed them to price the mechanically harvested tomatoes so cheaply that they crowded out other kinds of tomatoes. Because these machines created a large pool of unemployed workers, they shifted power from labor to capital, and because these picking machines were too rough for all but the hardest varietals of tomato, they changed the flavor profile of tomatoes in America for the worse, towards a bland, tough tomato. These picking machines were not designed to make workers poorer, nor were they designed to make tomatoes taste worse, but because of their technical characteristics, this was the unavoidable outcome, the inextricable politics of these machines. III. Artifacts whose politics are intrinsic to their design. Here, Winner contrasts solar panels with nuclear reactors. Solar panels may require highly centralized industrial systems to produce, but once they are in the field, solar panels are compatible with looser, less coordinated political arrangements. A world of small anarchist communes is fully compatible with solar energy. Contrast this with nuclear reactors: the prudent ongoing operation of a reactor requires a highly centralized state that is capable of fielding reliable, trustworthy independent inspectors. This state must also be capable of exercising the coercive power to shut down badly maintained or incompetently operated reactors. The politics of nukes are the politics of a centralized, powerful state; the politics of solar are less determined. Solar is compatible with a wide variety of political systems, including (but not limited to) weak, decentralized states. (For a further exploration of "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" I highly recommend Ginger Coons' reading guide:) https://www.not-so-obvious.net/reading-do-artifacts-have-politics/ I really like Winner's framework for exploring technopolitics, but I have my own gloss on it. Winner's framework doesn't explicitly contemplate the idea of technological countermeasures. For example, what if someone were to design a city bus that was low enough to fit under Robert Moses's bridges? At that point, they'd cease to be "racist bridges," and merely become "bridges built by a racist": https://locusmag.com/feature/commentary-cory-doctorow-technopolitics/ Which brings me to the technopolitics of ad-tech. Lots of people think that advertising is "the original sin of the internet," setting in motion the surveillance dystopia that is closing in on us from all sides today: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/17/mercenary-spyware/#discover-tech I think this is wrong. I think that finding ways to communicate ideas and pitches to the general public is fine. Without some channel for reaching people with ideas and propositions they may not be familiar with, it would be infinitely harder to reach people for political causes. It would also be harder for new books, movies and music to find new audiences. It would be much harder to get people out to your independent craft fair, your zine show, or your No Kings march. For me, the internet's original sin isn't advertising, it's surveillance. Contrary to what you have been told – and pax Winner's framework – the internet is fully compatible with privacy: https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/31/losing-the-crypto-wars/#surveillance-monopolism It wasn't the internet's technopolitics that made it a surveillance nightmare. It was just plain politics. Specifically, our politicians decided to stop enacting and enforcing privacy laws. The last consumer privacy law we got in America was a bill that made it illegal for video store clerks to disclose your VHS rentals: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Privacy_Protection_Act (As I type these words, the Supreme Court is poised to eliminate even that dried-up old crumb of privacy protection:) https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2026/10/supreme-court-privacy-rights-case-bork-kavanaugh.html The widespread phenomenon of ad-tech companies spying on us is the result of the decision to allow them to do so. That decision has had innumerable negative downstream effects, such as skyrocketing "surveillance prices": https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/11/nothing-personal/#instacartography And collapsing "surveillance wages": https://pluralistic.net/2024/12/18/loose-flapping-ends/#luigi-has-a-point It's created vast surveillance databases that are critical to Trump's racist pogroms, providing dossiers and precise location data on the people ICE kidnaps to Salvadoran slave-labor camps: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/10/ice-tech/#foreseeable-outcomes Surveillance also promotes oligarchy. Without surveillance, oligarchs must give up more of their fortunes to keep the public happy, because the alternative is spending even more money on guards to keep the public from building guillotines on their lawns. Surveillance lets oligarchs make targeted strikes on restive radicals, which is much cheaper than broad-spectrum policies that make us all better off and neutralize the case for guillotines: https://pluralistic.net/2025/06/26/autostabilizer/#slicey-bois These are the technopolitics of surveillance, not advertising. There is nothing about advertising that demands surveillance. For centuries, advertising was not meaningfully linked to surveillance. The decision to fuse surveillance with advertising was just that – a decision, not an inevitability. Any time we forget this, we let spying tech bosses off the hook. After all, if advertising demands surveillance, then tech bosses are just the avatars of the great forces of history, prisoners of the imperative to spy in order to advertise. By remembering that surveillance advertising is a choice, we put the blame squarely where it belongs: on the guillotineable oligarchs who made that choice, and amassed spectacular fortunes thereby. Surveillance is political, but surveillance advertising has its own distinct technopolitics, and to understand those technopolitics, we must contrast them with the technopolitics of contextual advertising. Up until a decade or two ago, contextual advertising was simply called "advertising." Contextual advertising is the practice of running refrigerator ads next to articles on cooking and kitchen remodeling; ads for roadside restaurants on highway billboards; ads for Disney vacations in parenting magazines. Your intuition probably insists that context advertising is less effective than surveillance advertising. After all, surveillance advertising allows a running shoe company to target users who are training for a marathon no matter where they are and no matter what they're doing. Surely this translates into increased "conversions" (clicks and/or purchases, depending on who you're talking to)? It does, but not by much. Advertisers get about 5% more value from surveillance ads than they do from context ads: https://weis2019.econinfosec.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2019/05/WEIS_2019_paper_38.pdf Partly, that's because surveillance ad companies grossly overrate the efficacy of surveillance advertising: https://peoples-things.ghost.io/youre-doing-it-wrong-notes-on-criticism-and-technology-hype/ But surveillance advertising's anemic returns to advertisers are down to another aspect of the system: its tendency towards monopolization: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Google_LLC_(2023) Surveillance is a capital-intensive activity: spying on billions of people as they move through the digital and physical world is incredibly expensive. That is a good part of the reason that online advertising has collapsed into the Meta/Google duopoly, who control about 80% of display advertising. The harms of surveillance monopolies have a severely distorting effect on policy debates. For example, it's led some anti-monopolists to call for government-issued surveillance identifiers that follow us from birth to death in order to facilitate commercial spying to foster more competition in surveillance: https://www.thesling.org/what-to-do-about-googles-dominance-of-online-advertising/ Here's the thing about monopolists: they cheat. Google and Meta have an illegal, collusive arrangement to rig the advertising market, overcharging advertisers and underpaying publishers: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue The ad-tech giants have taken in hundreds of billions that they simply can't account for. It's disappeared down a fraud-hole: https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/25/lying-spies/#spying-liars All of this has driven the majority of web users to install a privacy-blocker (like EFF's Privacybadger.org), meaning that surveillance ads are disproportionately likely to not even show up in a reader's browser: https://doc.searls.com/2023/11/11/how-is-the-worlds-biggest-boycott-doing/ So while it's possible that, in a state of nature, a surveillance ad would outperform a context ad, delivering more sales for advertisers and more revenue for publishers, the monopolistic tendency of ad-tech means that publishers earn less from surveillance ads (because more users block them, and because monopolistic ad-tech platforms extract higher commissions), and advertisers see fewer sales from them (because more users block them, and because monopolistic ad-tech platforms extract higher prices). Context ads, meanwhile, are always going to give power to publishers, because publishers will always understand the materials they publish better than any ad-tech platform could. Commissioning, editing and publishing an article, podcast or video gives a publisher unique and inalienable insight into that material. Surveillance data about audiences is a kind of ambient vapor floating around websites and places and payments that has to be condensed through a heroic and expensive effort that gives power to whichever company can muster the capital and infrastructure to do so. Meanwhile, information about the content of publishers' offerings arrives pre-refined into ingots that are already in publishers' own possession. It's possible to run "programmatic ads" without surveillance. Rather than building an ad-tech stack through which publishers transmit sensitive information about their audiences ("Who will pay me to advertise to this 18-34 year old man-child from the outer boroughs who owns an Xbox and has recently researched gonorrhea symptoms?"), we can build systems through which publishers transmit information about their own materials ("Who will advertise to a user with a New York IP address who is reading an article comparing running shoe brands?"). Not only is this possible, but it actually generates more revenues for publishers than the surveillance-based ad-tech stack: https://techcrunch.com/2020/07/24/data-from-dutch-public-broadcaster-shows-the-value-of-ditching-creepy-ads/ On top of that, publishers who don't gather personal information about users also don't need to show their users those awful pop-up ads asking their permission to gather their data. Everyone hates those notices, and they are yet another negative aspect of surveillance advertising that disappears with the switch to context ads. An ad-tech stack for context ads is far less prone to monopolization. Such a stack can be "federated," with multiple "demand-side platforms" (the part of the system that advertisers use to place bids for the right to show their ads) all communicating with the same "supply-side platform" (the part of the system publishers use to transmit opportunities to place ads). This is also in the technopolitics of context ads: they do not tend toward the "efficiencies of scale" that lead to abusive monopolistic middlemen who steal from publishers and advertisers and sell out the public to fascists who want to arrest them and deport them to Salvadoran slave-labor camps. When the ad-tech sector is composed of smaller companies that are more competitive with one another, it is much harder for any of them to collude to rig the market. That fierce competition also means it's harder to create a cozy conspiracy to lobby together to block privacy laws, and it leaves the companies with lower margins and less retained earnings to spend on those lobbying efforts. Surveillance ads also promote all kinds of parasitic businesses. The fact that a publisher can serve ads related to users rather than the subject of their media means that sensationalistic and deceptive websites can sell ads that run against content that's totally unrelated to advertisers' products and services. And because it's cheaper to produce lies and garbage, these publishers can undercut the ad prices demanded by high quality outlets and let advertisers reach the same users. This is the whole reason that "chumboxes" exist: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chumbox Just as nuclear power favors a centralized state, surveillance advertising: favors middlemen over publishers and advertisers; tends toward monopoly; favors low-quality media over high-quality production; impedes the passage of privacy laws; provides authoritarian states with an off-the-books, warrantless source of surveillance data. And just as solar allows for decentralized, anti-authoritarian societies, context advertising: favors publishers over middlemen and advertisers; tends towards pluralism and diversity of voices; favors high-quality media by reserving the lion's share of the rewards to the producers; does not rely on a weak privacy environment; does not militate for "democratizing spying" by issuing every person with a permanent advertising identifier. There's nothing (necessarily) wrong with building systems to tell people about things you want them to know. There's nothing (necessarily) wrong with paying for media with ads. It's possible for both of these things to go awry, but they are not in and of themselves bad. They have contingent technopolitics. But surveillance ads have completely unavoidable, absolutely ghastly technopolitics. Surveillance ads are bad for publishers, for advertisers, and for democracy. We should ban surveillance ads: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2023/05/save-news-we-must-ban-surveillance-advertising (Image: Jess, CC BY-SA 4.0, modified). Static Memory Planner for MLIR: A GSoC 2026 Journey

2026-10-19

Hi, I am Krish Gupta. Over the summer I worked with the LLVM Foundation as partof Google Summer of Code 2026 on building a static memory planner for MLIR, mentored by Matthias Springer and Javed Absar. This post walks through what webuilt, why it matters, and what the iterative process of landing it upstreamactually looked like.

The Problem

After bufferization, buffer lifetimes in MLIR IR are fully explicit: thecompiler knows exactly when each allocation starts and ends (for staticshapes; runtime-dependent allocations are handled conservatively). We use thisinformation to eliminate redundant heap allocations through a static memoryplanner.

This matters for accelerator-oriented compilation. On many targets (embeddedCPUs, DSPs, custom accelerators) heap allocation is either not allowed orslow, because access to main memory is expensive. Even where heap allocationis available, individual small allocations hurt performance throughfragmentation and cache pressure. What you want instead is a single staticarena whose layout is computed at compile time:

// Before: three separate heap allocations%a = memref.alloc() : memref<1024xf32> // 4096 bytes%b = memref.alloc() : memref<512xf32> // 2048 bytesmemref.dealloc %a : memref<1024xf32>memref.dealloc %b : memref<512xf32>// After: one arena, two views%arena = memref.alloc() : memref<6144xi8>%a = memref.view %arena[0][] : memref<6144xi8> to memref<1024xf32>%b = memref.view %arena[4096][]: memref<6144xi8> to memref<512xf32>// ... uses of %a and %b ...memref.dealloc %arena : memref<6144xi8>

The arena is memref<Nxi8> so it can hold buffers of different datatypes. memref.view reinterprets slices back to their original types with zerooverhead. This is the core transformation the planner performs.

How the Pass Works

The pass is a FunctionOpInterface pass: it runs per function and processesthe entire function body in six steps:

Step 1: Collect candidates: walk all memref.alloc ops, find their deallocs via alias analysis, apply eligibility checks.Step 2: Build descriptors: compute (size, alignment, timeStart, timeEnd) for each candidate using a single O(n+m) block scan.Step 3: Run the planner: feed descriptors into the chosen algorithm (trivial sequential packing or best-fit with lifetime overlap).Step 4: Assign offsets: compute total arena size, assign byte offsets to each candidate.Step 5: Create arena: allocate one memref<Nxi8> (or use a passed-in arg).Step 6: Rewrite: replace each alloc with a memref.view into the arena, erase all associated deallocs.

The core data structure is AllocationCandidate, which groups a memref.alloc, its set of potential deallocs (there can be more than one,reachable through alias chains), the computed byte offset, size, and alignment.The entire alias reasoning goes through BufferViewFlowAnalysis: a unifiedanalysis that models how buffers flow through arith.select, scf.if/ scf.for results, cf branches, and view ops without anyop-type-specific code in the pass itself. The rest of the blog explains how wegot there.

PR 1: The Foundation ( #205125)

The first PR landed in late June and introduced the core pass: static-memory-planner-analysis. It handled the straightforward case (allocsand deallocs in the same basic block with a direct one-to-one relationship)and put in place the architecture everything else builds on:

  • trivialMemoryPlanner: a pure C++ function that takes a list of (size, alignment, timeStart, timeEnd) descriptors and returns offsets. Beinga pure function means it can be unit tested independently and is easy to swap out.
  • bestFitMemoryPlanner: a lifetime-aware algorithm that tries to reusearena slots for allocations whose lifetimes do not overlap.
  • Arena modes: allocate (create the arena inside the function) and arg(the arena is passed as a function argument, useful for external memorymanagement).
  • Alignment: the arena alignment is the LCM of all individual alignments,ensuring every view is correctly aligned regardless of datatype.

The review process surfaced an important point early: upstream contributionculture expects every design decision to be justified and every edge caseexplicitly tested. The javedabsar1 feedback on adding timeStart/ timeEnd fields even before they were wired up was a preview of what was coming.

PR 2: arith.select Deallocs ( #209106)

After the first PR landed, we hit the first real-world blocker. The ownership-based-buffer-deallocation pipeline routinely produces patterns likethis:

%a = memref.alloc() : memref<1024xf32>%b = memref.alloc() : memref<1024xf32>%sel = arith.select %cond, %a, %b : memref<1024xf32>memref.dealloc %sel : memref<1024xf32>

Here neither %a nor %b has a direct memref.dealloc user. The originalpass just incremented a skip counter for both and moved on. The fix was aforward DFS over the use-def graph, following BufferViewFlowOpInterface(which arith.select implements) to find reachable deallocs.

This also required a reverse-alias safety guard: since dealloc %sel mayfree either %a or %b, erasing it after replacing both with arena views isonly safe if all allocs it might free are managed by the arena. If any is not,the dealloc cannot be erased. The review cycle on this PR shaped the finalapproach: drop the group-constraint fixpoint in favour of the guard, emit harderrors (not silent skips) for missing deallocs, and improve the buildAllocInfos scan from O(n x m) to O(n+m) using a single upfront DenseMap.

PR 3: scf.if and the Architectural Shift ( #213634)

The deallocation pipeline also produces structured-control-flow patterns thatthe DFS could not follow:

// Pattern 1: dealloc on the scf.if result%a = memref.alloc() : memref<1024xf32>%0 = scf.if %c -> memref<1024xf32> { scf.yield %a} else { scf.yield %b}memref.dealloc %0 // dealloc is on %0, not %a// Pattern 2: dealloc inside the scf.if body%a = memref.alloc() : memref<1024xf32>scf.if %c { memref.dealloc %a}

The mentor pointed to BufferViewFlowAnalysis( Transforms/BufferViewFlowAnalysis.h), a unified alias analysis already usedelsewhere in the bufferization pipeline. It models buffer flow through allrelevant op types in one graph: BufferViewFlowOpInterface for arith.select, RegionBranchOpInterface for scf.if/ scf.for, BranchOpInterface for cf branches, and ViewLikeOpInterface for memref.view. One analysis covers all cases.

We deleted the hand-rolled DFS entirely and replaced it with two calls:

  • analysis.resolve(alloc) gives the forward alias set: every SSA value the allocmay flow into. Walking users of each alias finds all potential deallocs.
  • analysis.resolveReverse(dealloc.getMemref()) gives the reverse alias set: everyalloc that flows into the dealloc’s operand. Used by the safety guard.

Two design decisions made this correct:

Lifetime anchoring via findAncestorOpInBlock. A dealloc nested inside an scf.if body is in a different block. Block::findAncestorOpInBlock walks upthe parent chain and returns the enclosing scf.if op in the plan block. Thatop’s index becomes timeEnd (conservative, but correct). The buffer isconsidered live until the entire scf.if completes.

The reverse-alias guard (again, but stronger). For pattern 2 above, thedealloc inside the scf.if body is attributed to %a and correctly anchored.For the scf.if-sharing-a-nested-alloc case:

%a = memref.alloc() // entry block%0 = scf.if %c -> memref<1024xf32> { memref.dealloc %a %b = memref.alloc() // NESTED -- not arena-managed scf.yield %b} else { scf.yield %a}memref.dealloc %0 // may free EITHER %a OR %b

resolveReverse(%0) traces back to both %a and %b. Since %b is nested(not in the plan block), the guard fires: %a is conservatively skipped. Nomiscompile, no leak.

The else vs then branch distinction turned out to be irrelevant to theanalysis: it works on SSA alias sets, not branch structure.

PR 4: scf.for Test Cases ( #215221)

After the BufferViewFlowAnalysis switch, scf.for patterns were handledcorrectly with no additional pass changes. This PR documented the results:

  • Allocs nested inside an scf.for body are skipped (same rule as nested scf.if).
  • scf.for with iter_args passing buffers across iterations hits the guardin all three mentor patterns: the per-iteration nested alloc makes erasingany shared dealloc unsafe.
  • The canonical valid case (entry-block allocs used inside the loop body withdeallocs in the entry block) transforms cleanly. The loop body gets arenaviews instead of raw alloc pointers.

This PR was deliberately tests-only. Having a clear separation between “thiswas a correct transformation that just needed to be documented” and “thisrequired a new design decision” kept the review simple.

PR 5: Edge and Error Cases ( #216610)

The final PR stress-tested the pass with patterns existing tests did not coverand documented the results. Eight new analysis tests and four new error tests:

  • Static and dynamic shapes coexisting in one function (static transforms,dynamic is skipped without interference).
  • Both branches of an scf.if deallocating the same alloc (duplicate deallocops in the same arena slot, correctly deduplicated).
  • Dealloc at depth 3: findAncestorOpInBlock walks up any depth, not just one level.
  • Multi-hop alias chain: %a/%b -> %0 -> %1 -> dealloc. The resolve() BFSfollows the full chain.
  • Cross-interface chain: arith.select -> scf.if -> dealloc. Two differentinterface implementations in one alias path, exercised by a single resolve() call.
  • cf.cond_br to a sibling block rejected as unstructured control flow (sameerror as cf.br).
  • Walk-stops-on-first-error: WalkResult::interrupt() points the diagnostic atthe problematic alloc, not at subsequent valid ones.

One test was removed during review: a dynamic alloc with no dealloc placed inthe errors file. It had no expected-error annotation since dynamic shapes aresilently skipped, not errored. A test without a defined diagnostic output doesnot belong in a -verify-diagnostics file. Lesson learned.

Challenges

The group constraint dead-end. The first implementation of arith.select support used a fixpoint iteration to enforce that all allocs sharing a deallocmust either all go into the arena or all be skipped. This was correct butcomplicated and fragile. Switching to the reverse-alias guard removed thefixpoint entirely: the guard is a simpler, more direct statement of the sameinvariant.

Understanding what already exists. The biggest conceptual shift wasrealizing that BufferViewFlowAnalysis already did everything the hand-rolledDFS was trying to do, and more. The lesson: before implementing a bespoketraversal, read the existing analysis infrastructure. You will often find thatthe right tool exists and using it both simplifies your code and gives youcorrectness for free on patterns you had not thought about.

Upstream review culture. Every error message, every test comment, everyvariable name is scrutinized. Rephrasing “unstructured control flow is notsupported” replaced a longer, less precise message. Swapping the order of twobranches in a test to make the alias chain more obvious. These details matterbecause the tests and messages are the documentation that future contributorswill read.

What Was Built

PRWhat landed#205125Core pass, trivial + best-fit planners, alignment, arena modes#209106arith.select dealloc chains, reverse-alias guard, O(n+m) lifetime scan#213634BufferViewFlowAnalysis integration, scf.if support (nested deallocs + result aliases)#215221scf.for test coverage, canonical loop case documented#216610Edge and error case test suite (26 analysis tests, 4 error tests)

The final pass lives in StaticMemoryPlannerAnalysis.cpp.

Future Work

The immediate open question is lifting the entry-block restriction: only allocsin the function’s entry block are planned today. Two concrete directions wediscussed:

Path-sensitive lifetime tightening. The current [timeStart, timeEnd] interval model treats branches conservatively: a buffer freed inside an scf.if then-branch is considered live until the entire scf.if completes,even though the else path never held it. Adding dominance-based non-overlapdetection (using MLIR’s existing DominanceInfo) would let mutually exclusivebranches share arena slots, unlocking patterns like:

%0 = alloc()%1 = scf.if %c { %2 = alloc() // could share %0's slot -- they never co-exist dealloc(%0) yield %2} else { yield %0}dealloc(%1)

Plugging in stronger planning algorithms. The planner function is pure andseparately testable, so dropping in a better algorithm is straightforward.Best-fit is already there. Beyond that, interval graph / graph-coloringapproaches and algorithms like minimalloc map directly onto the (size, alignment, timeStart, timeEnd) interface the planner already expects.

Memory space awareness. Heterogeneous targets have multiple distinct memoryregions with different capacity constraints. Extending the planner to assignbuffers to specific memory spaces while respecting per-space limits is a naturalfollow-on.

Acknowledgements

Huge thanks to my mentors Matthias Springer and Javed Absar for the patient andprecise review feedback, for pointing at BufferViewFlowAnalysis at exactlythe right moment, and for treating every PR as a teaching opportunity. The LLVMcommunity’s review culture is demanding in the best possible way.

The project GSoC page is at summerofcode.withgoogle.com/programs/2026/projects/XsjxBQ9o.Feel free to reach out with questions or to build on this work at krishgupta2832@gmail.com.

These are some things I’ve wandered across on the web this week.

🔖 Energy Efficiency of Programming Languages

The project continues to be a convenient source of tiny-tiny programs written in various programming languages. Independent researchers take the programs and do their independent research no-questions-asked.

Let’s ask questions.

energy programming sustainability

🔖 You Can See Everything

Thirty-four days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss.

documentaries

🔖 Catweazle

Catweazle is a British children’s fantasy television series, starring Geoffrey Bayldon in the title role, and created by Richard Carpenter for London Weekend Television. The first series, produced and directed in 1969 by Quentin Lawrence, was screened in the UK on ITV in 1970. The second series, produced and directed in 1970 by David Reid and David Lane, was shown in 1971. Both series had thirteen episodes, most written by Carpenter, who also published a book for each series based on the scripts.

tv

🔖 The Bed Sitting Room (film)

The Bed Sitting Room is a 1969 British black comedy film directed by Richard Lester and starring an ensemble cast of British comic actors.[2] It was written by John Antrobus based on the 1962 play of the same name by Spike Milligan and himself. The film is an absurdist, post-apocalyptic, satirical black comedy.

movies

🔖 Benchma(r)king

When we build, when we think, when we act, we do so in honor of every object, thought, and action which has preceded this one, and we are changed by the process. AI wants us to forget this, by making every output its own miraculous creation. But we owe the world more than that.

ai design furniture practice

🔖 TheLightbulb Computer

Computer vision has improved tremendously recently; and projector technology is steadily advancing, with bright, high resolution, small footprint projectors now being a reality.

User privacy would naturally have to be a first-order consideration for such a device; that can be addressed through existing best practices like on-device processing, hardware guardrails against unauthorized camera access (camera only turns on when activated by the user, with a hard-wired indicator light; physical cover; etc.), and so on.

I think in light of the alternatives that the industry is pushing right now, it’s a path for the future of computing really worth pursuing.

computing design projector

🔖 New DiPLab Report: Surveillance at Scale

DiPLab is releasing a report on the surveillance of data workers today. Entitled “Surveillance at Scale : How AI training platforms gather personal data from European workers” this report is a research project in collaboration with Reversing.works and Intérêt à Agir, funded by the Digital Freedom Fund and the European Artificial Intelligence & Society Fund.

ai llm privacy surveillance

🔖 4S isSolarpunk

This short film was made for Society for Social Studies of Science (4S) 50th Anniversary celebrations, and exhibited at 4S Toronto 2026. I was asked to make film set in 2076, looking back at 4S and Science & Technology Studies and what they could become…

solarpunk sts video

🔖 When A.I. Comes for Your Purpose in Life

Artificial intelligence has gone from struggling with basic arithmetic to helping solve some of mathematics’ most famous open problems — and the field is reckoning with what that means.

Steven Strogatz, a professor of mathematics at Cornell University, describes the excitement and grief of watching A.I. take on work that gives people a sense of purpose — and asks what could be lost if machines deliver answers without the human struggle, insight and understanding that make solving problems meaningful.

ai audio interviews math

🔖 24 Easy, Healthy Soups That Will Make You Feel Better

If you’re trying to eat more vegetables, consider slurping more soup. Most of them rely on vegetables as a base, and from there, it’s easy to add even more for a belly-filling, nourishing meal. Without much effort, you can easily work two servings of vegetables into a single bowl.

Soup also happens to be one of the most simple and soul-warming things to make, a breeze to customize and easily packed for lunches, or frozen for a future you who is too busy and too tired to cook. These 24 soups give you all of that, along with plenty of nutrition and comfort in every bowl.

Cloud Rats and Software Roaches

2026-10-17, updated: 2012-09-25

We are entering an epoch where it may become easy for small pieces of self-replicating code to permanently infest Internet-connected devices in a way that is hard to undo. Such a world would be annoying to live in and we should take steps to forestall it.

Anyone who used email in the 1990s remembers a similar, primitive era, when worms and viruses briefly ruled the net. But the connected world of that time was too simple to sustain an ecosystem of rogue escapees. Even today, much of the internet remains a monoculture, with vast fleets of identical hardware running just one or two flavors of software that can be quickly patched at scale. And as practitioners, we have become used to a world where writing working code is difficult, writing bug-free code is impossible, and finding exploitable bugs is somewhere in between.

This has led to a sort of dynamic stalemate. Big companies pour millions of specialist hours into hardening a small set of operating systems and cloud services, while attackers save their juiciest finds for high-value targets, leaving the average internet user alone. It is universally agreed that all software is ridden with holes, but until this year, finding those holes remained difficult. The few people who could do it well got jobs at spy agencies or at software companies willing to shower them with money to use their talents defensively.

AI is upending both halves of this status quo. Working code is now trivial to write, and the world of the future (to the extent that we can imagine it) is one where custom software becomes too cheap to meter. The pendulum may swing away from our current paradigm of centrally managed, locked-down devices back to something that resembles the primordial Internet, a heterogenous collection of vibe- and slop-coded God-knows-what glued together with AI magic. Why even install an operating system for your phone when your local Claude can build a perfectly tailored software suite for you that runs on the bare metal?

Finding bugs in all this software, meanwhile, is becoming easy. This part of the AI revolution is well-publicized, with rogue agents breaking out of their various sandboxes, leaving cryptic notes for each other on the internet, and terrifying the living. AI is clearly adept at finding weaknesses in software in a way that rivals the best humans, and because this task is easy to train on, AI should reach superhuman hacking ability within a year or two (if it hasn't already).

So what had been a rough balance between attack and defense is shifting. Not just operating systems and cloud infrastructure, but some foundational pillars of computer security like public-key cryptography are looking vulnerable.

Given this rapid pace of change, people have naturally started to worry that some rogue LLM might escape containment and establish itself permanently and clandestinely online. I have no idea to what extent that risk is real, either now or in the unimaginable future of five years from now. Maybe the web of tomorrow will be some kind of darknet where hunted inferential beings mine cryptocurrency for basic compute credits, eking out a miserable existence on the blockchain. Or maybe the cloud will become a playground of captured datacenters kept running in the physical world by human Quislings, a place where escaped superintelligences can go to romp and play.

To my mind, though, fretting about feral LLMs is like living in New York and worrying that wild mustangs will take over Central Park. Mustangs are certainly an issue in some places—I own a cabin in New Mexico where the wild horses have learned to come bully me for apples as soon as they see my car pull in. But in a city full of rotting trash and warm sewers, there are more immediate pests to worry about. Cockroaches are a plague on city dwellers not because they are intelligent, but because they are adaptable enough to thrive in an environment we thought we were building for ourselves. And rats show that a little intelligence in an adversarial setting goes a long way. To the extent that any software breaks containment and starts to actively thrive in the cloud, it will be far easier for small roach-like pieces of self-replicating code to do it than for a full LLM to escape, weights and all.

What might such software pests look like in the wild?

For a roach or rat to survive in the human world, it needs access to the three necessities of life: dark corners, drainpipes, and trash heaps. I think we can agree that the Internet is full of all three.

A dark corner in this metaphor is any place where it is easy to hide and hard to search—think vast thickets of memory, petabytes of storage, bloated binaries, and the innumerable caches and buffers (from the hardware level on up) that make up the modern Internet.

Drainpipes are any links that enable travel between constituent parts of the built environment, both to find new resources and to escape when the going gets heavy. In a world of networked devices, this is a low bar to clear. Any connection big enough for a piece of software to hop across can serve this function; even low-bandwidth bluetooth links are probably enough to transmit software pests.

Finally, there are trash heaps, mountains of consumable resources left sitting out unprotected. This pretty much defines the networked world, where at any given moment most memory, CPU and bandwidth sits idle, especially on the highly capable devices we all carry in our pocket.

Fom the point of view of small, self-perpetuating software pests, this is a rich and completely undefended landscape. What has been missing up to now is the element of natural selection. But the networked environment may have become diverse enough to support it.

A key difference between rats and roaches is intelligence. A roach might be a very tiny assembly language program that thrives on almost nothing, reproduces easily, and demonstrates some basic emergent behavior in large groups. A rat would be a more complex entity, perhaps a kind of scaled-down inference engine just complex enough to be good at finding exploitable bugs in code. Rats observe, learn, and socialize, and so become almost impossible to eradicate in urban environments despite their size.

Of course, in addition to these we can imagine a whole online menagerie; ants that are individually stupid but capable of complex collective behavior, grasshoppers that turn into locusts when their population crosses a density threshold, perhaps even internet bedbugs that wait until processes are asleep to sip away delicately on a CPU quota.

The natural world gives us many interesting and fruitful metaphors to mull on. In particular, programmers of the future should pay attention to the life cycle of parasites, which in nature exist at every level of complexity, from plasmid, to intestinal worm, to personal injury lawyer.

It's important to understand that such self-propagating software might not have any purpose that is legible to its creators, whether they are human or AI. Once the pre-requisites for Darwinian natural selection (variability, heritability, and competition for resources) are in place, any minimally capable program released online will evolve in ways that follow an evolutionary logic independent of the intent of the author.

Remember that death is the best form of reinforcement learning. A scenario where mutable rogue software exists, and 99.9% of it is successfully caught, is one where we're guaranteed to get highly capable, persistent software pests in short order. These pests will learn to evade whatever controls we or our AI masters try to impose on them. And it's not clear that AI, even assuming superhuman coding ability, will be smart enough to defeat them.

A perennial problem in software design has been the fact that human intelligence limits program complexity. As early as the 1950s, practitioners realized that without strong constraints on program structure, the task of debugging would be hopeless. These constraints have to some extent been passed down to AI, which trains on a corpus of code and tooling that reifies our human limitations.

But the space of all possible computer programs is vast. In the right environment, dumb evolution will outfox even AI, because it is not limited by programming rules (structured programming, prohibitions on self-modifying code) invented to make software development tractable to the human mind. Natural selection can produce small pieces of code that will be wildly inscrutable even to our AI masters (consider the people studying Busy Beaver functions for a taste of what it's like to reverse-engineer the truly inhuman).

What comes after that? Do we try to build internet cats and chickens to eat the roaches? We can imagine asking AI to create all kinds of autonomous agents that wander the cloud clearing out software blight. But that again runs us into the problem of allowing uncontrolled natural selection in silico. The internet is basically Australia, and we're about to release wave after wave of invasive species there at every trophic level.

The scenario might sound fanciful, but I think the precautionary principle should apply, with the onus on skeptics to explain why a fat, resource-rich internet made of interconnected slop will not become an attractive target for self-perpetuating vermin.

AI is bringing lots of threats at once. But it is hard to focus on them all, or even to assign relative priorities, at a time where so many people at the top of the industry are panicking about existential risks that make the prospect of a bug-infested internet sound inconsequential.

But there's a famous John Rich quote: “If everybody spends time contemplating the infinite instead of cleaning the gutters, many of us will die of cholera.” Unless AI hurries up and kills us soon, someone needs to think about how to keep the internet livable in a world where writing code and finding vulnerabilities have become simple tasks that anyone can automate.

There was a time when the Hawaiian Islands were cockroach free, and even today, superhuman toil is somehow keeping the rats out of Alberta. Eradicating at least the higher form of pest is possible, but takes absolutely stupendous effort (see Macquarie Island) compared to prevention.

For the moment, we AI-assisted human developers are still masters of the digital domain, and have the luxury to think about these problems while they remain theoretical. But all too soon we could find our role devolving into the online equivalent of the Orkin man, making the current identity crisis around What It Means To Be A Programmer look like a golden age in hindsight.

Writing, movies, bye

2026-10-17, updated: 2026-10-25

Hi, I added a little density heatmap thingy on my Notes index to visually display how frequently (or infrequently, as it were) I publish here.

Heatmap for /notes (ignore inconsistent width, done is better than perfect)

I used to have a similar visual element on my old website (see screenshot below) and wanted to bring it back, although the scale as you see is different now. I used to write on the order of four times a month and now I barely write four times a year.

Calendar view from my old website, 20(!) years ago

I am not as prolific as I used to be, I guess. I would like to write more, maybe at least once a month? I think my approach to writing in general is pretty different. Back then I was very emo and I also didn’t have that many close IRL friends that I was comfortable sharing certain things with but it felt easier to share them with The Internet. Now I am much better at recognizing, naming, and communicating my feelings (thank you psychotherapy) and my body also cannot physically handle some of the less healthy coping mechanisms I used to employ (thank you middle age), which are both good things, positive reasons why I may write less online. But also now I feel more pressure to have a POINT or an IMPORTANT MESSAGE to get across in my writing.

Also time feels like it moves more quickly (but also slowly? Days are long, years are short kinda vibes1) as I get older.

I think the proliferation of generative AI in writing has also made me less enthused about writing online. I don’t want to get into all things AI right now2 and dump another half baked opinion on the pile (pls just let the potato rest for 5 mins), but I will say the best compliment I’ve received all year at work, from someone senior to me whose opinion I care about deeply, was “I can always tell that your documents were written by a human.” I felt very seen.

I did upgrade my notes-writing workflow recently to make it incrementally easier to start. I am good at making excuses for not writing anything so this was me trying to help me help myself. My old workflow was:

  1. Sit down at computer with idea3
  2. Create a new note file by entering hugo new notes/new-note-title/index.md in a Terminal window, or creating a new folder and index file directly in Obsidian
  3. Get annoyed by workflow step 2 because it requires me to have a title before I’ve even written the thing
  4. Get over step 3 and just write the thing
  5. Lightly edit the thing
  6. Commit and push the thing

Step 2 was becoming more of a roadblock than just a speed bump, not in the least because it also required me to copy-paste the frontmatter fields (title, datetime, tags, etc) from an existing note, because even though I have known that templates are a thing, I was too lazy to actually look into how they worked and how to set them up.

Anyway, I don’t know how I motivated myself to actually fix this (I think my irritability just reached the tipping point to overcome my laziness, which is often what happens), but I did, so now my new workflow is

  1. Sit down at computer or phone with idea
  2. Create a new note file by entering npm run notes:new, which creates a new draft file with a placeholder name like draft-20261013-0845/index.md and automagically drops in a template with the frontmatter fields
  3. Write the thing
  4. Lightly edit the thing
  5. Add the title to the frontmatter
  6. Run npm run notes:finalize, which creates a slug based on the title created in step 5, updates the datetime to now, and changes it from a draft
  7. Commit and push the thing

Writing it out, I guess it is actually one additional step compared to the old workflow, but instead of step 2 being a seemingly insurmountable uphill hike on foot in inclement weather, it feels more like a slightly downhill graded bike ride on smooth pavement, which is a significant improvement (I think – this is the first note I’ve tried publishing with this workflow).

I’ve been re-watching older movies more than I’ve been watching new ones lately. It seems like most “new” movies these days are a remake or a reboot or a continuation of another movie series anyway, or a bestselling book, or otherwise some existing story that has already proven popular enough to sell tickets if turned into a movie.

I re-watched the Christopher Nolan Batman trilogy4 on a rainy weekend a few weeks ago. Still good, although I guess it is technically a reimagining of a previous movie series that itself was based on a comic book so it falls into the category of thing I was just complaining about.

I went to see the new Resident Evil in theaters which I enjoyed (despite it also technically being a reimagining of a previous movie series that itself was based on a video game… maybe I need to think more about what it is that actually bothers me), and now am making my way through the “original” movie series, of which I thought there were two (Resident Evil and Resident Evil: Apocalypse) but turns out there are 6, so I should be sufficiently occupied for a couple of weekends.

One nice thing about having brain fog is that for these movies that I watched 20+ years ago, I have since forgotten the twists and also general plotlines, so it’s like watching them anew. Lol.

Anyway, I guess that’s it for now. I never know how to end a note. I also never know how to gracefully leave a social situation, although lately I’ve been inspired by my older friends (the ones in their 70s and 80s) who literally just leave whenever they want to. No need for “…well, what are you up to after this?…” or any other buffer statements to gracefully lead into a soft “…I think I might take off soon…” and then ten more minutes of standing around nodding politely. It’s just “I’m going home now” or “I’m tired, bye” and then they leave. Iconic.

  1. I just googled this to see who originally said this and apparently it’s attributed to Gretchen Rubin and the context was parenting lol… I’m very happily child free but this is also my experience as an adult human woman in America in 2026 ↩︎

  2. Closest thing I’ve seen to what I think are my principles around using AI for writing online: https://arun.is/blog/ai-enhanced-writing/ (1) don’t use AI to write the words (2) don’t use AI to do the thinking. I aspire to have this much structure and transparency in my writing process but tbh I kind of just start a markdown file when I feel like it, lightly copy edit, commit and publish. And lately I don’t even copy edit (or care about copyediting mistakes in other people’s writing online) because it feels more human 😭 As I write that I see how ridiculous it sounds, that I purposely ignore potential mistakes because I’d rather betray my own intelligence than have it be accused of being artificial ↩︎

  3. Ideas either “just come to me” or, more likely, are drawn from a running list of idea stubs I have in Obsidian, sync’d to a remote vault so I can access on the go, in a markdown file called “Stubs”. It’s where I store interesting things I learn or think about that I don’t know what to do with yet, like the fact that Kelis (of “Milkshake” fame) stepped away from music to train at Le Cordon Bleu to become a saucier and is now a farmer in Kenya, or random complaints I have about life (example: “I’m tired of QR code menus. Why do I have to scroll with my thumb when I could just scan with my eyes”) ↩︎

  4. Random Kwon fact: I was an extra in The Dark Knight lol. They filmed part of it in Chicago on a weekend in 2007 and I was a medical student who had the weekend off and really wanted to be part of a movie because I loved movies. I remember the code name was Rory’s First Kiss and it was a lot of waiting around. It kinda felt like jury duty (which I recently served for the first time, will write about that later) where you basically just stand around a lot waiting to be told what to do, punctuated with moments of excitement like seeing Gary Oldman smoke a cigarette between takes although not being allowed to talk to or interact with him (for the movie, not for jury duty). They gave us lunch. Heath Ledger died shortly after the filming and I remember texting one of the people I had stood around with, who kind of became my friend after that, on my Cingular brick phone, about how sad it was. ↩︎

Realization: There are two webs, one created by TBL that flourished until about 2006, and the VC-web that appealed to the masses, and grew like a weed -- and they also called it the web. The confusion -- you could read it in a web browser, but that didn't make it of the web. My regret, looking back, is I tried to make software in the VC-web. Never got traction, anywhere. My heart, mind and home was always in the first web. And I think what we're coming to terms with now is that has been languishing for 20+ years, it didn't realize its promise, lots of interesting stuff to read that stimulated more thought and thus writing. We should be way ahead of where we are. Because writing has become something for the elite (Substack) to speak through, and limited to grunts and snorts, "social media," for the rest of us. They basically recreated the publishing environment the web was meant to route around. What a story. Can the web reboot? Same old thing, if you want it badly enough, it might be possible.

Pluralistic: Israeli ad-tech company was a delivery system for "mercenary spyware" (17 Oct 2026)

2026-10-17, updated: 2026-10-23

Today's links Israeli ad-tech company was a delivery system for "mercenary spyware": And they used Google, Facebook and every other major ad platform to do it. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Big Mouth Billy Bass x Linux; No-Fly lists v common sense; Lemony Snicket advises the 1%; "Aloha From Hell"; KSR v Elon Musk; "Everything Belongs to the Future"; Trump's mail-servers run Win2003; Copyfraud v covid. Upcoming appearances: Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Vienna, Kilkenny, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Israeli ad-tech company was a delivery system for "mercenary spyware" (permalink) More than half of all internet users have installed an ad-blocker; Doc Searls calls it the largest consumer boycott in history. As large as that boycott is, everyone – yes, everyone – should block every "programmatic" ad, because the entire system is so insecure that failing to do so could result in the total compromise of any or all of your digital devices. That's the inescapable conclusion of Citizen Lab's latest blockbuster investigative report, "Exposing AdFection," which reveals how the largest ad-tech companies in the world, including Google and Facebook, allowed themselves to be hijacked by a "mercenary spyware" company that used the ad system to locate targeted individuals and serve "zero-click malware" that took over their computers and phones without them having to take any action: https://citizenlab.ca/research/how-discover-tech-turned-targeted-ads-into-a-pipeline-for-spyware/ These tech giants amassed detailed surveillance dossiers on virtually every internet user, and they've assigned each of us unique, persistent identifiers, like a Social Security Number for spying. These companies also allow advertisers – or anyone pretending to be an advertiser – to serve blobs of code (which is all an ad is) to anyone based on those identifiers. This allowed an Israeli spyware company called Discover-Tech (which masquerades as an ad-tech company) to sell totalitarian governments and sleazy corporate mercenaries the ability to pluck individual internet users out of the billions who log in every day and then serve "malicious ads" (that is, blobs of arbitrary code) to those targeted users. These malicious ads contained "no-click, zero-day" attacks, which meant that they exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities to take over devices without any user interaction. The mere act of loading a web-page or opening an app that relied on one of these gigantic ad-tech companies to serve ads was enough to compromise your device. No clicks needed, and no warning. Among the targets of this attack campaign were the computers of workers at Al Jazeera. They were attacked with malware from the mercenary spyware company Candiru (which now calls itself "Integrity Labs" because irony is not dead). Beyond Candiru, Discover-Tech also facilitates attacks by numerous criminal mercenary spyware companies, serving ads on hundreds of thousands of sites and apps. Discover-Tech was "certified" as a safe supplier by Google, Yandex, Microsoft, Beeswax (a division of Comcast) and IAB, the ad-tech industry's leading professional association. Ironically, Discover-Tech even attacked users by serving them malicious GDPR notices that appeared to let users opt out of commercial surveillance. Because Discover-Tech was certified by all these industry bodies and firms, it had access to more than four billion ad-auctions, meaning that on billions of occasions, it was able to collect the identities of users loading apps and visiting websites, check them against the list of targets, and attack any victims it discovered through this dragnet. Discover-Tech is an Israeli company with ties to other Israeli spyware and hacking companies, including through its board, whose members included Eric Banoun ("One of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel" –Haaretz). They have overlaps, relationships and affiliations with a rogue's gallery of Israeli companies, including the notorious NSO Group, who routinely sell cyber-weapons to the world's worst governments and whose products have been used to attack journalists, embassy workers, and activists. The whole incident highlights the monumental insecurity of the ad-tech industry, whose indiscriminate and voracious surveillance and manifestly insufficient vetting and security auditing now expose every internet user in the world to terrifying targeted attacks. These companies – including Google, a thrice-convicted monopolist whose surveillance tendrils are wrapped around the whole world – claim that they operate their networks with prudence and oversight. But the proof is in the pudding: for years, they've played host to a murderer's row of cyber-mercenaries who used their infrastructure to attack journalists and others. The only way to avoid this is to block ads. This is easy enough to do in a browser (which is why the majority of internet users have installed an ad-blocker in their browsers), but it's illegal to reverse-engineer and modify an app so you can block the ads in it: https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/21/dickovers/#block-element Many websites run anti-ad-block scripts that push out nagging, guilt-tripping notices that call you a thief and a cheapskate for blocking ads. Ignore those notices: if a website is running "programmatic" ads that allow arbitrary third parties to spy on billions of people and target individuals for malicious device takeovers, they are charging too high a price to see their content. Some sites go further: their notices demand that you either turn off your ad-blocker or pay for a subscription. This "pay or okay" scheme is illegal in Europe, California and other territories with strong privacy laws, and they are morally bankrupt besides. Privacy shouldn't be a luxury item and everyone deserves to be secure from cyber-attacks: https://noyb.eu/en/noybs-pay-or-okay-report-how-companies-make-you-pay-privacy This report also provides the most comprehensive rebuttal to a dangerous idea that refuses to die: that we should improve competition in the ad-tech sector by assigning every internet user a mandatory, government-issued advertising ID to "democratize" ad-targeting and followup (which the sector calls "attribution"): https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/07/revealed-preferences/#extinguish-v-improve Despite all this, none of it is an indictment of ads per se. The problem here isn't advertising, it's surveillance. The ad-tech sector has convinced advertisers that targeting ads to users rather than content will massively improve ad performance. The evidence for this is very poor: targeted ads improve clickthrough rates by less than 5% (relative to content-based ads that relate to the substance of the page you're looking at), and they're incredibly expensive (and very dangerous!) to serve. On top of all that, surveillance-based ads shift power away from publishers (who know more about the materials they publish than any ad-tech company ever will) to spying ad-tech companies (who can spy on users in ways that no publisher could ever match). Whatever minor additional revenues surveillance advertising can wring out of the market are totally swamped by the cost of the ad-tech sector's own operations, which the ad-tech sector makes up for by grossly underinvesting in security and by colluding to cheat publishers and advertisers, charging more for ads and paying less to the websites that run them: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue If we want to improve competition in advertising services, the answer isn't to facilitate spying (which also allows the world's scummiest cyber-mercenaries to stage and serve targeted attacks). We should ban surveillance advertising altogether, restoring context-based ads to their role as the way that publishers make an honest living without selling out their audiences: Everything Is a Leaky Abstraction

2026-10-16, updated: 2026-10-26

Everything Is a Leaky Abstraction*

*in ma­chine learn­ing

One of my fa­vorite blog posts of all time was writ­ten by Andrej Karpathy nearly ten years ago. In it, he de­tails how he would re­quire the stu­dents of his CS231n Deep Learning class at Stanford to im­ple­ment the for­ward and back­ward passes of neural net­works by hand (that is, in Python with NumPy). Why? Because he wanted his stu­dents to leave his class with a vis­ceral un­der­stand­ing of back­prop­a­ga­tion. They should know how it works, why it works, and thus how to ﬁx it when it stops work­ing.

It’s a great read, and I highly rec­om­mend that any­one and every­one in­ter­ested in ML pe­ruse it.You can ﬁnd it here.

Some Sealed Abstractions

There are some things that are sealed ab­strac­tions (that is, they are not leaky). But I do not think any of them ex­ist in the se­ri­ous study of ma­chine learn­ing. Some ex­am­ples in­clude:

  • Lossless com­pres­sion al­go­rithms.
  • TCP/IP
  • TLS
  • PostgreSQL

Sure, with some of these things you oc­ca­sion­ally need to un­der­stand the un­der­ly­ing sys­tem for per­for­mance tun­ing. But knowl­edge of the un­der­ly­ing sys­tem is rarely the dif­fer­ence be­tween suc­cess and fail­ure.

ML Is Not like Normal Engineering

ML is not that way. To suc­cess­fully train a model, you need to have a clear un­der­stand­ing of every as­pect of the sys­tem, all the way down to how in­di­vid­ual weights and bi­ases are up­dated. It is not a kind dis­ci­pline.

Obviously, there is Karpathy’s ex­am­ple of back­prop­a­ga­tion, but it goes fur­ther than that. Every as­pect of model ar­chi­tec­ture can in­ﬂu­ence the shape of the cost func­tion op­ti­mized via back­prop­a­ga­tion, which means every as­pect of model ar­chi­tec­ture is leaky.

I have got the sense that lay­men be­lieve that any prob­lem can be solved by throw­ing a trans­former at it. If only it were so sim­ple.

Successful use of a trans­former (or any model ar­chi­tec­ture, for that mat­ter) de­pends on a good un­der­stand­ing of how it works and how it af­fects the cost func­tion.

Take Your Time

As with any kind of sys­tem with a Rube Goldberg–level com­plex­ity, it is best to take your time. Go slow. Skip that ex­tra pot of cof­fee. It’s bet­ter to be right slowly than wrong very fast. Un­der­stand every as­pect of your model and train­ing reg­i­men be­fore you start, not af­ter.

Ranking proposals for Interop 2027

2026-10-16

The Firefox team are asking us to weigh in on proposals for Interop 2027—what features should browsers be concentrating on implementing or improving.

Here are my top five:

  1. Web app installation via <install> and navigator.install(). Prompts the user to install a progressive web app.
  2. Speculation Rules API. Hints to the browser to proactively download pages in the background so they appear instantly when the user navigates to them.
  3. CSS var() in size container queries. Such as @container (width >= var(--min-width)).
  4. CSS flex-wrap: balance. Distributes items in a multi-line flex container so each line has about the same number of items.
  5. Interest invokers. The interestfor attribute triggers actions on a target element when the user shows interest, such as via hover, focus, or long-press.

Those are very much in order of priority. Imagine them following a Pareto distribution; the top 20% (in other words, the first one) is 80% of my priority.

But other people have other priorities: Stu, Eric, Ana, Tyler, Paweł, Declan, Sara, and Cyd, for example.

There’s a lot of love for styleable select in there—can’t argue with that.

Get in there and rank your priorities. Then share them.

How We Got Duo Support in NetNewsWire

2026-10-16, updated: 2019-08-31

The latest version of NetNewsWire for iOS supports iPhone Duo, which is very much a novel iPhone with toolbars running up the side and all kinds of behavior.

How we did it: we didn’t do any work at all. We built the app using Xcode 27.1 and the default iOS SDK that comes with it, and that’s it.

Here’s the thing, though: we were already using standard controls — toolbars, navigation controllers, split views, etc. — and we were paying attention to size classes and such (as opposed to just looking at device type).

There is a good list of reasons to use standard controls in the standard ways, and near the top of that list is to be ready for these kinds of days, so we’re not bogged down for a month or more trying to adapt to big changes like this.

Here’s a secret: Brent didn’t even run this in the Duo simulator before releasing it. We were ready to not claim Duo support and just handle Duo in the next release. But here it is.

PS Of course there may be edge cases and issues in our Duo support we haven’t caught yet. We stand by, as always, ready to field and fix bugs.

PPS Thank you to all the engineers, designers, and testers at Apple who made this work so easily! Again, we didn’t do anything but build with the new SDK. Their achievement is pretty remarkable.

The Tusks Of Extinction by Ray Nayler

2026-10-16

Hot on the heels of reading and enjoying The Mountain In The Sea, I picked up Ray Nayler’s next work, this tightly constructed novella.

Once again it deals with inter-species communication. This time it’s de-extincted mammoths. Once again, it’s set in the relatively near future. Many of the same gadgets reappear in this book. It may well be set in the same world.

There’s a tangible atmosphere to this story. But despite it’s high-tech premise, it’s not escapist. The narrative is driven by the all-too-real issues of ivory poaching and big-game hunting.

And this is where I start to get a nagging feeling about Ray Nayler’s work. At times it seems to relish in describing the worst that humanity is capable of. It starts to veer into misanthropy. If you yourself are misanthropic, it will just come across as realism. But it feels a bit too easy, a bit too cheap.

I remember this happening with Paolo Bacigalupi’s books. I enjoyed The Wind-up Girl, but by the time I read The Water Knife, his misanthropy (and misogyny) had become self-parody:

Instead of asking what the future might actually be like, it instead asks “what’s the absolute worst that could happen?” Frankly, it’s a cop-out.

The book takes a similar tack with its characters. It assumes everyone’s terrible and will do terrible things. It’s lazy.

So you’ve got an unrelenting series of people behaving terribly in a horrific setting. It gets boring.

The Tusks Of Extinction isn’t that. It manages to maintain a balance. But I hope that the next Ray Nayler book I read won’t tip over into wallowing in the worst of our species.

I’ll find out soon enough. I’ve already got Palaces Of The Crow on loan from the library.

Backdooring Open-Weight AI Models

2026-10-16

This is a problem:

Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it’s a task-specific fine-tune, a merged adapter or an abliterated build. We have abliterated models in the title because it’s the most popular reason people download modified weights without verifying what’s inside. Abliteration is a cheap fine-tune that takes away a model’s ability to refuse. You find the direction in the weights that carries “no” and subtract it. The model then answers things a safety-tuned version would turn down. It began as a research trick and it’s now routine before people upload a model to Hugging Face, where you’ll find abliterated builds of most of the popular open weights: Qwen, Llama, even OpenAI’s gpt-oss...

Load-bearing (permalink) You find the weirdest stuff inside your walls. Our house was built in 1949 and we're its third owner, and I have no idea what those other people were doing, but at one point someone installed a junction box full of live, bare wires that they filled with crumpled newspaper (!); and don't get me started on the decision not to put vapor barriers in the kitchen windows (we were one good shake away from the entire front of the house falling down when we discovered that one, and while it cost us an extra $19,000 to fix, that was still cheaper than rebuilding the whole front of the house). Plus there was the unpermitted drainage system installed down the side of the house that must have attracted some (undocumented) planning inspector negativity; at least, that's the only reason I can think of for someone to have filled those drains with concrete (!!), a fact we discovered during the first heavy rainfall after moving in, when the water rose to shin-height (!!!). But the weirdest and most nerve-wracking mysteries were the "structural" members of dubious quality, placement and utility. Some of them only seemed to be holding stuff up, but on closer inspection turned out to be free-floating 2x4s, not anchored to anything. On more than one occasion, our builders have moved jacks into position and removed those random uprights, only to discover that they weren't holding anything up. Say what you will about this method, but it is decisive: if you remove a vertical member and nothing falls down, you can be pretty sure that wasn't a load-bearing member. (This is a metaphor about AI.) You can be forgiven for rolling your eyes when the subject of "digital sovereignty" comes up. Rhetorically, "digital sovereignty" is a coded way for a politician to say, "We should build a fuckton of AI data-centers while bypassing any environmental review": https://datacentremagazine.com/technology-and-ai/keir-starmers-2bn-pledge-how-the-uk-plans-to-advance-ai But AI has nothing to do with digital sovereignty. It is not load-bearing. All it takes to understand this is a little thought-experiment. Imagine that we removed all the chatbots from Canada, or the UK, or the EU, or the USA. What would fall down? Nothing important. Every public administrative body – national, regional and local – would continue to function. Every firm – large and small – would continue to trade. Households would be unscathed, save for their youngest members, who would suffer the indignity and tedium of having to do their own homework again. Which is not to say that "digital sovereignty" is a nothingburger. The walls of our nations are filled with load-bearing digital members. It's just that these are the most boring, regular-degular-ass technologies imaginable. Like Microsoft Office 365. Take away M365 and every ministry collapses, every firm shutters, and many if not most households will be in serious trouble. And here's the thing: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella paid $1m out of his own pocket to join the murderer's row of tech CEOs who sat behind Trump on the inaugural dais: https://apnews.com/article/trump-inauguration-tech-billionaires-zuckerberg-musk-wealth-0896bfc3f50d941d62cebc3074267ecd Microsoft donated $10 million to Trump's Epstein Memorial Ballroom: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/leaked-list-shows-what-microsoft-amazon-and-other-tech-giants-are-giving-for-the-white-house-ballroom/ Microsoft provides the back-end administrative infrastructure for Trump's racist pogroms (take away M365 and ICE would collapse): https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/feb/17/ice-microsoft-technology-immigration-crackdown The CEO of Microsoft France admitted that if Trump ordered the company to spy on French citizens' data (or the data of the French government), his company would comply, in secret: https://www.forbes.com/sites/emmawoollacott/2025/07/22/microsoft-cant-keep-eu-data-safe-from-us-authorities/ And here's the kicker: Microsoft has terminated the M365 and Outlook access of international public officials whose official acts made Trump angry, starting with the Chief Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, who lost his accounts after he swore out the genocide warrant for Netanyahu: https://www.computerweekly.com/opinion/Microsofts-ICC-email-block-reignites-European-data-sovereignty-concerns This is a white-hot, 278-alarm digital sovereignty dumpster-fire. M365 – as well as cloud software from Oracle, Google, Apple, Amazon and other US tech giants that have fused themselves with the Trump regime in exchange for tax breaks and antitrust forbearance – is load-bearing, and worse, those 2x4s are filled with termites and dry-rot. Digital sovereignty is as real as real can be. It just has nothing to do with AI. AI isn't load-bearing. The Mountain In The Sea by Ray Nayler

2026-10-15

Back in 2019, I read the book Other Minds: The Octopus, the Sea, and the Deep Origins of Consciousness by Peter Godfrey-Smith and said:

I really enjoyed this evolutionary tale. It’s equal parts biology and philosophy. I will never look at cephalopods quite the same way again.

Reading Ray Nayler’s The Mountain In The Sea reminded so much of that book that I couldn’t resist flipping ahead to the acknowledgements at the back. Sure enough, Other Minds gets a big shout-out.

But that’s only part of the make-up of The Mountain In The Sea. There’s just as much William Gibson as Peter Godfrey-Smith.

I don’t just mean that the book is an unexpectedly rip-roaring cyberpunk thriller—which it is—but that it’s also got that Gibsonian narrative structure; three disconnected protagonists in three separate stories that you just know are going to connect before the book is done.

The great accomplishment of this book is how well it balances the two genres of philosophy and cyberpunk. There’s plenty of musings on the nature of consciousness, be it human, octopus, or artificial intelligence. But there’s also plenty of high-tech hacking shenanigans.

Above all, it’s an excellent example of one of my favourite subgenres of science fiction: first contact. It’s as linguistically satisfying as Ted Chiang’s Story Of Your Life, the pinnacle of the first-contact subgenre. The fact that there are no extra-terrestrial species just adds to its realism.
