Clear the Terminal Like a Pro

2026-10-15

sclide is an implementation of a wipe effect for terminals. It draws a horizontal line that sweeps across the screen, accompanied by a trail with four levels of shading. Then, when requested, it uses the same effect to progressively clear the terminal, line by line.

The project was designed to be small, straightforward, and easy to integrate into other C++ programs.

Key features:

  • 24-bit RGB colors: customize the colors of the line and the trail using RGB values or hexadecimal codes.
  • Four-level trail: uses the characters █, ▓, ▒, and ░ to create a visual gradient.
  • Configurable speed: control the interval between animation steps.
  • Animated clearing: erase the terminal contents with a vertical transition.
  • Character customization: replace the symbols used in the trail.
  • Lean implementation: does not depend on external libraries and pre-calculates the animation sequences to reduce work during rendering.

In action:

Installation

sclide is distributed as C++ source code, and its installation basically consists of obtaining the sclide.cpp file and incorporating it into your project. There is no need to install an additional library.

Windows

The recommended path is to use WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux), since the project uses POSIX calls to query the terminal dimensions and write output.

1. Install WSL, if it is not already available, using PowerShell run as administrator:

wsl --install

2. Open the installed Linux distribution and install the compilation tools:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install git g++ build-essential

3. Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/intriXlabs/sclide.git
cd sclide

4. Copy the sclide.cpp file into your C++ project directory and follow the usage example presented in the next section.

You can also compile C++ projects natively on Windows with other tools, but sclide’s operation in that environment is not guaranteed by the original project.

macOS

On macOS, you can use Clang provided by Apple’s command-line tools.

1. Install the development tools, if necessary:

xcode-select --install

2. Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/intriXlabs/sclide.git
cd sclide

3. Copy the sclide.cpp file into your project directory.

4. Compile your application using clang++ or g++, with support for C++11 or higher.

GNU/Linux

On Debian- or Ubuntu-based distributions, install Git and the compiler:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install git g++

Then, obtain the source code:

git clone https://github.com/intriXlabs/sclide.git
cd sclide

Copy sclide.cpp into your project and compile the application as shown in the following example.

On other distributions, install the C++ compiler and Git using the corresponding package manager.

Getting started

The sclide API is simple: create an object, configure the colors and speed, and call clean() to run the animation.

Create a file named main.cpp in the same directory as sclide.cpp:

#include "sclide.cpp"

int main(){
    // Sets the starting line of the animation.
    sclide wipe(5);

    // Main color: teal.
    wipe.setSclideColor("#00FFAA");

    // Color toward which the trail will fade.
    wipe.setShadeDegradingColor("#001111");

    // Time between steps, in seconds.
    wipe.setSpeed(0.05);

    // Runs the animation and clears the terminal.
    wipe.clean();

    return 0;
}

Compile the program in the terminal:

g++ -O3 -std=c++11 main.cpp -o example

Run it on macOS or GNU/Linux:

./example

On Windows, run the binary inside the WSL environment:

./example

The result is an animated line with a colored trail, followed by the progressive clearing of the screen. Since clean() erases the terminal contents, run the example in a test session.

Customizing the animation

sclide provides methods to adjust the effect during execution.

MethodPurposesetSclideColor()Sets the main color of the line.setShadeDegradingColor()Sets the final color of the gradient.resetSclideColor()Restores the main color to white.setSpeed()Adjusts the interval between steps.changeShades()Replaces the four trail characters.clean()Runs the animation and clears the terminal.

Colors can be configured with hexadecimal codes, such as "#FF6600", or with RGB components. To create different styles, try combining a vibrant main color with a dark degrading color or one close to the terminal’s background color.

For more information, visit the repository

We Need All the Disciplines

2026-10-15

From where I sit, figuring out what to build, building it, and shipping it are all part of the art of making software.

Many disciplines have emerged through the years to facilitate this work: product, design, engineering, devops, etc.

We need all these disciplines to make great, dependable software (granted, in different doses). Each brings different values and judgments; each sees things the others don’t.

And including all might mean going a bit slower.

Human collaboration may seem less “efficient” than handing the work over entirely to the machines.

But inefficiency may be the cost of collaborating with humans, rather than extracting an output from a machine. We gain not only from their judgment and expertise in a particular discipline, but from the relationship, trust, and shared understanding that blossoms from making something together.

As the old proverb says: “If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”

Reformulated for today: If you want to go fast, go with the LLM. If you want to go far, go with your fellow humans.

Dark GPUs

2026-10-15, updated: 2026-10-25

Laying dark fiber

Stealth Communications CC-BY-SA Wikipedia's Dark Fibre article starts:

Dark fibre originally referred to the potential network capacity of telecommunication infrastructure. Because the marginal cost of installing additional fibre optic cables is very low once a trench has been dug or conduit laid, a great excess of fibre was installed in the US during the telecom boom of the late 1990s and early 2000s. This excess capacity was later referred to as dark fibre following the dot-com crash of the early 2000s that briefly reduced demand for high-speed data transmission.

These unused fibre optic cables later created a new market for unique private services that could not be accommodated on lit fibre cables (i.e., cables used in traditional long-distance communication).

Many are analogizing the current AI bubble to the dot-com era, pointing out that although the dark fiber eventually became very valuable infrastructure, the companies that invested in laying it suffered. Wikipedia notes that the buildout:

was based on the assumption that telecoms traffic, particularly data traffic, would continue to grow exponentially for the foreseeable future. The advent of wavelength-division multiplexing reduced the demand for fibre by increasing the capacity of a single fibre by a factor of as much as 100.

According to Gerry Butters, the former head of Lucent Technologies's Optical Networking Group at Bell Labs, the amount of data that could be carried by an optical fibre was doubling every nine months at the time. This progress in the ability to carry data over fibre reduced the need for more fibres. As a result, the wholesale price for data communications collapsed and a number of these companies filed for bankruptcy protection. Global Crossing and Worldcom are two high-profile examples in the United States.

The analogy being suggested is that the AI data centers will eventually be valuable infrastructure even if delays in construction and lack of real demand mean that the companies building them will suffer.

Below the fold I investigate this analogy.

Flawed Analogy

There are some significant problems with the analogy between dark fiber and AI data centers:

  • Depreciation: Decades later the fiber in the ground was still fully functional. The capacity could be sold for very little additional investment. Estimates are that about 40% of the cost of an AI data center is the physical infrastructure (buildings, power connections, cooling, etc.) which might still be useful a decade later. But 60% of the cost is the (mostly Nvidia) racks full of state-of-the-art chips.

    Source Companies typically depreciate their racks linearly over 5 or 6 years. But, as I wrote in Mind The GAAP Again and its predecessors, this is unrealistic. Because:

    • There is intense price competition in AI.
    • Power is a major cost of both inference and training. Power effectively sets the price floor for inference.
    • Each technology generation improves power efficiency by a significant factor.
    • Thus the profit from running a rack doesn't decay linearly, but exponentially.
    • Thus racks more than a couple of generations old are uneconomic.
    • Nvidia has announced that they plan to move from a two-year product cadence to a one-year product cadence.

  • Overproduction: Wikipedia correctly notes what drove the massive overproduction of dark fiber:

    Because the marginal cost of installing additional fibre optic cables is very low once a trench has been dug or conduit laid, a great excess of fibre was installed

    Building data centers does not have the same low marginal cost. While it is true that there are economies of scale in construction driving up the size of AI data centers, these are both much smaller than for laying fiber and apply only to the smaller part of the overall cost.

  • Carrying Costs: The fiber in the ground required very little maintenance. The physical infrastructure of unused AI data centers could survive until eventual re-use only with significant maintenance costs.

  • Technology evolution: Developments in optical technology increased the capacity of the unused fiber with no additional investment. The evolution of AI racks has meant that data centers built a few years ago cannot host current racks, and that the design of data centers for Nvidia's future racks is a research problem.

Dark fiber thus had two important attributes that AI data centers lack; the surplus initial capacity was both long-lived and cheap.

Construction Delays

Building and activating an AI data center is a much bigger, more expensive and long drawn-out task than digging a trench and laying a cable in it. This problem grabbed the headlines when, as Sridhar Natarajan et al reported, Oracle Cites ‘Force Majeure’ to Shield Itself on Controversial Data Center. Almost two years into the project:

the campus designed to handle 2.45 gigawatts — enough electricity to power roughly 1.8 million homes at any given moment — has hit serious setbacks including the denial of a permit key to its plans for energy resources. It’s becoming a symbol of the growing backlash against the broader AI data center boom and a political flashpoint ahead of the US midterm elections that threatens to turn races into referendums over the build-out.

The amount of "construction in progress" for the hyperscales, representing data centers they are struggling to bring on-line, is enormous. Ed Zitron writes:

Considering Oracle’s CIP number from its latest quarterly earnings was at $48.5 billion and Google’s Q2 2026 “assets not yet in service” were at an astonishing $122.8 billion, up from $108.5 billion in Q1 2026 and $78.5 billion at the end of 2025, it’s reasonable to believe that Microsoft has at least $50 billion of construction in progress. I also think it’s fair to assume that Amazon has, since the beginning of 2026, added at least $25 billion to CIP, though we’ll find out at the end of the year.

Zitron quotes a Frebruary 2026 estimate from Sightline Climate:

We’re tracking 190GW across 777 large data centers and AI factories (>50MW) announced since 2024. At least 16GW of capacity is slated to come online in 2026 across roughly 140 projects. Yet only about 5GW is currently under construction. Around 11GW remains in the announced stage with no visible construction progress, despite typical build timelines of 12–18 months.

Anyone who has built themselves a house will understand that construction takes longer than it takes.

Overproduction

Of course, only 40-50% of this "construction in progress" is actual construction, the rest is the racks. There are two ways to estimate what proportion of the racks Nvidia has shipped are actually powered on in a data center as opposed to sitting in a warehouse waiting for the construction to stop being "in progress".

Ed Zitron bases his estimate on the financial picture. He adds up the "construction in progress" and assumes 50% is the racks:

if we assume the number is roughly $374 billion, plus (at minimum) $50 billion from Microsoft, plus another (at minimum) $20 billion from Amazon, that puts us around $444 billion, with Google’s share — $120.8 billion — being 60% GPUs and related hardware, for a total of $72.48 billion, putting us at ... an estimated $234 billion in GPUs and TPUs sitting in warehouses.

He goes on to compare this $234B number with the value of the racks sold since the start of 2023, which he estimates at $561.5B. Clearly, the systems that shipped early in this time-span are likely to have been powered up, so he estimates that around 50% of recent shipments are idle. He looks in detail at Microsoft's financials and and estimates:

Nadella mentioned in November 2025 that he had “...a bunch of chips sitting in inventory that [he couldn’t plug in],” but didn’t make any mention of how many there were.

In other words, Microsoft is warehousing anywhere from $50 billion to $100 billion in GPUs, and has barely gotten $50 billion worth installed in the last four years.

If Microsoft is struggling, everybody’s struggling, and we may have a very inconvenient truth: that NVIDIA has potentially sold hundreds of billions of GPUs years in advance.

Source The other way to estimate this proportion is to compare the power demand of the racks that have been shipped to the data centers that are supposed to house them. In OK, so where are all these data centres?, Bryce Elder wrote:

A theme we’ve touched on a few times is the mismatch between consensus forecasts for chip sales and US data centre completions.

Morgan Stanley measured the gap earlier this week by estimating the shortfall in available power, concluding that more than half of the GPU servers sold between 2026 and 2028 might not have anywhere to be plugged in. New research from Jefferies analysts reaches a similar conclusion using a very top-down method: space.

Tracking US data centre construction sites by satellite imagery shows between 16 and 18 gigawatts of gross capacity that can be energised this year, the broker says, citing SynMax Intelligence. (Gross capacity means the site’s all-in power requirement, not just the draw for IT equipment.)

...

In the longer term, power availability is still the bottleneck — along with labour. And transformers. And cooling equipment. And backup generation. As Jefferies says: “The gap between planned capacity and physical execution remains the central issue.”

Thus there is an emerging consensus that something like a quarter of the AI investment boom is going into rapidly depreciating equipment quite unlike the dark fiber.

Demand Overestimation

The frontier labs and the hyperscalers claim that there is overwhelming demand for AI compute, which justifies the planned AI data center buildout. But the frontier labs are private and don't publish audited numbers to back up their claims. The hyperscalers are public but their accounts don't include explicit numbers for their AI compute. Nvidia is public and its audited accounts reveal the number of AI systems it shipped each quarter. So the easy way to estimate the demand for AI compute is to base it on Nvidia's shipments.

There are three problems with such estimates. Assume this estimate is D and the real demand from end-users is D':

  • As we have seen, it appears that about half of Nvidia's shipments go to a warehouse not a data center. Thus D' = D/2.

  • Ed Zitron estimates that 80% of D comes from OpnAI and Anthropic. So D/10 comes from other sources, which we will generously assume is all end-user demand.

  • In Thoughts on The Curve and the Future of AI Thomas Wright reported an estimate:

    that the labs spend 58% of their compute on R & D and 32% on servicing customers.

    Thus the labs end-user demand is D*0.8*0.32, or about D/4.

Adding these, we have D' = D*0.35. The real end-user demand is likely only around 1/3 of the estimates.

Source If there was overwhelming demand from customers, one would expect that the vendors would have pricing power. But in What’s really going on with AI token price deflation?, Bryce Elder points out that they don't:

The data [Jay Goldberg] collects shows a similar pattern to the Silicon Data index, with token prices plunging for frontier LLMs from $50 per million tokens in late 2023 to about $6 now. More interestingly, he finds the median token price has held fairly steady at just below $1 per million since mid-2024 as the LLM marketplace became more competitive. A floor price of about $0.11 (basically just the cost of electricity) has barely budged.

@arakharazian tweets data from Ramp::

AI Spend FALLS in the latest Ramp AI Index.

Price cuts at the frontier, in addition to cheaper and more efficient models at standard and lite levels, are pushing down the cost of using AI.

Open source models remain <5% of business spend. This decline in spend is driven almost exclusively by competition between OpenAI + Anthropic

The Ramp data does show increased token volume, but flat to decreasing spending. The increased colume is likely due to successive models burning more tokens per query.

Market Reaction

We now have some evidence showing how the big banks rate GPUs as collateral for loans, i.e. how useful they are likely to be down the road.

On 5th October Paula Seligson and Gowri Gurumurthy reported that JPMorgan Dangles 11% Yield on Volta’s $5 Billion AI Loan Sale:

JPMorgan Chase & Co. is pitching a yield of about 11% on a $5 billion leveraged-loan sale on behalf of Volta Infrastructure Holdings Ltd., one of the highest borrowing costs seen in the market for risky debt that’s become popular for financing the AI boom.

...

A $3.7 billion chip loan will be used to purchase about 36,000 graphics processing units, or GPUs, made by Nvidia Corp., according to the people. A $1.3 billion loan will cash collateralize a letter of credit for a data center lease, meaning the money will be held in an account and used to make lease payments to Bitdeer to use the data center, the people said.

11% is a pretty high interest rate, indicating a signinificant risk of default. A week later Claire Ruckin reported that JPMorgan, Goldman Curb Exposure on $5 Billion Volta AI Loan:

JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. have taken a rare move to limit their exposure on a $5 billion loan sale for AI startup Volta Infrastructure Holdings Ltd. as investors demand higher yields for risky debt tied to the artificial intelligence boom.

The two banks are leading the loan offering for Volta, a new artificial intelligence cloud company. The banks have underwritten a $1.3 billion term loan for Volta, while a $3.7 billion chip loan is not underwritten by the banks — a move to protect themselves from potential risks, according to people familiar with the deal.

In other words, these banks are happy to lend at 11% against cash collateral, but not at 11% against GPU collateral. The loan is said to be oversubscribed, but the part with GPU collateral is for the private credit suckers.

Source 11% may not be that high after all. On 14th October Rachel Graf and Katherine Schwartz reported that CoreWeave’s Bonds Turn Distressed, Drawing ‘Yikes’ From Musk:

The AI cloud-computing provider’s unsecured debt due in 2032 traded below 80 cents on the dollar on Wednesday, according to Trace pricing data. That’s widely considered the threshold for when a borrower is financially strained.

At that price, the bonds yield more than 15% — a figure noted by Palihapitiya that led Musk to respond “yikes” on his social media platform.

Shares of the company, which rents out access to leading AI chips, fell as much as 17% on Wednesday. Even though its bonds are trading at distressed levels, CoreWeave’s stock is up more than 60% since its initial public offering in March 2025 and its market value is more than $36.5 billion.

Ruckin noted that:

CoreWeave’s credit-default swaps are back at a record high, and at current levels are pricing in a more than 50% chance of default within the next five years.

CoreWeave is the original "neocloud". As I understand it, its assets against its debts are (a) a set of commitments from companies like Microsoft and Oracle to pay for future access to compute, and (b) a set of data centers full of GPUs. The market is betting that these assets won't be "money good" in the near future.

Coda: A Sun Microsystems Story

Nvidia is just the most successful of the vast number of companies spawned by Sun Microsystems. In the run-up of the dot-com bubble Sun's Starfire systems powered the Web the way Nvidia's GPUs power AI today. But this market dominance was a double-edged sword. Once the dot-com bubble burst, the bankrupt Web companies flooded the market with barely-used Starfire systems. So not merely did much of the customer base vanish, but the remaining customers bought from the second-hand market at huge discounts. Demand for new systems collapsed, and Sun never really recovered. That's not the only reason Sun died. Scott McNealy admitted in a fascinating podcast that during the boom he lost control of Sun's spending. It is hard to maintain discipline when you are being flooded with cash.

Once the bubble bursts, Nvidia will face a similar problem. First, their customers will stop ordering new racks, because:

  • Companies like CoreWeave that exist to get debt off the AI companies' balance sheets will be bankrupt because their customers can't afford their commitments.
  • The assets of these bankrupt companies will be sold off at a loss, flooding the market with barely-used data centers and stopping construction of new ones.
  • It has proven harder than expected to build data centers quickly because of public opposition, lack of skilled tradespeople, difficulties in securing power and so on. Thus it is likely that there will be warehouses full of Nvidia racks that were waiting for a data center to be built when the bubble burst. These unused racks will also be sold off, crashing the price of the barely-used ones further.

Second, in some ways the problem will be worse for Nvidia than Sun. Nvidia will have invested heavily in developing and securing wafer slots for their next-generation GPUs. Although these will be faster and more power-efficient than those in the written-down data centers, they won't be able to compete on price-performance. The pipeline between committing to a new design and market entry is now much longer than it was in the '90s. Nvidia will have relatively more capital tied up in the product pipeline than Sun did.

A Newsletter of Humorous Writing #465

2026-10-15, updated: 2026-10-22

For October 7-13, 2026

Hello and welcome to A Newsletter of Humorous Writing, a roundup of the week's finest short humor pieces and funny articles, and a celebration of the fantastic writers who wrote them. One note: In this week’s Brian Agler Old Favorite writeup, there’s a line that says the piece is the perfect thing “to read as you watch the World Series.” We are aware that the World Series is not yet underway, but because of the schedule of the newsletter, if we didn’t use the pick this week, we’d have to wait to run it until October 29th, at which point the World Series might already be over. So please bookmark that piece to read once the World Series has started, and please do not read it UNTIL the World Series has started. (We’re relying on the honor system here, folks.) Thank you for your attention to this matter.

What We Enjoyed This Week

Crossword Clues Where It’s Clear the Puzzle’s Creator Got Themselves into a Jam Letter-wise by Tyler Gooch (McSweeney’s) What can we say? If you’re a regular reader of the newsletter, you know Tyler’s been on a real roll lately, and his streak continues with this piece. We’re big fans of crossword puzzles (both regular and cryptic), so this was serious catnip for us. There’s a ton to like in this piece, but we particularly love the syntax and rhythm of “Got Themselves into a Jam Letter-wise.”

Skeleton Actors Guild (SAG) Grievances Regarding Your Front Lawn Halloween Production by Lisa Pertoso (Points in Case) There are some really great spooky skeleton details in here: “We are skilled artists with wide ranges who are pigeon-holed into the same derivative roles every season of restaurant hostess, chef who cooks human organs, bartenders who sling creepy-crawly martinis, waltzing restaurant patrons, and an off-game customer whose head has been replaced as a pumpkin.” And we hope it goes without saying, but we stand in solidarity with the skeleton actors, and hope that the homeowners come to the bargaining table in good faith to bring this dispute to a speedy resolution.

I’m the Guy Who Writes the Assembly Instructions for Kids’ Toys, You Stupid Idiot by David Distenfeld (McSweeney’s) This piece is packed with tremendous lines: “Try not to lose your place in my little novella, you pathetic imbecile.” “I identify the sixteen screws in your package as A, B, C, D, E, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N, P, Q, and R. There is no F. There is no O. Why? Go fuck yourself, that’s why.“ The use of foul language in a humor piece can often feel like a crutch—an attempt to add oomph to a punchline that would otherwise fall flat. That’s not the case here: The use of cursing and insults is completely earned, and feels deeply rooted in the narrator’s character.

-- ADS --

2026-10-14 The state of the world

Has Israel stopped the genocide?

Has Russia stopped invading Ukraine?

Pluralistic: Expedia amazoned hotel rooms (15 Oct 2026)

2026-10-15, updated: 2026-10-23

Today's links Expedia amazoned hotel rooms: Everything more expensive for everyone, monopolies everywhere, and we're all screwed. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Delta v dovening; "Play Money"; Alabama's ethnic cleansing; We trust neuroscience over psychology; Billionaires' anti-homeless pogrom; Game devs v DRM; What security means; Microsoft, tear down that wall! Publisher won't revert rights; SNL's Trump/Clinton debate; Chicago Tribune's murder; AI after AI. Upcoming appearances: Paris, Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Vienna, Kilkenny, Oxford, Sheffield, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Expedia amazoned hotel rooms (permalink) No matter where you shop, you're getting screwed by Amazon. Amazon has found a way to make everything you buy – at Target, at a mom-and-pop shop, even direct from the manufacturer – more expensive. And they're not the only one: Expedia's done the same thing, but for hotel rooms. Here's how Amazon broke the economy: first, they locked in a key group of shoppers. The vast majority of affluent shoppers in the USA have Amazon Prime accounts. Having prepaid for a year's shipping in advance, those Prime subscribers start their purchasing journey by searching Amazon, and if they find what they're looking for, that's where it ends. America's affluent top decile – the 10% of richest Americans – do the majority of America's shopping, a phenomenon that has only been accelerated by America's precipitous slide into oligarchy, which has exhausted the savings and the credit-card limits and the home equity of the majority of Americans, who increasingly can't afford to buy anything: https://dreamagainusa.org/ If you want to sell things in America, you must sell them in the place where the top decile shops, and that's Amazon. For merchants, that is an incredibly expensive proposition: 51-60% of every dollar you spend with an independent merchant on Amazon is claimed by Amazon through junk fees, listing fees, commissions, processing fees and other scams: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/04/cheating-at-fraud/#absentee-rentier Merchants don't have 51-60% margins they can afford to turn over to Amazon. To remain viable while selling on Amazon, they have to raise prices. Amazon doesn't mind if prices go up, so long as Amazon's price remains competitive. So Amazon imposes a requirement on its suppliers called "most favored nation," which requires sellers to offer their best price on Amazon: https://pluralistic.net/2026/02/25/most-favored-nation/#price-fixing Practically speaking, that means that when you raise your price on Amazon, you must raise your prices everywhere by the same amount, which means that no matter where you shop (Target, Walmart, the corner store or direct from the factory), you pay the Amazon Tax. The Amazon Tax is a prime (you should forgive the expression) example of enshittification, in which an intermediary (a business that sits between buyers and sellers, AKA, "a platform") screws both customers and sellers to benefit itself. But Amazon isn't the only example of a powerful digital intermediary that has used its market power to impose an economy-wide tax. Wherever you look online, you find digital giants who grew the way Amazon grew (buying all of their competitors) and then did what Amazon did (squeezing buyers and sellers, making prices higher everywhere). That's what happened with Expedia. Almost every travel site you can find online has been purchased by Expedia (Hotels.com, Travelocity, and Orbitz), and the ones that aren't Expedia subsidiaries were acquired by its main rival, Priceline (Booking.com, Kayak, Agoda and even Opentable). Nearly all the hotel rooms are booked by a tiny minority of travelers – largely that same top decile that Amazon has so thoroughly captured and locked in – and hoteliers can't live without their business, and they're almost all Expedia and/or Priceline customers. Expedia accounts for 80% of all hotel bookings by dollar value. Expedia's position, in other words, is basically Amazon's position, so Expedia is doing exactly what Amazon is doing: they charge huge fees to hotels, and then force the hotels to raise their prices everywhere through a "most favored nation" deal: https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.wawd.369601/gov.uscourts.wawd.369601.1.0.pdf But – as Lee Hepner writes for the BIG newsletter – Expedia has figured out ways to out-Amazon Amazon. They've copied one of Amazon's sleaziest businesses, and made it worse: https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/how-expedia-rigs-travel-markets-and Here's Amazon's sleaziest commercial practice: when you search Amazon, the top results for your search aren't the best matches for your queries; they're products sold by the companies willing to pay the most for search placement, in a "real-time auction" that runs every time you search. The cost of winning that auction comes out of your pocket through higher prices: the first result for an Amazon query is, on average, 29% more expensive than the best match. The top row is 25% more expensive. On average, the best match for your query is 17 positions down the screen, on the second page, where almost no one ever bothers to scroll: https://pluralistic.net/2023/11/03/subprime-attention-rent-crisis/#euthanize-rentiers This rip-off is Amazon's most profitable line of business, more profitable than AWS or Prime. It makes the company more than $80b/year. And – incredibly – Expedia's found a way to make it even worse. Like Amazon, Expedia auctions off its search results. They call this their "VIP listing" program. Practically speaking, hotels have to pay for this, because it boosts booking rates by 42% (the first ten results on an Expedia search-results page get 62% of the clicks). VIP listing is expensive for the merchant – but it's even more expensive for you and me. That's because Expedia requires hotels in its VIP listings programs to raise their prices on non-Expedia sites by 10-25%…INDEFINITELY. Let me repeat that: to stay in business, hotels need to be on Expedia. To stay in business on Expedia, hotels have to raise their prices to pay Expedia's junk fees, but they have to raise their prices everywhere else. But to really stay in business on Expedia, hotels have to use the VIP program, which is even more expensive. And – one more time – hotels in the VIP program have to jack up their prices everywhere else, INDEFINITELY. This means that, throughout the economy, hotel prices are rising at a superinflationary rate, because Expedia – who command 80% of the market – are pushing those prices up. This goes a long way to explaining why US hotel rates rose 58% from a 2020 average of $103/night to a 2025 average of $162/night. It explains why hotel prices rose by 5% last year, which is double the rate of inflation. And this is why Expedia stock is up 65% since the start of the Iran war, a fact that Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin attributes to "higher margins" from "higher prices": https://s202.q4cdn.com/757635260/files/doc_financials/2026/q2/Q2-2026-Earnings-Presentation-Final.pdf In his coverage of the Expedia lawsuit – which brought many of these details to light – Hepner notes that hotels themselves have undergone near-total cartelization, with Hilton, Marriott, and Choice International owning the majority of all hotels after a string of acquisitions that went largely unchallenged by slumbering antitrust regulators around the world. These consolidated chains have also jacked up prices and enshittified their service, slashing housekeeping and check-in staff and allowing their facilities to slip into disrepair. This, too, is characteristic of monopolization: whenever a monopoly takes over part of its supply chain, the rest of the supply chain consolidates to prevent itself from being ripped off by the new giant. This is the story of publishers consolidating to defend themselves from Borders/B&N, Walmart and Costco, then Amazon; and it's the story of literary agencies consolidating to resist the power of those overgrown publishers. And it's the story of health-care, which saw consolidation in pharmaceuticals leading to mergers among hospitals, who screwed the insurers, who also consolidated. In every case, it's the workers and the people who rely on them that get the shitty end of the stick. Hotel guests, readers and patients pay more for inferior products. Writers, editors, doctors, nurses, hotel staff and housekeepers get lower pay and worse working-conditions: https://pluralistic.net/2024/12/18/loose-flapping-ends/#luigi-has-a-point There is nothing wrong with the idea of an intermediary. Most writers can't publish and sell their own books, and few travelers can navigate finding hotels in strange cities without help. The problem of intermediaries is that when intermediaries gain monopoly power – by buying their rivals and capturing buyers and sellers – they are able to squeeze both. As Tim Wu says, this is the moment when a company that's supposed to be helping becomes a predator, acquires "main character syndrome" and makes every transaction all about the middleman, at the expense of the people buying and selling: https://pluralistic.net/2026/08/05/absentee-landlord/ There are so many reasons for inflation and the cost of living crisis: wage stagnation, wars of choice in Iran, environmental cataclysm after environmental cataclysm. But under cover of these real factors is a cohort of what Matt Stoller calls "economic termites," parasites that have infested the walls of our economy and are devouring it from within. You can't solve this by shopping. Calling the hotel direct won't fix it: they have to be on Expedia to survive, and to be on Expedia, they have to sign up for VIP service, and to keep VIP service, they have to make their prices higher everywhere. To fix this, we need systemic action: the corporate death penalty for the companies that are consuming the structural members of our society. Dogs of New York

2026-10-14, updated: 2026-10-25

I recently updated nycdogs, a data package for R that I originally made for teaching purposes. It bundles up New York City’s dog licensing and dog bite datasets into an R package. The data is already provided by the city in a directly usable way (as CSV files), but packaging it up makes it easier to integrate with other packages and get things moving a little more quickly in class.

The nyc_license table looks like this:

nyc_license
#> # A tibble: 819,323 × 12
#>    animal_name animal_gender animal_birth_year breed_name       breed_rc zip_code zip   license_issued_date license_expired_date extract_year borough city
#>    <chr>       <chr>                     <int> <chr>            <chr>    <chr>    <chr> <date>              <date>                      <int> <chr>   <chr>
#>  1 Paige       F                          2014 American Pit Bu… Pit Bul… 10035    10035 2014-09-12          2017-09-12                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  2 Yogi        M                          2010 Boxer            Boxer    10465    10465 2014-09-12          2017-10-02                   2016 Bronx   Bronx
#>  3 Ali         M                          2014 Basenji          Basenji  10013    10013 2014-09-12          2019-09-12                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  4 Queen       F                          2013 Akita Crossbreed Akita C… 10013    10013 2014-09-12          2017-09-12                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  5 Lola        F                          2009 Maltese          Maltese  10028    10028 2014-09-12          2017-10-09                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  6 Ian         M                          2006 Unknown          Unknown  10013    10013 2014-09-12          2019-10-30                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  7 Buddy       M                          2008 Unknown          Unknown  10025    10025 2014-09-12          2017-10-20                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  8 Chewbacca   F                          2012 Labrador Retrie… Labrado… 10013    10013 2014-09-12          2019-10-01                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  9 Heidi-bo    F                          2007 Dachshund Smoot… Dachshu… 11215    11215 2014-09-13          2017-04-16                   2016 Brookl… Broo…
#> 10 Massimo     M                          2009 Bull Dog, French French … 11201    11201 2014-09-13          2017-09-17                   2016 Brookl… Broo…
#> # ℹ 819,313 more rows

The dataset is good for teaching with for several reasons. First, people like dogs. Second, it has about 800,000 records, which is a lot in many ways but also trivial for a modern laptop to work with. Third, the data are pretty clean, but they’re not that clean. There are various things going on in there that invite us to explore it but also to be careful about what we can and can’t be confident about.

The first thing we ask about any data set like this is: what is each row in this table? In the case of nyc_license, each row is a record of one time-limited license for a dog. A row is not necessarily the record of a unique dog. When an owner renews a dog’s license, the dog will appear one time for each license period. In New York City, dog licenses can be issued for one year or five years. The table does not provide any dog_id column that ties sequences of licenses to individual dogs.

Second, the table contains several “extracts” of the license data. It seems like the way the provider updates the NYC Open Data record is to periodically pull from its internal database every year or so and append it to the existing, previously-released version. The extract_year column identifies the extract, so at least we know that. But it’s also the case that a license that was active in more than one extract year appears in each extract. As a result, the table has a large number of duplicate rows.

Third, license information is provided by dog owners. This means that there’s a fair amount of noise in the records, because people make typos and other errors. For instance, the ZIP code data has incomplete ZIPs. Some people provide invalid ZIP codes (e.g. ones that are fewer than five digits long). Others (about 3,300 records) have ZIP codes that are not in New York City. Eighty percent of these (about 2,700) are ZIP codes located elsewhere in New York state. Another 77 are located in Florida, which I kind of like. Five of them live in Boca Raton, for example. Their kids never call. You’d think it would be easy for them to just pick up the bone, I mean phone, but you never hear from them.

About 650 rows have valid ZIP codes that are in Manhattan, but these ZIPs are notZCTAs. The trouble with ZIP codes is that people think of them as areas, as polygons, but in fact they are lines. They are defined by the Post Office as postal routes, i.e. as journeys a mail carrier takes. While they tend to form closed polygons, they are absolutely not guaranteed to. But people know their ZIP code and all kinds of analysts (from marketers to political operatives) like thinking in terms of ZIP codes. So the Census defines ZIP Code Tabulation
Areas that are a kind of best-effort at answering the question “What if this ZIP code were a closed polygon?” ZCTAs exclude every P.O. box and single-address ZIP nationwide. Manhattan has several buildings that have their own ZIP code. New York City also defines MODZCTAs that merge some low- or no-population ZCTAs with their neighbors. I use these below.

Fourth, beyond the ZIP codes, owners also provide information about the age and sex of their dogs, the dog’s name, and the dog’s breed. Again, this kind of information tends to be a little noisy. For example, people vary in how they spell names. They also vary in how they classify their dog by breed. Beyond the list of “recognized” breeds (itself something that dog owners variably conform to), some people might describe their dog as, e.g., “Labrador-Sheltie mix” while others might just say “Unknown”. The dataset includes the breed_name column from the original dataset and also breed_rc, which is a recoding by me to clean up equivalent terms (“Yorkshire Terrier” and “Terrier, Yorkshire”, for example) along with a few other coding decisions.

Finally, and only because I’m choosing to stop here, the table just shows the number of licensed dogs in New York City. That is definitely not the same as the number of dogs there. Moreover, license compliance varies quite a bit in ways that are related to characteristics of the owner that we can’t observe, and also ones that we partially can, like where they live.

All of which is related to the fact that one of the lolsob-mantras of courses I teach is “Now you know the true meaning of data”. In the graphs and maps below, I’ve done the best I can, where appropriate, to uniquely identify individual dogs in the dataset (even though ultimately we cannot).

Popular Breeds

With that out of the way, it’s time to indulge your prejudices about Dogs, New Yorkers, and New York Dogs. The most common “breed” of dog in New York is “Unknown”, as befits a city of immigrants, hustlers, scrappy up-and-comers, and dogs seeking to leave their small-town past behind and remake their identities. Somewhere between eight and ten percent of records each year have “Unknown” recorded as their breed. There’s some change over time (a declining share), but I think this is an artifact of how breeds are getting recorded rather than a change in the composition of the dog population. If we leave the Unknowns out, here are the trends in annual licenses issued to the twenty most popular breeds.

Some breeds are pretty steadily popular. Smaller breeds do well in a city full of apartments. We can also see some evidence here of trends in popularity. However, these annual numbers are what we might call the prevalence of dogs, rather than the incidence of new dogs. If we want to get a better sense of fashion trends in dog breeds, we should look at puppies. (Who doesn’t want to look at puppies?) Because of the structure of the data we can’t quite do this. The best we can do, based on the dog’s age, is to examine licenses issued to dogs younger than a year old. Let’s pick out some breeds that seem to be rising, a few that seem relatively steady, and a few that might be declining. I’ve indexed these changes relative to each breed in 2016 by setting the value for that year to 100. Even though our range is narrow, we use a log scale on the y-axis because, e.g., a rise in a breed’s index from 100 to 200 reflects the same relative change as a fall from 100 to 50.

Maltipoos and Goldendoodles seem to be doing pretty well for themselves. Golden Retrievers remain steadily popular. Meanwhile, Shiba Inus, beloved fad-breed of the 2010s, seem to have been affected by their association with crypto and are strongly in decline. Much drop. Very diminish. Wow. Beagles are also doing poorly. Good grief.

Where Breeds Live

We can look at the relative prevalence of breeds by their ZIP code (strictly speaking, by their MODZCTA). I hesitate a little on this just because, even with 800,000 licenses, we’ll run out of degrees of freedom fairly quickly if we break things down by breed and ZIP. Relatedly, we should ask what sort of metric we’re trying to show here. What’s the denominator? (A surprising amount of Statistics, I claim, is essentially exploring the question “What happens if I divide bythis number instead of that number?”) Popular dogs are, to a first approximation, pretty popular all over the city. Most ZIP codes have a solid contingent of Yorkies. If, for each popular breed, we calculate the share of that breed as a percentage of all dogs in the ZIP code, we’ll see some ZIP-by-ZIP variation come out.

It would also be nice to adjust for the fact that different ZIP codes have quite different shares of the total number of dogs licensed in the city. (Which, again, is not the same as share of the total number of dogs in the city.) So we calculate the within-ZIP share and make a ratio of it by dividing that number by the breed’s citywide share. The ratio is 1 when the breed is just as common in that ZIP code as it is across the whole city. If it’s 2, the breed is twice as common in that ZIP as it is across the city. If it’s 0.5, the breed is half as common in that ZIP as it is in the city as a whole. The main downside of ratios like this is that they can exaggerate differences a little, especially if the base rates are small. We have enough breeds in each zip code to make me feel OK about doing this. But if you refer to the bar charts above you can see that even for disproportionately popular breeds in zips, you’re looking at changes like “twice as common with respect to a baseline of five percent of all dogs”. Here’s the map:

We see some plausible evidence that breeds are distributed across ZIP codes in a manner that tracks the demography of owners. French Bulldogs in Chelsea, Soho, and TriBeCa. Havanese on the Upper East Side. Pit Bulls in the Bronx. German Shepherds on Staten Island. Goldendoodles and King Charles Spaniels in Manhattan south of 96th.

The Diffusion of Goldendoodles

Let’s take a closer look at the Goldendoodles. In 2015, Goldendoodles weren’t that common. We can ask: where were they initially popular? Did they diffuse across New York City from focal points where people were more likely to set trends in breed fashion? Restricting ourselves to young dogs, we can try to look at each ZIP’s share of all Goldendoodle puppies licensed each year from 2015 to 2025. Here’s what that looks like:

In 2015, Goldendoodle puppies are licensed in a relatively small number of ZIP codes, mostly in Manhattan. Most ZIP codes are doodle-free. Over the next five years, they gradually spread across the city. By 2023 or 2024, most—though still not all—ZIP codes are licensing young Goldendoodles.

Again, the underlying numbers aren’t huge. So take all of this with a delicious treat. I mean, grain of salt. I also wonder what the next few years are going to look like in terms of dog popularity. Based on the maps above, I think Australian Shepherds are likely to continue to rise in popularity amongst owners looking to acquire a fashionable breed. And while they’re not on any of the maps above, the data also suggest that theJindo, a Korean breed that is a relatively recent arrival in the US, has been sharply on the rise. If you ask me, though, if you’re in New York City and planning to get a dog, you should throw in your lot with Unknown and get a good, solid, dog-shaped mutt. Preferably one with strong views on the state of the Subway these days, or who knows a guy who can get you a deal on some shirts, or the special ramen, or tickets. Not tickets for anything in particular. Just, like, tickets. Works out of an upstairs bar downtown on Water St. Trust me.

2026-10-14 English

2026-10-14

2026-10-14 English

I write in English, both at work and at home. I read a ton of English. It’s still my second language as far as proficiency is concerned. I guess it’s also only the fourth language I learned, growing up.

When people tell me about the correct pronunciation of this or that, or make fun of somebody who doesn’t speak their British or American variant of English, I usually like to point out that the majority of English speakers probably live in India. English is for everyone. All languages are for everybody.

Sometimes we learn a language and learn about the culture of a certain country. When I grew up, we learned English and learned about England. We learned French and learned about France. It is only now that I realize how toxic this is. What a colonizer mindset!

It’s probably why I don’t react well when people talk about German this or German that or Germans here and Germans there. Just Germans? Or German-speaking? I am a former Austrian living in Switzerland with a handful of German ancestors. Of course it’s not just Germany. The language is for everybody.

Today I saw a crushing comeback to somebody who was making fun of grammar mistakes:

“You speak English because its the only language you know. I speak English because its the only language you know. We are not the same.” – MeisterVaxl

2026-10-13 Fascism is against the rules

2026-10-13

2026-10-13 Fascism is against the rules

This rule was written by Olivia Hill and first appeared in the game #iHunt by Olivia Hill and Filamena Young:

If you’re a fascist, you’re not welcome to play this game. It’s against the rules. If you’re reading this and thinking, “You just call everyone you disagree with a fascist,” then you’re probably a fascist, or incapable of drawing inferences from context and acknowledging a dangerous political climate that causes the oppressed to be hyperbolic. Don’t play this game. Heal yourself. Grow. Learn. Watch some Mr. Rogers’ Neighborhood or something. – No fascists

I love it.

@pathunstrom posted about this a few months ago and added:

anyone questioning the rule “no f fascists” directly is going to be a problem. There are no “false positives” because the signal is “willing to argue with a no fascist policy” not “full throated fascists!”

The conversation turned to somebody who ran afoul of the rule by saying they “question everything.” That reminds me of the constant struggle about words in our society. If whatever wording works for one side, it doesn’t take long until the other side coopts it. And so we have to keep reinventing new words, new jargon, new phrases. That’s just the way it works.

When I grew up, we felt that skepticism was new and we wielded it against the religious fundamentalists. Now a new generation is growing up and wields it against us.

@elexia had an excellent response, however:

it’s always fine too question rules on your own time. that’s good and fine and healthy to do cause in the process you can learn why rules are in place and what rules and values are important to the community and to you. but if you join a community and then try to re-litigate every rule they established without even knowing why they exist or how they work in practice, you become a problem for those trying to run a community smoothly with limited time and energy. be respectful of other people’s time and energy and make an effort to understand things before you bother them about it.

A sign showing a human throwing a swastika into the trash.Keep your environment clean!

All of this because people still haven’t read the Ur-Fascism essay by Umberto Eco or something similarly good that explains how the fascists don’t want to argue in order to be right. They argue for the spectacle of it. It’s a game of who needs to bend their knee. They flood the zone with shit and if you’re trying to argue, you’re wasting your time – and they get the spectacle they enjoy watching. Liberals and leftists squirming, trying to keep up the political correctness and the necessary decorum. That’s why the Olivia Hill rule is cool. It identifies the initial impulse before the fight gets an audience. The urge to argue about this is what gets you banned.

That’s why the “message of the day” for the IRC server I run says “This server is only for anti-fascists. If you are a fascist, you are not welcome here.”

Crowding Out

2026-10-13, updated: 2026-10-25

In Downgrades and Competition For Capital I discussed how AI's insatiable appetite for funds was raising interest rates not just for AI-related debt, but also for everyone else. The impact of these rate increases will take time to become evident, as borrowers roll over existing debt or raise new debt.

Below the fold I look at impacts that we don't have to wait for, because they are already happening on a large scale.

Krugman Chart 1 Now, Paul Krugman's AI Versus Everything Else presents a different aspect of the competiton for capital — it is "crowding out" investment in everything else:

Evidence of that crowding out is revealed by a recent article in the New York Times, which noted that the AI Boom is not being slowed by these soaring rates. Yet the spike in interest rates is being felt throughout the non-AI economy. In other words, all that money going into construction of datacenters and purchasing foreign produced semiconductors comes at the expense of investment in everything else.

The chart at the top of this post, which I borrowed from Steve Rattner, clearly makes this point: construction of datacenters appears to be diverting funds and resources from the construction of housing, office buildings, and factories — more or less everything that isn’t AI-related.

That said, AI-related construction — building the structures that house datacenters — is only a fraction of the AI spending boom. Most of the money is going for equipment and software. In fact, that’s one main reason AI spending is so resistant to high interest rates: Borrowing costs matter much less for assets like GPUs, which depreciate rapidly in any case, than they do for long-lived assets like buildings.

Krugman Chart 2 Rattner's chart only showed the effects within the construction industry, which absorbs only about 40% of the spending on AI data centers. Krugman's Chart 2 shows the effects on the other 60% of the spending:

I look at business investment in “tech” — information processing and software — measured as a percentage of GDP. The blue line in the graph below shows how much that measure of tech spending has changed since the beginning of 2023. I compare that with the corresponding change in all other investment. This chart clearly reveals dramatic crowding out by tech spending of all other investment:

Krugman Chart 3 Interestingly, given the analogies being drawn between the AI boom and the dot-com boom, Krugman shows that the effects of AI spending aren't just much bigger but also different:

Chart 3 shows the same calculation as Chart 2, but applied to the tech boom of the 1990s, and it doesn’t show any crowding out at all — in fact, non-tech investment rose:

Source In Crowding out pits sovereigns against AI, Ryan Avent agrees with Krugman that the crowding out is happening:

Low interest rates imply that people will swap their claims on today’s productive potential for a song. In such cases, a debt-financed investment plan need not yield very much to pencil out. As rates rise, however, the expected return on an investment plan needed to justify the borrowing costs also goes up. Decent investments get squeezed out, then good investments, and then maybe really excellent investments that stand to deliver big economic benefits. So it goes.

We are experiencing this today, and you’ll never guess which part of the economy is responsible for the pronounced and sustained rise in desired borrowing.

But Avent argues that the "part of the economy" isn't AI but governments:

Anyway, gross government debt across advanced economies rose from 67 per cent of GDP in 2001 to 108 per cent today. So one could say that AI borrowing is crowding out other private investment, but one could also, and perhaps more reasonably, say that government borrowing is stymieing what might otherwise be a very broad-based, AI-driven, private sector investment boom.

If this turns out to be the better way to think about it, we’ll know soon enough. Firms in non-AI sectors may abandon efforts to claim more of the economy’s productive potential in the face of rising interest rates, but governments almost certainly won’t. For governments to give way, budget deficits need to fall. Accomplishing this means disappointing people who are expecting to receive claims from the government. It also means people have to give up more of their own claims to the government through higher taxes. In this fractious age, governments that do such things tend to be tossed out in favour of crazier governments which are even less able to do the needful.

Unfortunately, this likely means that we are on one of two paths. Either the AI complex ultimately smashes itself against the irresistible borrowing needs of the public sector and is forced to retrench, with potentially unpleasant consequences for growth, or rising interest rates cause one or another sovereign to slip into a market-destabilising crisis first.

The re-direction of investments toward AI would not be a problem if two conditions were satisfied. First, that the AI investments were more productive than those they crowded out. Skepticism on this question is warranted. There is a distinct lack of empirical evidence that AI is increasing productivity in the economy as a whole. Krugman expresses this skepticism:

Moreover, we shouldn’t assume that the private sector knows what it’s doing. There’s often a double standard when thinking about bad investments, in which public investments that go bad are treated as evidence that the government can’t do anything right, while private malinvestment is brushed off as no big deal.

Think about the $80 billion that Meta, formerly known as Facebook, spent on the “metaverse,” only to basically abandon the concept. A government program that spent $80 billion on a failed project would be the subject of endless Congressional hearings. Yet the waste from a failed private investment is equally real.

Second, that the enhanced productivity from the AI investments was at least as durable as that from those they crowded out. But the benefits of the 60% of the iAI investment that goes into IT hardware decay very rapidly, as I discussed inMind The GAAP Again and its predecessors.

Krugman concludes:

So it’s clear that crowding out by the AI boom is happening on a very large scale. And unlike the risks of technological unemployment or a burst bubble, this isn’t a hypothetical risk. It’s happening right now.

Subsequently, Krugman also asked Will AI Crowd Out Jobs?, pointing out that a data center that might cost around $8B might only employ about 100 workers, mostly in low-skill jobs like security:

deploying $8 billion in capital, the cost of a data center, in a non-AI sector will, on average, support more than 10,000 jobs, while investing that money in a data center will support only around 100 jobs. Or to put it another way, money spent building data centers will, on average, create only around one percent as many jobs as investing the same sum in other industries would have created.

Citing this paper, Krugman explains the effect of the crowding out:

Van Nieuwerbergh estimates that through 2032 hyperscalers will spend more than $10 trillion on data centers — capital expenditure that, all the evidence suggests, will come at the expense of investment elsewhere in the economy. And because data centers employ so few people, a back-of-the-envelope estimate yields a number that made even my eyes bug out: the capital invested in data centers will employ roughly ten million fewer workers than that capital would have employed if invested elsewhere.

This doesn’t mean that unemployment will rise by 10 million. It means, instead, that reduced demand for labor will put downward pressure on wages and shift the balance of economic power, which has already been moving against labor, even more in capital’s favor. Even before the rise of AI, we were experiencing a rapid decline in the share of national income going to wages relative to profits, along with rising oligarchy. The anti-labor effects of AI will accelerate that trend.

For the AI companies' managements, this seems like a feature not a bug.

Source Rattner's and Krugman's charts show a rapid increase in the crowding out effect. But the worrying thing that Krugman doesn't mention is that the AI investments that have already had such a marked crowding out effect are small compared to those planned for the next few years. This chart, from Big Tech will fund more than a third of its AI investments with debt in 2027, Goldman Sachs predicts by Jake Conley, reports Goldman Sachs' estimates of the scale of the investments by the hyperscalers, and how much they expect them to borrow:

hyperscalers have turned increasingly toward debt markets. In 2025, investment-grade-rated global bond issuance from the hyperscalers totaled $108 billion, per Goldman Sachs, or roughly 26% of capex. Through the first half of 2026, those companies have already issued $194 billion of IG-rated debt, with that figure expected to reach roughly $250 billion in debt issuance, or roughly 33% of capex.

In 2027, Goldman Sachs said, the share of debt-funded capex is likely to rise even further, with $400 billion in expected global IG bond issuance from the hyperscalers against an estimated $1.14 trillion in capex, or a roughly 35% share.

If these investment plans materialize, the crowding out effect will greatly accelerate. In the 18 months from January 2025 it reduced non-AI construction spending by $132B, or about six week's worth. The chart suggests that spendig will double from around $700B to around $1.4T in 2028. That might equate to crowding out 12 weeks worth of non-AI construction in 2028, or about a quarter. That would be a significant hit to the broader economy

Fortunately, Ed Zitron's Credit Crunch provides a basis for predicting that:

the AI complex ultimately smashes itself against the irresistible borrowing needs of the public sector and is forced to retrench,

Zitron is skeptical that these investment plans will materialize:

In any case, AI data center debt is way more expensive now by virtue of the current state of treasuries, with costs compounded by the anxiety around them in general.

This means that any “virgin” projects — those that aren’t directly backstopped or co-signed by hyperscalers — are guaranteed to hit egregiously-high, 9% to 14% rates, which makes ( as I discussed a few weeks ago in my two-part debt series) it near-impossible to make the already-questionable economics of running a data center work.

This means that any AI data center debt being raised right now is doing so under stricter credit conditions and doing so at unrealistic, unsustainable prices, if they’re going to be able to raise at all. This makes the $174 billion in debt that SB Energy needs to raise to fund its theoretical data center project with OpenAI — even when backstopped by NVIDIA — either horrendously expensive or impossible to complete, as does it mean that any future large, multi-gigawatt projects will add billions of dollars in interest payments to already-expensive debt.

This all makes pontifications that data center spending will increase to $32 trillion by 2050 equal parts stupid and wasteful, on top of the overall problem that there isn’t even enough demand right now for hyperscalers to break even on their 2026 and 2027 capex plans.

OpenAI and Anthropic have made huge, non-cancelable "take-or-pay" commitments to the hyperscalers. These form the basis of a vast amount of the hyperscalers' backlog. The compute these commitments cover is for both training, a cost, and inference, which generates revenue. In Thoughts on The Curve and the Future of AI Thomas Wright reported an estimate:

that the labs spend 58% of their compute on R & D and 32% on servicing customers.

Zitron estimates that OpenAI and Anthropic represent 80% of the total demand for compute. Thus about half of the total demand for compute is OpenAI and Anthropic's training and attacking other companies. Halving their internal compute budget would allow for about a 50% increase in compute for customers with no need for additional investment. This is why they are using the claim that their products are too dangerous to release to call for a pause and regulation.

Source But even if the competitors could agree, and they weren't worried about the Chinese catching up, halving their training budget wouldn't work because the demand doesn't exist:

As a result of their $1.3 trillion in compute commitments, neither company can become “capital efficient” by cutting their training costs, because said training costs are the only means of further growth outside of massive price increases that are unlikely to grow their businesses.

To make matters worse, both are cutting prices to compete with each other, and per Ramp, said price cuts aren’t increasing usage:

Price cuts, flat usage, cutting R&D and revenue disappointments aren't a good look when you're planning a $2T IPO or a $30B funding round at a $1.4T valuation. Skepticism about the projected capex spending, and the increased crowding out is reasonable. But the effects on the broader market of the bubble deflating will be severe.

In AI Bubble Risks Worst S&P 500 Crash Since 2008, Strategist Says, Levin Stamm and Sagarika Jaisinghani report that:

Panmure Liberum’s Joachim Klement said his base case is for that trade to disintegrate as soon as 2027, sending stocks sharply lower.

“My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement said in an interview. Hyperscalers’ free cash flows are largely depleted, while the cost of debt is rising quickly and becoming prohibitive for these firms, he said.

Klement’s 2027 year-end target of 5,000 points for the S&P 500 implies 36% downside from current levels. ... Klement sees Europe’s Stoxx 600 falling to 430 points, more than 30% below current levels.

There are many more pessimistic forecasts. Hang on to your hats.
