Pluralistic: Bundestrojaner (13 Oct 2026)

2026-10-13, updated: 2026-10-23

Today's links Bundestrojaner: You can't make people more secure by making them less secure. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: 9/11 sitcom; Jon Norman v Philcon; Bruce Sterling's post-9/11 geopolitics; Polaroid bankrupt; David Mamet x Shel Silverstein; "Great Big Beautiful Tomorrow"; Canadian government calls abortion doctors "terrorists"; Shanghai Ikea kicks out lonely, loitering seniors; Black Panther self-care. Upcoming appearances: Paris, Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Vienna, Kilkenny, Oxford, Sheffield, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Bundestrojaner (permalink) Every morning, I revisit my blog headlines from this date, going back 25 years, 20 years, 15 years, 10 years, 5 years, and one year. I publish the most interesting ones in a section of my newsletter that I call "object permanence," and I think it's the most useful part of my day. "Object permanence," of course, is a reference to the stage in an infant's development when they acquire the ability to connect events in the past to events in the present, which is why it's the point at which babies cease to be amazed by peek-a-boo. I've been blogging for more than a quarter century, and these daily trawls through the things I considered important enough to share are an unexpectedly powerful way to connect the events of the past to the events of the present. Take cybersecurity, a subject that is filling today's headlines, primarily due to a spate of poorly understood (and criminally poorly explained) incidents in which AI companies' hacking tools broke into various servers on the internet, sometimes trashing them: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake In my discussions of this subject, I've been at pains to tease apart two different aspects of these incidents: first, that it's wrong to speak of bots "going rogue" here (they're doing what they're designed to do); but second, that the alarming thing about these incidents is that they illustrate how deeply unserious our approach to information security has been, and remains. This is important context, and context is what gives us the object permanence we need to both understand and address real problems, like the two related facts that a) our IT systems are poorly constructed and indifferently maintained; and b) the people who are supposed to be fixing this keep making it worse. The worst culprits here are governments, though the private sector is also terrible (in truth, our cybersecurity nightmare is something of a private-public partnership from hell). Governments are deeply compromised when it comes to digital security because they have an irreconcilable conflict of interest: on the one hand, they want to defend their countries' administrative systems, firms and households from digital attacks. But on the other hand, they really want to be able to launch attacks on their adversaries, both foreign and domestic. Worse: because governments don't know who those adversaries might be (or might become at some later date), the state security apparatuses of the world's governments keep insisting that all working computer security must be dismantled, so they can spy on all of us in order to figure out whom among us is a Bad Guy, and then "travel back in time" through each newly discovered "bad guy's" communications to identify their confederates and detail their nefarious plots. This is an old, old, old fight. It was arguably the first policy fight of the digital era: the fight over whether we could have working encryption at all. Old hands call this era "the crypto wars" (from when "crypto" meant "cryptography"), when the NSA classed working encryption code as a "munition" and criminalized civilian access to it. That was a very hard-fought fight, and it was won decisively by the Electronic Frontier Foundation and our just-retired executive director Cindy Cohn, who, as a young lawyer, litigated the "Bernstein case" that established that code was a form of expressive speech protected by the First Amendment. If you're interested in learning more about this, you should read Cindy's newly published memoir, Privacy's Defender (all profits go to EFF): https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262051248/privacys-defender/ Before Cindy came on the scene, the crypto wars were being fought primarily by the "cypherpunks," a motley gang of computer security enthusiasts of many political stripes who were unified by their conviction that the most important aspect of security was defensive. The fact that the NSA wanted to be able to read the private messages and files of their adversaries (the "Four Horsemen of the Infocalypse": terrorists, drug traffickers, child pornographers and organized crime) must not be allowed to trump the fact that any encryption that the NSA could pierce could also be pierced by bad guys: corporate spies, state-sponsored spies, griefers, petty criminals, stalkers, identity thieves and other creeps. This argument was so indisputable, it's a tautology: "You cannot make a computer user more secure by making their computers less secure." We don't know how to make a computer that only "good guys" can break into, but which "bad guys" bounce off of. Either we make computers more secure, or we don't. We didn't. In the decades since the crypto wars, governments have embarked upon an uninterrupted program to weaken the security of our computers, with catastrophic effect. The most spectacular example is unquestionably the spy agencies' doctrine called "NOBUS," which stands for "no one but us"; as in "No one but us is smart enough to find this bug, which means that we can withhold its discovery from the manufacturer, which will allow us to weaponize this bug and use it to attack our enemies. Because no one but us is smart enough to find this bug, none of those enemies will ever discover it, weaponize it, and use it to attack the people who pay our salaries, who expect us to keep them safe." This turns out to be both catastrophically wrong and catastrophically dangerous. A series of leaks of computer vulnerabilities hoarded by both the NSA and CIA under NOBUS confirmed that these bugs were independently rediscovered by criminals and state actors at the rate of about 20% per year. Worse, though, is that these bugs don't need to be independently rediscovered, because the NSA and CIA both leaked them. The highest-profile leak was an NSA-hoarded vulnerability in Windows they codenamed "Eternal Blue." Eternal Blue leaked in 2017, whereupon cybercriminals hybridized it with some otherwise undistinguished ransomware to create Wannacry, a devastating piece of malware that took down hospitals, banks and oil pipelines, as well as the entire city government of Baltimore and the British Library: https://cdn.sanity.io/files/v5dwkion/production/99206a2d1e9f07b35712b78f7d75fbb09560c08d.pdf But NOBUS isn't the only example of spy agencies making our computers less secure in the name of making us more secure. Perhaps the most egregious example of that are the Bundestrojaners, malicious software purchased by the German government, whose customs agents secretly installed it on the computers of unsuspecting people during border inspections. This "lawful interception" software was hugely invasive: it could grab your screen, plunder your hard drive, and install and execute software on your computer, all with the utmost stealth, intended to keep you from knowing it was installed and operating on your computer. But it wasn't merely invasive – it was insecure, so anyone (rival spies, criminals, stalkers) could scan the internet for infected computers and take them over: https://www.ccc.de/en/updates/2011/staatstrojaner You really couldn't ask for a more perfect example of the maxim that you can't make computer users more secure by making their computers less secure. Despite this, governments continue to demand the introduction of grave, universal secure vulnerabilities into our digital lives. Take "chat control," a proposal to force every device manufacturer to install software that continuously scans your devices for child sex abuse material (AKA "child porn"): https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/04/eu-parliament-blocks-mass-scanning-our-chats-whats-next There are plenty of things wrong with this, starting with the fact that it requires your device to secretly grab and transmit sensitive images from your phone, which might include sensitive images of your kids that were requested by their doctors. This isn't a hypothetical: it's something that happened to a dad who subsequently lost his email, his login to every other account, his phone number, all of his files (including his tax records and his business data), and every photo he had ever taken of his family, without appeal, after Google automatically detected a photo he took of his son to send to the family pediatrician. Google also falsely accused this man of sexually abusing his child and sicced the SFPD on him: https://pluralistic.net/2022/08/22/allopathic-risk/#snitches-get-stitches But even if you're not worried about this, you should still have the object permanence to recall the lessons of NOBUS and the Bundestrojaner. We can't make computer users more secure by making their computers less secure, and it's hard to imagine something more insecure than a computer that you entrust with every sensitive detail of your life that is designed to run computer code in secret that you can neither inspect nor terminate (let alone delete). Hardly a day goes by without some country demanding that your computer's security be weakened in the name of protecting you. For years, both Conservative and Labour UK governments have been steaming towards a total ban on working encryption in the name of catching bad guys: https://pluralistic.net/2023/03/05/theyre-still-trying-to-ban-cryptography/ It's happening in Canada, too, where somehow "digital sovereignty" means "making every device used in Canada vulnerable to foreign spies so that our own spies can access our private communications": https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/05/canadas-bill-c-22-repackaged-version-last-years-surveillance-nightmare Then there's the "age verification" laws proliferating all around the world. Remember, there's no such thing as "age verification," there's only "spying on everyone, all the time, to figure out who the kids are": https://pluralistic.net/2026/06/23/destroy-the-village/#to-save-it Age verification requires multiple entities to assemble vast corpuses of the kinds of sensitive identification papers that would allow identity thieves to destroy the finances and lives of everyone in the country, and (as foretold) every time it's tried, these files leak. Someday, this will lead to doxing whole countries: https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/02/discord-faces-backlash-over-age-checks-after-data-breach-exposed-70000-ids/ Age verification is the latest and worst stage in governments' fraught relationship with private sector data-collection. The USA is the worst offender here: it is the largest, richest country in the world that has essentially no privacy protections. The last time the US updated its federal privacy law was in 1988, when the Video Privacy Protection Act banned the disclosure of your VHS rentals. Tech companies spy on you for the same reason your dog licks its balls – because they can, and no one stops them: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/10/ice-tech/#foreseeable-outcomes Which raises an obvious question: why hasn't Congress updated privacy law? And why hasn't the EU figured out how to force the US companies that pretend to be Irish to obey European privacy law? The answer is that governments love private sector data-collection, because it gives them a cheap, off-the-books source of warrantless access to information they aren't legally allowed to acquire: https://pluralistic.net/2021/04/13/public-interest-pharma/#axciom From Flock cameras to ICE's use of Google data in its ethnic cleansing campaign, the US government and the commercial surveillance industry have created a public-private partnership from hell, where governments refuse to block commercial spying and companies hand their commercial surveillance data over to governments in return. From there, it was a short leap to governments insisting that the private sector gather our data. That's the right way to think about age verification, chat control, and other mandates for corporations to spy on us using our devices and our accounts: a government requirement for private-sector mass surveillance. I have plenty of hostility to corporate overreach, but to have any hope of fighting that overreach, we need governments to be on our side. But for our governments, when it comes to cybersecurity, we are the enemy, and spying corporations are our governments' allies. Sometimes, that's utterly, literally true. Governments around the world are addicted to buying spyware from cyber-arms dealers, mostly headquartered in Israel and the UAE (with the odd Italian and British company for variety). These arms-dealers practice NOBUS-by-proxy, wherein they discover or pay bounties for bugs in widely used hardware, operating systems and applications and – rather than reporting them to the manufacturer – hoard them and weaponize them, and then sell the weapons to criminals, corporations, and our governments, who give them billions of our money to ensure that our computers have huge, glaring defects in them that leave us terribly vulnerable: https://citizenlab.ca/focus-area/targeted-surveillance/ In a world where our governments' national security apparatuses were genuinely committed to our safety and security, they would criminally prosecute these companies, not make their owners into billionaires. This is the context we should all be thinking about when it comes to these "rogue AI hacking agents." The IT systems that these irresponsibly deployed software products have trashed were already terrifyingly vulnerable…by design. Rather than fix these systems, our governmental "security" agencies have spent the past 40 years making them less secure, in order to make it easier for them to catch "bad guys," who now find it trivial to attack us through systems we are all totally reliant upon. In every way, in every area of law, governments fail to take our security seriously. That even includes copyright law. All over the world, the US Trade Representative has ensured that every country has an "anti-circumvention" law that makes it a crime to reverse-engineer and modify software without permission: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition From the very start, these have been a security nightmare. Remember the "Sony Rootkit?" Between 2005-2007, Sony-BMG Music distributed over 6m CDs that were deliberately infected with a piece of malicious software called a "rootkit" that was used to disable your computer's ability to rip (copy) music CDs. The way this rootkit did so was depraved in its indifference to the security of Sony-BMG's customers: at the same time as Sony-BMG's malware installed its secret anti-ripping program, it also altered their computers' operating systems to make them incapable of detecting any program or file whose name started with $SYS$. Immediately, malicious software authors started adding $SYS$ to the start of all their filenames, and that malicious software was therefore undetectable to millions of users' computers. It was even invisible to anti-virus software. Worse: Sony-BMG's rootkit infected 200,000-300,000 US government and military networks: https://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2005/11/sonys_drm_rootk.html Even worse: after the scandal broke, security researchers all over the world came forward to say that they'd discovered the Sony Rootkit months before it became common knowledge, but their lawyers had told them they weren't allowed to disclose its existence because doing so would fall afoul of anti-circumvention law. For months, this official, deliberate malware epidemic spread in secret because of anti-circumvention law. It's been more than 20 years since the Sony Rootkit, and anti-circumvention law is now worse than it was in the oughts: now it applies to far more devices from far more vendors. Today, it's common for corporations to threaten their own customers with civil and criminal liability if they have the temerity to hire outside auditors to evaluate the software they entrust their businesses to for security defects. And oh God, it's even worse, because the worst offender is Oracle, who are now the de facto IT czars of America: https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2015/08/oracle-security-chief-to-customers-stop-checking-our-code-for-vulnerabilities/ I'm not saying that these are the only problems with our IT security. What I am saying is that the hacking bots everyone's freaking out about didn't appear out of nowhere. If you have just a little object permanence, you can see that they are the terminal stage of a pathology that governments have only ever worsened: by hoarding and weaponizing vulnerabilities; by paying others to hoard and weaponize vulnerabilities; by criminalizing security audits; by insisting that every computer we rely on be equipped with deliberate vulnerabilities in software we can't inspect, terminate or delete. Yeah, there should be criminal and civil liability for OpenAI, Amazon, Anthropic and every other company whose bots "went rogue" and attacked servers. But that will do nothing to fix our IT. The table-stakes for a secure digital world are: public agencies that try to make our computers as secure as possible, including by administering the corporate death-penalty to any company that hoards and weaponizes information about bugs in our computer. We should protect and reward individuals and firms who come forward with true disclosures about bugs in systems we rely upon. We should not give companies the right to silence and punish those critics who want to warn us about their defective products. And we should not require that companies make us less secure in the name of making it easier for spies and cops to catch the bad guys. I used to have a 'Swiss Army Knife' when I was young, lost it long ago, and have just ordered another.

In the intervening time, the web has happened, and it turns out there are a vast multitude of pocket-knife enthusiasts out there discussing their preferred EDC ('Every Day Carry') penknives, arguing over which manufacturers use the best steel, and, even within the Victorinox fold, debating the relative merits of the Mountaineer, the Rambler or the Super Tinker. Victorinox have dozens of models to choose from, and, though there are many other options — I'm a big fan of my Leatherman Wave, for example — the company does seem to inspire particular loyalty.

But if you have one of their larger offerings and have been wondering just why you might need the little hook, the awl (or even, these days, the corkscrew) then you might enjoy this example of the kind of helpful material now available for those wanting to make the most of their EDC.

Gruber is right. The only way for the others to compete with Twitter is to start innovating. Get rid of the limits. The funny thing is Twitter, the dominant leader, is moving forward and getting rid of character limits, and introducing styles and links. They're acting like the little guy while the others, Bluesky, Mastodon, Threads, aren't doing anything to be more useful. That whole market is stuck in 2006 and the myth that 140 chars somehow was magic. It wasn't. It killed the web as a writer's platform. If you want to compete with Twitter, drop your proprietary protocols, hook up to the web standards, and peer with your competitors. I wouldn't be surprised if Twitter joined you. They have the same kind of competitive spirit that successful big companies have. It's time for their competitors to not win users through guilt, rather by providing a better service. Back in the day, we hated Microsoft's plan to suffocate the web, but we admired their tenacity and the way they kept the pressure on their competitors. We've had 20 years of stagnation in social networking. Time to stop being so sensitive. Bluesky made huge promises, and they aren't happening, and that was already years ago. Time for Plan B. I don't really care about the others, Masto isn't going to move and Threads? Wtf is that. Inbound and outbound RSS 2.0, is the way to go. And Markdown is the way you do text. This is what matters, you all are making something that's really simple so unbearably complicated.

2026-09-27 Still loving the MNT Pocket Reform

2026-10-12

2026-09-27 Still loving the MNT Pocket Reform

I still use the MNT Pocket Reform a lot. I recently took it along on a trip, as my “emergency” laptop, but also as my chill-out activity late at night in the hotel room, working on a little something instead of reading a book.

At home, I use it as my secondary laptop in the living room. My wife loves to sit on the couch and read and sit on the floor. Here, reception is not too good and so I use an Ethernet cable to get connected.

During our recent trip, Wi-Fi reception was never an issue.

The charging problems I used to have disappeared with a recent upgrade. So I can plug and unplug the laptop while it runs with no issues.

I sometimes run into the situation where the laptop keyboard seems dead. It’s not entirely dead because I can still use Hyper+Enter to call up and navigate the OLED menu. What almost always seems to help is closing and opening the lid. Other people havereported that they reset the keyboard multiple times using the OLED menu. Eventually, it works. As long as the situation does not deteriorate, I can live with it.

I also made my peace with Debian unstable. I haven’t run into any problems in a very long time, now.

#Pocket #Reform

2026-10-03. I’m holding off from upgrading the CPU of my MNT Pocket Reform because I feel that half the promise of buying this laptop was that it could act as some sort of long-term laptop with me being able to replace pieces as they fail. Should it turn out that the upgrade treadmill is worse than in my iPhone, however, with software upgrades demanding CPU upgrades every so many years, then there’d be no advantage to buying this laptop. I’m holding off with the upgrade in order to prove to myself that it is possible. I hope that it is possible. Yay for the i.MX8MP Module!

2026-10-04. Something that’s also on my mind is frugal computing. Having old hardware that is still supported by modern software is important to me. And working with it, finding the best programs, is part if this.

MuPDF instead of Evince or Okular.

Midnight Commander instead of Thunar; Thunar instead of Nautilus.

irssi and tmux instead of a web-based IRC cloent; IRC instead of Discord.

That kind of thing.

2026-10-06. @wim_v12e just published Frugal computing revisited.

In Manhattan, I lived on 57th St and Eighth Ave. Best location. The Columbus Circle subway station is under the building. Whole Foods a block away. Three Starbucks one block or less from the apartment (one was on 58th on the same block). Central Park has a six mile bike-only road (at least that's how bikers view it) and down the hill there's a much longer path along the Hudson River. Everywhere you look, a skyscraper is going up. Two were visible from my 50th floor window. New York is an amazing city because it can start up a huge gravity-defying construction project with almost no impact on the surrounding area. If I didn't know where to look I'd never see it. One of the biggest industries in the city is building the city. It's never finished. That's the way good software is too. And we just got a whole new tool for software construction, and it's like nothing we've ever had before.

Pluralistic: How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist (12 Oct 2026)

2026-10-12, updated: 2026-10-23

Today's links How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist: If you care about labor justice and artists' rights, stop focusing on copyright. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: China unblocks Wikipedia; CCC cracks the Bundestrojaner; "Children of the Sky"; "Messy"; Every top Icelandic banker is guilty; Climate activism x digital activism; Gene Kan on P2P's future; Larry Ellison x mass surveillance; W3C v patents; "Work from home" in the cybercrime supply-chain; "Nursery Rhyme Comics"; Glitchy tea-set; Tourist Guy; Vista v reinstallation; Ryanair v your bladder; Wells Fargo CEO loves "sales culture"; "Attention Merchants"; Orban v free press; AI v GIGO; Dylan wins the Nobel; India's starving kids app; Adobe's spyware copyfraud; Charter blackmails customers with bad credit threats; Fix UK housing. Upcoming appearances: Paris, Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Kilkenny, Sheffield, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist (permalink) If you work in the media, you have doubtless had a lifetime of encouragement to treat copyright as your primary source of economic protection, and doubtless you've been told that this protection arises from the fact that copyright is a property right – specifically, it's a subspecies of "intellectual property": https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-ip/ Property rights are capitalism's holy sacrament, so of course, it's natural to treasure any property right you can lay claim to. But this is a trap. Creative workers aren't asset speculators, we're workers. When we bargain with a media company to sell them our copyright, we're just bargaining to sell our labor, not our property. This is a distinction with a difference. Property rights are alienable. When you negotiate to sell your property to someone else, you propose to transfer the title to that property. If you sell your house, you don't get to move back in if you change your mind later. Sell your car, and you must not get in and drive it away. Nominally, creative workers only bargain away some of their copyright, because copyright is also divisible. You can sell US English print rights to a novel, a one-month license to synch a song to an advertisement, or the right to display a painting for a year. But here's the thing about property rights: the most reliable predictor of how many property rights you must give up in a sale isn't how many property rights you started with – it's how much bargaining power you have. For 50 years, governments have expanded copyright in every way, making it last longer, cover more works and restrict more uses, all backstopped by ever-steepening penalties. 50 years later, media companies – our bosses – are larger and more profitable than they've ever been, and we're poorer than we've ever been. The share of the money generated by our labor has declined, even as our rights over the product of that labor have expanded. How to make sense of this? It's easy, once you factor in power. In a world of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies and a single ebook/audiobook company, getting more copyright to bargain with just means getting more copyright to bargain away. When copyright's term expanded from "life plus 50 years" to "life plus 70 years," our bosses simply demanded the entirety of the new term, and didn't offer us a dime more. This is the thesis of Chokepoint Capitalism, the book on Big Tech, Big Media, and creative labor markets Rebecca Giblin and I published in 2022: https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx Chokepoint Capitalism is broken into two parts: the first half of the book is a series of pitiless, plain-language dissections of the baroque scams that media companies have used to make themselves richer from our work, from Spotify to Amazon to Livenation and beyond. From reader feedback, I can tell you that these chapters will make you very angry, because once you strip away all the deliberate obfuscation, all you're left with is one screw-job after another, each of which makes the creators you love poorer even as you pay more for their work. But then there's the second half of the book. This section is devoted to "shovel-ready" policy solutions, each of which is designed to change the "distribution" of the spoils of the media industry, putting more money in workers' pockets at the expense of our bosses. None of these are things you can do as a "conscious consumer." The monopolistic destruction of creators' livelihoods is a systemic problem and you can't solve it by shopping better. The point of these chapters is to lay out what we must demand from our policymakers when (inevitably), they propose to "solve" the problem of worsening straits for creative workers – and to help creative workers understand that when our bosses demand more copyright, that's not there to benefit us. One of these systemic solutions is "termination of transfer," a simple and radical idea that has a proven track-record of making creative workers richer at our bosses' expense. Simply put, "termination of transfer" is the statutory right to void any contract you've signed to transfer your copyright to someone else. In the USA, the 1976 Copyright Act introduced a 35-year termination right. 35 years after you sign any copyright contract, you can file some paperwork with the US Copyright Office and get that copyright back, no matter what your contract says. Now, most creative works don't have a commercial life after 35 years (very few works are commercially viable even after the original US copyright term of 14 years), but for those that do, termination of transfer is a reliable way to address the extremely common situation in which a creator signs away their rights for a low price, not knowing that it will become a lasting hit. Once you've scored that hit, you can probably get a better deal from your next work, but the deal for that hit is done and can't be altered. Termination solves this. From The Babysitters Club to the early Stephen King novels to George Clinton's entire catalog, termination of transfer has put lots of money into creative workers' pockets at the expense of corporations that ripped them off at the start of their careers. From the start, there was no question whether termination of transfer would make it into Chokepoint Capitalism. Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject, having co-authored the definitive study of termination: https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/ In the book, we note that – unlike longer copyright terms – termination has a proven track record of putting groceries on creators' tables, braces on their kids' teeth, and a roof over their heads. We go over the legislative history of termination in the 1976 Act, noting that it was originally supposed to be automatic and kick in after just 20 years. If we want to make creative workers richer, changing the 35-year administrative right into an automatic 20-year termination right is a no-brainer amendment to copyright law. How did an automatic right that kicked in after 20 years turn into a right you have to apply for after 35 years? Simple: our bosses hate termination. How much do they hate it? Well, take Mitch Glazier, the head of the Recording Industry Association of America, where he draws a $1.3m annual salary to represent the record labels. Before Glazier got the RIAA gig, he was an obscure Congressional staffer, but he was forced out of the job after he snuck a clause into an otherwise unrelated bill that killed termination of transfer for recording artists. This was so outrageous that Congress actually convened a special session so they could rip out Glazier's amendment, and Glazier got a new job as a millionaire lobbyist for the recording industry: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/03/its-a-trap-2/#inheres-at-the-moment-of-fixation Termination is hugely useful and quite radical. Last year saw Gary K Wolf, creator of the novel Who Censored Roger Rabbit? (later adapted by Disney as Who Framed Roger Rabbit?) claw back his rights to the book and its characters, in order to continue the series: https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way In 2023, Bill Willingham terminated the transfer of his wildly successful graphic novel series Fables from DC and released the copyright into the public domain: https://pluralistic.net/2023/09/15/fairy-use-tales/#sampling-license And now, Richard Garriott, AKA "Lord British," has claimed back the rights to the groundbreaking Ultima series of computer role-playing games, which he sold to Electronic Arts in 1992: https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/richard-garriott-is-officially-regaining-control-of-the-ultima-series/ On the Techjess podcast, Garriott marveled at how easy the process was: "there’s a really weird United States copyright law that says if you are the original holder of a copyright and you assign it or sell it to any publisher or any other entity, after 35 years, you can just take it back": https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2El7VtPuSzs EA killed off Ultima in 2000, and it has languished since, despite an ardent fandom. Garriott has vowed to reissue the old games and is mulling new ones. All this brings me back to property rights. Property rights are uniquely unsuitable to this kind of arrangement. You don't get to move back into the house your parents sold 35 years ago, and if you did, the photographer who took the family portrait in the hallway wouldn't be allowed to break in and take it away 35 years after you sat for it. Termination of transfer isn't an "IP right" – it's a labor right. It belongs to the large class of rights that are far more important and useful than mere property rights, such as privacy rights and human rights: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/28/cost-of-everything/#value-of-nothing If copyright were just about property rights, then termination of transfer would be inconceivable. Termination is a vestigial labor right at the very periphery of copyright. It protects artists, and it can only do so because it is not a property right. This is one of the themes in The Bezzle, my 2024 historical technothriller, starring my two-fisted forensic accountant hero Martin Hench who uses termination to help an artist claw back his rights from an unscrupulous former manager who forged his signature decades before (this plotline is based on the true story of Parliament/Funkadelic's George Clinton!): https://craphound.com/bezzle/ If you signed away your rights 35 years ago and want to get them back, check out the Authors Alliance, a nonprofit whose advisory board I volunteer for. We produced a tool that automates all the hardest parts of terminating your transfers and getting your rights back: https://www.authorsalliance.org/resources/termination-of-transfer/ Some of our most ardent fans are academics, whose publicly funded papers are published in journals dominated by a cartel of giant companies that do not pay the authors, nor the editors, nor the reviewers, but still claim all rights and charge the institutions that funded the research they publish tens of thousands of dollars per journal to access that research: https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/16/the-public-sphere/#not-the-elsevier But it's not just academics who have an interest in termination of transfer. It's video game authors, novelists, musicians – and maybe you, someday! Access and Trust

2026-10-12, updated: 2026-10-26

I had the good fortune to attend an Archiving the Black Web meeting last week. The main focus of the few days in St Louis was for fellows to share stories of web archiving work that they had been involved with. A few themes emerged for me while listening to these presentations. We weren’t using Chatham House
Rules, but I didn’t ask anyone if I could write about their work here, so these are broad strokes.

  • Fellows were often trying to contact website creators to negotiate consent. This process seemed like it was quite time intensive, and difficult, especially when contact needed to be established, and formal process was being followed.

  • Some fellows were archiving within their existing trust networks, where consent wasn’t such a big hurdle, and seemed to be established in a more informal way.

  • Helping website creators understand what it meant for their websites to be archived was challenging. Communicating why they would want to have a web archive of their content was also non-intuitive.

  • There was often a desire to create new websites that arranged the web archives along with additional materials, such as oral histories, maps, and other descriptive material.

  • There was also a need to limit access to a community of known users. These communities aligned with existing trust networks. I inferred from this that limiting access was one avenue to gaining consent.

  • Many of the fellows were using Browsertrix to create web archives, and some were also using ArchiveWebPage to do more detailed patch crawling. It seemed like there had also been some initial early work using Archive-It.

  • When it came to integrating access to archived content, fellows were often linking to the playback mechanism inside of Browsertrix itself.

  • Sometimes the website creators were given access to archived web content, while offering to serve as a backup.

  • A few were thinking about the sustainability of the web archiving work in terms of having their practice become more of a service. I had an interesting side conversation about how a cooperative model could potentially help grow a web archiving practice as a form of mutual aid.

Given the interest in creating web sites for the archived web content, and administering access to them, I mentioned to one of the organizers that it would be super if the fellows could be introduced to how toembed WACZ files in their own sites using the ReplayWebPage web component. I learned that they were already planning on doing this, and that it just hadn’t happened yet since the focus so far had been on creating the web archives. I still think Webrecorder’s innovation of allowing archived web content to be replayed anywhere on the web is one of their most transformative ideas.

I think it’s super interesting how methods of access seems to sometimes gate the types of material, and whose material, gets archived. Understanding goals in terms of access, such as where the web archives live, and who can see them, seems to shape the types of content that can be archived? I think this has a counterpart in traditional archives where the deed of gift often stipulates how and when records can be accessed.

Donors introduce a dynamic element to the archival process, bringing their own values, ideas, and interests. Examining donors through the concept of agency, as developed in the social sciences, reveals that they exercise significant influence on key archival functions, which in our theoretical models are generally treated as the sole purview of archival professionals. ( Fisher, 2015)

I heard from at least one fellow that they were working with Omeka, and that being able to embed WACZ files in Omeka could be desirable. Omeka S has a WebArchive plugin that supports WACZ replay, but I noticed that Omeka Classic did not, and it is still being actively used (and maintained).

Since I had some time to fill while waiting for my plane back I “used” Claude to create a WebArchive plugin for
Omeka Classic. It was just 80 lines of PHP, and I haven’t written PHP in over a decade, so I was grateful for the help. Once you’ve installed the plugin you can upload WACZ files and replay them directly in Omeka, where the data is stored, and you can use Omeka’s access control settings to set who can see them. Everything old is new again…

References

Fisher, R. (2015). Donors and donor agency: Implications for private archives theory and practice. Archivaria, 79, 91–119. Retrieved from https://archivaria.ca/index.php/archivaria/article/view/13528

GSoC 2026: Improving lit

2026-10-12, updated: 2026-10-19

This summer I worked on improving lit, the LLVM Integrated Tester, as part of Google Summer of Code 2026.

I got interested in compilers after seeing how much heavy lifting happens underneath a single line of code, especially on parallel accelerators like GPUs.Two courses at IIT Bombay, SysML and Advanced Computer Architecture, turned that from a passing interest into something I actually wanted to work on.I’d like to eventually move toward compilers or microarchitecture for parallel compute engines as a career, and LLVM felt like the right place to start: it’s the compiler infrastructure behind a large share of the toolchains people actually use, so performance work here doesn’t stay contained to one project.lit specifically appealed to me because the problems in it turned out to be systems problems, process scheduling, IPC, syscall overhead, GIL contention, not surface-level scripting fixes, which is exactly the kind of low-level work I wanted hands-on experience with before jumping into compiler internals directly.

My mentors were Aiden Grossman, Paul Kirth, and Petr Hosek.

The Project

lit is LLVM’s test runner. RUN: lines look like shell commands, but lit’s own internal shell parses and runs them itself.A 2024 RFC made that the default everywhere, arguing it’s faster and more consistent across platforms than spawning an actual shell process for every line ( RFC).The option to spawn a shell process instead still exists in the code, but now raises an error unless explicitly forced, and is on track for removal.By the time I started this project, it was lit’s own Python code, not a spawned shell process, parsing and executing every RUN: line, in every subproject in the monorepo, under ninja check-* (lit also runs a smaller set of tests in GoogleTest’s format, which skip RUN: entirely).None of that, parsing and executing RUN: lines, compiles or checks anything on its own.It’s the overhead sitting between a developer pushing a change and finding out whether it passed.lit hadn’t gotten much dedicated performance work before this project, even though every second it spends is a second not spent running an actual test.It’s testing infrastructure, and testing infrastructure tends to get left alone once it works well enough.

Petr Hosek’s project idea flagged three areas as worth a closer look:

  1. Excessive process creation: Builtin shell utilities like cat, diff, and resource-limit wrappers were spawning fresh Python interpreter subprocesses for every single invocation line.
  2. Execution engine & IPC bottlenecks: Locking and queueing overhead in the execution engine ( multiprocessing.Pool), causing scaling limits on modern high core count systems.
  3. Legacy codebase idioms: Python 2 patterns, redundant string concatenations, and sub-optimal loop structures remaining across lit’s execution paths.

Before writing the GSoC proposal, I ran lit under a debugger to see how testing actually happened underneath: where it spent its time, which paths were hot, and which of those hot paths had obviously unoptimized code sitting in them.That debugging pass is what the proposal’s four parts below are built from:

  1. Modernizing the Python implementation: cleaning up legacy Python 2 idioms and picking up things like @dataclass(slots=True) and functools.cache on lit’s hot paths.
  2. Reducing process overhead: moving the execution engine off multiprocessing.Pool and onto asyncio.
  3. Improving internal shell utilities: moving cat and diff in-process, and fixing a pipeline bug in env.
  4. Performance tuning via profiling: using Scalene to catch whatever the first three parts didn’t.

The sections below go through what actually happened once those turned into pull requests over the summer, which was not always what the proposal predicted.

The figure above shows how these fit together.Profiling (part 4) sits at the top because it feeds the other three tracks: Python modernization (part 1), reduced process overhead (part 2) and shell utility correctness (part 3).All four aim at one goal, making lit faster without changing test verdicts.The sections below are organized by these same four areas.I also wrote a small script around hyperfine early on, and later added a peak-RSS measurement pass to it.Most of the timing numbers below come from it.

Modernizing the Codebase

The first two weeks focused on eliminating legacy Python 2 idioms remaining in lit’s codebase, found by reading through every file in lit/ end to end:

  • A suffix map implemented as a plain dict was replaced with an IntEnum.The dict mapped a fixed set of parser kinds to values with no structure tying them together.An enum names each member, gives it one definition site, and makes membership and iteration explicit.This was an idiom change and I did not measure a speed difference.
  • zip(range(len(x)), x) loops were refactored to enumerate(x).Both yield (index, item) pairs, but enumerate says so directly and drops the separate range and len calls.Again an idiom change with no measured difference.
  • Explicit argument calls like super(Class, self) were updated to modern super().The two-argument form repeats the class name, so renaming the class silently breaks it.The Python 3 form has no such coupling.
  • String concatenation in the shell lexer’s ( ShLexer) hottest method was changed from repeated += string building to list joins.This one was a performance fix, covered below.

ShLexer was one of the hot paths that my initial profiling turned up: it runs on every character of every RUN: line, across every test file in the suite, and it built each token with str += inside a character loop continually reallocating intermediate strings, worst-case O(N²) on long tokens.That made its string-construction method worth optimizing and benchmarking directly.

It reduced the CodeGen/X86 test suite execution time from 99.31s to 94.96s (4.35s, a 4.4% improvement) and the Transforms suite from 51.46s to 50.89s (0.57s, a 1.1% improvement).

The proposal also planned to put @dataclass(slots=True) on lit’s hot data objects ( ShellCommandResult, ShellEnvironment, DiffFlags).These get created once per test, and a slotted class drops the per-instance __dict__, which cuts memory and speeds up attribute access.That part did not go according to the plan because slots=True on @dataclass needs Python 3.10, and the minimum Python version LLVM supports is 3.8.I used plain __slots__ instead, which works on 3.8 and gets the same benefit, and left a # Replace __slots__ with @dataclass(slots=True) comment in the code pointing at GitHub issue #200531, filed so the switch happens once the minimum version is raised.This kept coming up over the summer: the 3.8 minimum ruled out several other modern constructs too, and each time the resolution was the same, ship the best version 3.8 supports with a code comment naming what should replace it once the minimum moves.

Two other part 1 items were nice-to-have cleanups that didn’t ship early: replacing the hand-rolled _caching_re_compile with functools.lru_cache, and switching discovery.py from os.listdir() plus isdir() to os.scandir().I didn’t have numbers showing either one would matter yet, so I put time into the changes above instead, and both only came back months later, once Scalene profiling near the end of the summer gave me the numbers to justify them.They’re under Future Work below.

Pull Requests

  • optimize ShLexer string construction
  • modernize ParserKind implementation using Python3 IntEnum
  • replace zip(range(len(x)), x) with enumerate(x) in ProgressBar
  • refactor super() calls in ResultCode
  • add __slots__ to hot shell execution objects
  • handle config loading safely
  • make MetricValue a proper abstract base class
  • remove redundant f.close() in TestingConfig

Moving lit to ProcessPoolExecutor

At the start of the project, lit dispatched tests through multiprocessing.Pool and collected results in a loop calling ar.get(timeout).

That collection loop contained two issues:

  1. The timeout was calculated once before entering the loop, meaning --timeout did not anchor to a single absolute deadline as intended.
  2. Test results were matched back to tests by list index rather than by identity, meaning out-of-order task completions could attribute results to the wrong test.

Migrating to concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor fixed both, through as_completed() and an explicit mapping from futures to tests.For the first issue, as_completed() takes the deadline once and yields each future as it finishes.The remaining time is then always measured against a single absolute point in time, so --timeout means what it says.For the second issue, each future is a handle to exactly one submitted test.A future: test dict therefore returns the right test whichever order tasks finish in, where the old code relied on list position.It also decoupled lit’s execution engine from the rest of the runner.That’s what let me swap in different backends later without touching anything else, more on that further down.

Part 2 of the proposal aimed to reduce process overhead in the execution engine, which came from two costs paid for every test.The first is pickling: the main process serializes each Test object to send it to a worker over a pipe, and the worker serializes the result to send it back, so every test crosses the process boundary twice.The second is process creation: running a test means forking and exec-ing a fresh process for the tools in its RUN: lines, and that cost is paid again for every test.The proposal’s plan was to attack both by changing the execution engine.It sketched this migration as wrapping the whole thing in asyncio from the start, an async def _execute_async coroutine awaiting asyncio.as_completed() inside asyncio.run().What actually shipped left asyncio out entirely: a synchronous loop around plain concurrent.futures.as_completed(), since that alone fixed both bugs. asyncio did come back later, but as a completely separate experimental engine rather than this migration, covered further down.

The initial PR landed as a neutral refactor.Nine days later it got reverted, it had triggered two bugs in CPython’s concurrent.futures.process that multiprocessing.Pool had never hit.

First, Douglas Yung reported an AArch64 macOS bot hanging on ninja check-all, which David Candler reproduced on downstream Ubuntu/AArch64 hardware. ProcessPoolExecutor.shutdown(wait=True) calls call_queue.join_thread() before it joins the worker processes with p.join().On macOS, the feeder thread behind join_thread() can’t finish draining until the workers are joined, so it ends up blocking on a step that hasn’t happened yet.CPython’s own source has carried a comment about this exact macOS deadlock risk since 2018, which is why p.join() exists, it’s just sequenced on the wrong side of join_thread().

Second, lit was submitting every test future to the executor up front.Each submission writes an empty send_bytes(b"") call into the executor’s internal wakeup pipe, and even though the payload itself is nothing, CPython’s framing still costs 4 bytes per write for the length header.The OS pipe buffer defaults to 64 KiB, and 65,536 bytes divided by 4 bytes per write is exactly 16,384 writes before it fills, at which point submit() blocks while holding _shutdown_lock, which the manager thread also needs to drain the pipe ( CPython gh-105829).Running check-llvm submits ~64,500 tests, far exceeding that pipe limit.

The fix implements windowed submission.lit first submits a window of tests, 8 times the worker count by default ( SUBMISSION_WINDOW_PER_WORKER in run.py), then waits for completions.Each time a future finishes, lit submits exactly one more test, so the number of outstanding futures never exceeds the window.Since every submission writes one entry into the wakeup pipe and the manager thread drains it as work completes, the undrained writes are bounded by the window rather than by the suite size, so the pipe cannot reach the 16,384 write limit and submit() never blocks while holding _shutdown_lock.The window still exceeds the worker count, so every worker stays busy.After verification across macOS and AArch64 test environments, the relanded migration merged cleanly.

Pull Requests

  • migrate lit to ProcessPoolExecutor
  • reland “migrate lit to ProcessPoolExecutor”

A Regression on High Core Count Machines

In August, Cullen Rhodes reported a scaling regression: check-llvm ran 56% slower on a 64-core AArch64 Graviton2 machine (72.98s vs a 46.70s baseline).Benchmarks on 10-core (macOS) and 16-core (Linux) test setups had shown only a 0.2% to 0.5% difference against baseline, indicating the slowdown was specific to high core count scaling rather than a universal regression.

The cause stemmed from concurrent.futures.wait().Calling wait() re-registers listener callbacks against every outstanding future on each iteration, causing repeated $O(N)$ scanning cost per completion as concurrency grows.

Replacing the wait() rescan with a SimpleQueue and add_done_callback(), registered once per future at submit time instead of rescanning the whole pending set, reduced the 56% regression on 64 cores down to ~8%.

My mentor, Paul Kirth, built on that, adding worker-side task batching ( execute_batch()) on top of the same SimpleQueue model.Paul had access to a 64-core Threadripper workstation, so it was easy for him to test scaling well past what I could reach, and he measured check-llvm dropping from 105.2s to 48.38s, 4.6% faster than the pre-migration baseline of 50.7s.

Pull Requests

  • collect completed tests via callbacks, not wait() (closed, superseded by Paul Kirth’s fix below)
  • address scaling problems with ProcessPoolExecutor (Paul Kirth)

Evaluating Execution Engine Architectures

With the ProcessPoolExecutor migration in place, and Part 2 already calling out an asyncio engine as worth trying, I built and benchmarked three alternative execution engine designs to see if process creation overhead or IPC pickling costs could be cut further.

Thread-Based Execution ( ThreadPoolExecutor)

Even with the windowed-submission fix above, every test still meant a full process fork plus a pickle round-trip of its Test object and result.A Scalene profile of llvm-mca at -j1 showed the fork/exec syscall alone costing 4.5% of wall-clock time, more than every line of lit’s own Python combined.The combined process-and-pickle dispatch overhead was attributable for 5.23% of wall-clock at -j1, rising to 22.25% at -j40 as concurrency increased.The most direct way to cut that cost is to stop paying for a process per test at all, and rather use worker threads.In theory, a single process with multiple threads running tests should perform much better.

Before testing this, I had to fix three thread-safety issues in lit: os.umask (which is process-global and was mutated around every subprocess launch), the regex compilation cache in _caching_re_compile (an unlocked dictionary), and the per-suite environment dictionary in GoogleTest formats.

Once those races were fixed, I benchmarked ThreadPoolExecutor on check-llvm:

  • Apple M5 (10 cores): 401s with threads versus 216s with processes (1.86x slower)
  • Intel i5-13450HX (Ubuntu 24.04): 591.21s with threads versus 109.15s with processes (5.42x slower)

Profiling with Scalene at -j1 and -j10 revealed why threads performed so much worse than processes.Plain Python bytecode’s share of time barely changed, but native and C extension time rose from 10.28% to 34.12% on macOS, and from 16.35% to 43.79% on Linux, concentrated in subprocess.py, threading.py, and posixpath.py.Because lit spends most of its time spawning and waiting on subprocesses, worker threads continuously contend for Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL).With ten worker threads running concurrently, GIL contention dominated runtime.Until free-threaded Python (PEP 703) becomes standard, threads are not viable for lit.

Phase-Pipeline Execution

In lit today, a single worker process executes all five phases of a test from start to finish: parsing the test script, applying substitutions, parsing shell syntax, running the commands, and formatting results.I experimented with a phase-pipeline design where each phase runs in its own process, passing work down a queue like a hardware CPU pipeline.

Timing execution phases in TestRunner.py showed that the actual execution phase (spawning and waiting on llc or FileCheck) accounts for 84% to 89% of total runtime.The remaining four phases combined make up only ~10.7% of execution time.By Amdahl’s Law ($\frac{1}{1 - 0.107} \approx 1.12\times$), even if we perfectly overlapped those four phases with zero IPC overhead, the theoretical maximum speedup is about 1.12x.

When I built the prototype, wall-clock time came out virtually identical to the default process backend, within 0% to 4% noise.It also required four pickle crossings per test instead of two, and didn’t reduce the process count either.Not worth the added complexity, so I dropped it.

Asyncio Single-Process Engine

To eliminate worker processes and IPC pickling entirely, I wrote a single-process execution engine using Python’s asyncio.

In an asyncio engine, test objects never leave the main process.To prevent asyncio.create_subprocess_exec from spawning a helper thread per child process (which would re-introduce GIL contention), I explicitly set SafeChildWatcher so process reaping happens on the main event loop via signal handlers.

The benchmark results depended heavily on core count:

  • At -j1: 1.8x to 2.3x faster than process pools, because there is no IPC, pickling, or process pool overhead.
  • At -j4+: 1.5x to 1.9x slower, because a single Python event loop cannot run tasks across multiple CPU cores in parallel.

The crossover point falls between -j2 and -j3 on the machine I tested this on.Below that, asyncio wins because there’s no IPC to pay for.Above it, one Python process just can’t keep enough cores fed.

Dispatch Chunking

I also tested dispatch chunking, where the main process submits multiple tests in a single ProcessPoolExecutor.submit() task call to reduce pickling frequency.

Because --order=smart sorts tests by descending historical duration, a contiguous chunk of consecutive tests concentrates several of the slowest tests onto one worker while other workers finish early and sit idle.Chunk sizes above 1 require --order=random instead, to avoid exactly that.

On llvm-mca at -j10, the smart-order baseline was 3.15s.Chunk sizes of 1, 8, and 32 under random order measured 3.29s, 3.14s, and 3.21s.None of that is a difference worth asking reviewers to take on a hard --order=random requirement, so I left it as a draft instead of pushing it through review.

Summary of Engine Experiments

Engine DesignMechanismBenchmark PerformanceResult**ProcessPoolExecutor (Baseline)**Worker process pool with windowed submissionBaseline ( check-llvm: ~50.7s)Shipped as default****ThreadPoolExecutorWorker thread pool1.86x to 5.42x slowerRejected (GIL contention)Phase-Pipeline EngineDedicated process per test phase0% to 4% difference vs baselineRejected (adds pickle crossings)Asyncio EngineSingle-process event loop1.8x–2.3x faster at -j1, slower at -j4+Not pursued further (doesn’t scale past a few cores)Dispatch ChunkingSubmitting test batches per worker taskNo measurable win at -j10 under --order=randomLeft as a draft

Pull Requests

  • migrate lit to ThreadPoolExecutor (closed)
  • add dispatch chunking to the worker pool (draft)

Running cat and diff In-Process

By late June, cat and diff were the shell builtins spawning external subprocesses, incurring Python interpreter startup overhead for file I/O operations.

To run them in-process while maintaining pipeline compatibility ( | and 2>&1), I structured the implementation across three PRs:

  1. Refactored cat.py and diff.py so main() delegates execution to a run(argv, stdin, stdout, stderr, cwd) function that takes IO streams as arguments.
  2. Implemented an InProcessPipe shim (duck-typed to subprocess.Popen) allowing TestRunner.py’s pipeline executor to treat in-process builtins transparently alongside spawned tools.
  3. Enabled in-process cat and diff execution by default.

Benchmarking in-process cat and diff across six builtin-heavy test suites ( UpdateTestChecks, Interpreter, Integer, Feature, ClangScanDeps, and ExtractAPI) showed median wall-clock runtime dropping from 67.66s down to 63.02s (a 6.9% speedup) with zero RSS increase and byte-identical test output.

Pull Requests

  • add stream-injectable run() core to builtin cat
  • use provided streams in builtin diff
  • run builtin cat / diff in-process instead of spawning

The env Short-Circuit Bug

LLVM issue #115578 identified a bug where a bare env command with no subcommand returned early from the pipeline executor, silently dropping subsequent commands (causing lines like env | FileCheck to skip validation).

The proposal’s plan for this was to separate env processing out of the main command loop.By the time I actually got to it, that wasn’t necessary anymore: the InProcessPipe helper built earlier in the summer for the cat/ diff work above gave me a pipeline-stage abstraction that didn’t exist when the proposal was written, so I ran bare env through that instead of building the bespoke fix originally planned.Fixing the bug meant FileCheck finally ran on lines it had always been silently skipping.That surfaced three previously-invisible bugs across six test fixtures: a KEY = VALUE vs KEY=VALUE format mismatch, two check-prefix typos, and one FileCheck-empty-input case needing --allow-empty.All three had been masked by the same class of failure the GitHub issue itself described.

Pull Requests

  • stop bare env from short-circuiting the pipeline

Overview

  • Cleaned up the legacy Python 2 idioms still left in lit’s codebase.
  • Migrated lit to ProcessPoolExecutor.Found and fixed two CPython concurrency bugs along the way, and helped on the follow-up fix for the high-core-count regression.
  • Tried a thread-based backend.It performed far worse than processes because of GIL contention, and I wrote up why instead of just dropping it quietly.
  • Moved cat and diff to run in-process instead of spawning a subprocess per invocation.
  • Built and benchmarked three more execution engine designs on top of that.
  • Fixed the env pipeline short-circuit bug, which turned up a handful of latent test bugs on the way.

Future Work

  • Type Annotations: Adding type annotations across lit to improve maintainability and catch type errors early.
  • Testing PPE under Random Ordering: Evaluating ProcessPoolExecutor with --order=random by default or exploring better load-balancing heuristics for batched execution.
  • Executor and IPC Overhead at Full-Suite Scale: A separate Scalene profile of the full check-llvm suite showed ProcessPoolExecutor’s own manager thread and the pickled-result IPC pipe write together account for about 71% of CPU time, while lit’s own code stays under 16%.Filed as issue #218095: the IPC share grows with test count, from about 2% on llvm-mca to about 10% on check-llvm, rather than staying fixed.

An earlier, smaller-scale round of Scalene profiling had already turned up three more targeted fixes:

  • LRU Cache regex compilation: Replacing TestRunner.py’s custom _caching_re_compile with functools.lru_cache saves ~0.10s self-CPU time on llvm-mca.Already upstreamed: use functools.lru_cache instead of lit.util.memoize, followed by removing the now-unused memoize function itself.
  • Directory scanning with os.scandir(): Replacing os.listdir() + os.path.isdir() with os.scandir() avoids redundant stat() calls during test discovery, cutting ~18% of warm discovery overhead on llvm/test and clang/test.
  • Pre-compiling kPdbgRegex: Compiling kPdbgRegex once at module load saves 108MB in allocations and ~0.048s on full llvm-mca test runs.

Profiling ruled some things out too.The proposal listed breaking up TestRunner.py, over 2,400 lines in one file, as a possible refactor if profiling justified it.I tried a few substitution-engine rewrites on top of the lru_cache fix above and none of them measured faster than run-to-run variance, so there wasn’t a real case for it, and it’s still one file.

What I’ve Learned

  • CPython concurrency internals: chasing the macOS shutdown-ordering deadlock and the wakeup-pipe deadlock forced me to actually learn how CPython handles multi-process shutdown and IPC, not just treat concurrent.futures as a black box.
  • Syscall overhead and the GIL: Scalene made it obvious why threads lost.Syscall-heavy work spends most of its time exactly where threads can’t help.
  • Duck-typed abstractions: InProcessPipe mimicking subprocess.Popen meant the rest of the pipeline code didn’t need to know or care that cat and diff weren’t spawning a process anymore.

Beyond GSoC, I’d like to keep contributing to LLVM’s testing infrastructure, particularly digging into the executor and IPC overhead from issue #218095, and the type-annotation pass listed under Future Work above.

I’ve also been reading up on MLIR on the side this summer, working through it with an LLM whenever I got stuck, and I’d like to get more directly involved there next, especially on the GPU-facing dialects.It’s a jump from testing infrastructure to compiler internals, but it’s the direction I actually want my work to go in.

Acknowledgements

Thank you to my mentors, Aiden Grossman, Paul Kirth, and Petr Hosek, for their guidance throughout the summer.

Thanks also to Douglas Yung and David Candler for reporting and verifying the macOS/AArch64 shutdown fixes, Cullen Rhodes for identifying and verifying the high core count scaling regression, and Alexander Richardson for reviewing several pull requests throughout the summer.

Thank you to the LLVM Foundation for organizing everything, and to Google Summer of Code for the opportunity.

The Fascinating World of Domains

2026-10-11

Pete Millspaugh has a lovely article over on WIRED that peers into the world of domains. (If you’re as interested in the esoteric details of domains as I am, follow Pete’s writing at Dot Com Press.)

You should just read the article, but here are a few things that stood out to me.

The .com Registry

Did you know who the registry for .com is? I didn’t.

The registry that owns .com, Verisign, makes a billion and a half dollars every year just by keeping the lights on. To Verisign’s credit, the lights never go out: It reports 100 percent uptime over the past 28 years. It’s a pretty slick business model, watching over a database of words and collecting annual renewal fees. Warren Buffett thought so too, investing in Verisign in 2012, when its stock price was about one-eighth what it is today.

Why is it simultaneously surprising and not surprising that the company running .com makes billions and has 100% uptime over almost three decades?

Maybe GitHub should reach out for some advice, lol.

Buying Domains Is a Spy Thriller

Apparently the last time you could buy generic top-level domains (gTLDs) was in 2012.

So now that ICANN is providing another window of purchases in 2026 — and nobody knows when another window will open — there’s a lot of interest in capitalizing on these moments for new gTLDs.

most organizations [are] extremely secretive about their plans. One applicant from the last round tells me companies were flying around the world, meeting in person to avoid any risk of digital leaks, avoiding Gmail for fear of Google spying. Instead of email or video calls, she flew to London, then to Madrid. “We did it all in person. People got a little weird and scary, super paranoid.”

There’s a certain irony to this — people flying around the world to conduct business on owning a piece of the internet because they don’t trust the internet.

It appears the future of the internet is to be negotiated offline lol.

More Domains = More Online Handles

We haven’t had new gTLDs since 2012. Why do we need more?

I can imagine a future where expressive top-level domains become our personal brands, identities on the internet. This is already true in some nerdy corners of the web, like on Bluesky, where your domain is your username. I don’t call my internet friends Neal and Luke, I call them neal.fun and luke.zip. Instead of joining the land rush to grab our username on each new social media site, we’ll carry our domain around the web with us.

I’m telling you, domains are the OG handles on the internet.

More domains mean more opportunities for individual expression at the root layer of internet infrastructure — that makes sense for a web that’s meant to be worldwide!

You Think You Have a Domain Vice?

As developers, we often joke about our addiction to buying domain names for our side projects.

But buying a domain name — e.g. my-side-project.com — is child’s play compared to buying a generic top-level domain name (gTLD). That’s where the domain whales are.

ICANN charges a $227,000 application fee for each string, to recover the cost of running the program. The $36 million or so that Nova will need to cover those fees […] is coming from the personal bank account of Yoni Belousov, a reclusive domain investor (industry jargon: “domainer”) who’s been in the business since he was 14 years old.

Next time somebody asks me what I’d do with an insane amount of wealth, I now have the jargon for an answer: “I’d become a domainer.”

A Few Fun Facts to Close

A few things about domains I didn’t know until I read this:

all two-letter extensions are off the table. Those belong to countries, like .co in Colombia and .me in Montenegro and .ai in Anguilla.

If you want to run a geographic TLD, like .nyc or .paris, you need approval from that municipality

your string can’t be too similar to an existing one (.corn is a no-go; looks too much like .com)

certain special strings are off limits, like .icann and .www (wouldn’t that be a trip).

www.www would be a baller domain! Just think of the recursion you could do with that on the subdomain level.

Tom Ellison On “Serious Writing” and Humor

2026-10-11, updated: 2026-10-22

Welcome to the Subscription Edition of A Newsletter of Humorous Writing. Our paid subscribers keep the weekly newsletter running, and we’re deeply grateful for your support. (And if you’re not already subscribed, you can sign up here .)

This week we’re turning off the paywall and turning things over to Tom Ellison . Tom is a humor writer who has a new book coming out on November 10th, a satire of the manosphere called MAN-THOLOGY: 365 Alpha Maxims Guaranteed to Help You Know Everything, Feel Nothing, Get Jacked, and Never Die, by Chud Buffly. Tom’s also hosting live events for the book in NYC and Washington, DC .

Tom’s guest-writing this edition to talk about how “serious” writing can be more relevant to humor writing than you might think. And if you’re interested in learning more, Tom’s also got a class on the subject coming up on October 24th .

After that, we’ve got a couple of recommendations of things we’ve been into lately: A radio program and a film soundtrack that’s perfect for working.

On “Serious Writing” and Humor

“Serious” writing may not be the most common route to short humor writing, but it can be valuable experience if you know what translates and what doesn’t.

By “serious” writing, I don’t mean just anything non-humor, like literary fiction or poetry. I mean specifically non-creative, non-fiction writing--legal analyses, financial assessments, news articles, and the like. This is a topic I know something about, because before I started humor writing, I was trained in writing intelligence assessments as a CIA analyst.

In that former life, I spent much more time on clear, accurate, informative writing than Jason Bourne-esque spycraft. This kind of writing is not exactly Mark Twain, unless you find yourself thrilled and entertained by prose like “Egypt: Situation Report, 3 July 2013” or “ISIS: ______ing to __ _______ ___ in ______. But that kind of “serious writing” exists across law, medicine, business, policy analysis, news reporting–anywhere writing aims to communicate information clearly and persuasively rather than evoke a visceral or emotional response.

People With Square Jobs Can Still Be Funny

For my lawyers, doctors, analysts, and other fellow Professional Lame-Os, this part is the pep talk.

When I backed my way into humor writing, I felt out of place. Unsurprisingly, many of my writing peers have backgrounds in cooler creative or comedic fields. They do sketch, improv, or stand-up. They work in the fine arts, or pop culture criticism, or advertising.

But in fact, I eventually realized there’s also lots of us straddling the Serious←→Silly worlds. The hilarious Gracie Beaver-Kairis works in finance! McSweeney’s regular Tiffany Li is a tech policy expert! New Yorker humorist Miriam Jayaratna is a clinical psychology PhD! Belladonna Managing Editor Alice Phillips is a lawyer! Funny writers Gary Altmeter and Nick Morgan are… also lawyers! Actually, I think Tiffany Li might be a lawyer too? Wow, lots of lawyers, are lawyers doing ok? Do I need a J.D.?

The point is: people who write dry, serious stuff can, and do, write funny.

What Translates

Here are the main Serious Writing skills that transfer to short humor writing, in my experience.

Structure & Format: A lot of serious writing matches a preset template to the writing topic or task at hand, rather than starting from a blank page. Contracts, obituaries, government memos, grant proposals–they all start with off-the-shelf templates. Short humor is similarly much easier when you have a toolbox of existing templates to graft your jokes onto, whether literal ( FAQs About ____, Daily Itinerary of a _____, etc.) or conceptual ( Juxtaposition of COMMON EXPERIENCE with CONTRASTING CHARACTER/POV, Exaggerated Expression of BAD OPINION BEING SATIRIZED).

Precision of Language: Serious Writing hinges on precision of language. “Extremist” vs. “Terrorist.” “Agreement” vs. “Treaty.” The differences matter. Likewise for humor, word choice matters. If your comedic monologue is from a “Mobster” vs. a “Gang Member,” how might that change what the audience reads into your jokes?

Co-writing: Being a good collaborator helps any kind of writing. Most Pulitzer-winning journalism, Nobel prize-winning science, or world shaping government policy come from teams, not one guy on a laptop. The same goes for lots of humor–collaborative pieces like this, or co-written books like New Erotica for Feminists, Jokes to Offend Men, or Obey in Advance. And besides, co-writing is a great way to meet people and have fun, which is the point, right? I hope it’s not the money.

Audience Awareness: Finally, in humor you have to know your audience, just like in Serious Writing. What am I assuming the reader already knows and believes, for these jokes to be funny? Is this premise better for McSweeney’s or Reductress? You answer these questions using the same skills you use to answer “What arguments will this judge find persuasive?” or “What does the Ambassador need to know today, and what can wait until next week?”

What Might Not Translate

Despite all the commonalities above, funny and serious writing are different. There are a few areas to be deliberate about breaking free from any “Serious Writing” habits you have.

Neutrality: A lot of journalistic, government, and other writing wants you to be sober, neutral, and consider all sides as good-faith. Humor writing should not do this. In satire, you want to pick a point of view and commit to it hard. Likewise, in general humor you want to heighten and cut loose--no one ever says “that was so hilarious and restrained.”

Tone: Relatedly, journalism and a lot of Serious Writing encourages the “View from Nowhere” (whether it should is its own debate). No emotional language, no value-laden terms, no regional slang, etc. “Widespread human rights shortfalls,” not “massacres.” “Scientifically unsupported claims,” not “unhinged bullshit.” But this gets in the way of hard-hitting satire, funny specifics, and a well-defined POV.

Overanalysis: Many of the skills in the section above are very analytical and left-brained, because that is the nature of Serious Writing. They lend themselves better to satire (humor making a point) than to general humor (funniness for its own sake). But I adore writing by people like Colin Nissan, Lillian Stone, Sean McGowan, and Riane Konc who can take just a word or scene and make it hilarious. Pieces like this or this probably did not start with a structured analysis. It’s helpful not to overthink or pre-edit yourself, and to also explore more judgment-free, off-the-rails, wacky types of writing. This is something I’m still working on!

A Note on Professional Personas

One last thought. If you are pursuing humor writing, while also doing your Serious Job, it’s worth considering your professional persona(s). Will you have two, or will they be merged? Will you take on a professional split personality, or will you list your legal practice under the same name as your McSweeney’s pieces, the ones with the cum jokes?

There are benefits to both approaches. I’m still finding the right balance between segregating and combining my humor writing with my professional presence on climate change. Would it be better or worse if I wrote as Tom Goodwin (my middle name)? Tom Deckhard (my aspirational movie character name)? Tom Higglebum (my actual movie character name, realistically)? Something to consider.

Some Recommendations From Luke and James

Luke recommends Links Intuition with Ashley Clark . Ashley, former director of film programming at BAM and current Criterion Collection curatorial director, is not just a great writer and film critic—he also has great taste in music. In this hour-long program, Ashley takes listeners through an eclectic mix of tunes, providing thoughtful commentary and interesting context along the way. In addition to tracks from some familiar friends, I suspect you’ll also find at least one new fave in this bunch. Pharoah Sanders’ “ Greeting To Saud (Brother McCoy Tyner)” was a particularly delightful discovery for me.

James recommends the Tangerine Dream soundtrack to the 1981 Michael Mann movie Thief. A great movie with a great soundtrack, that’s perfect to put on in the background for work/chores/plotting a robbery/etc. Tangerine dream is a killer ‘60s German electronic band, so you know the tracks are good. But the fact that they’re written to score a neo-noir means they have just enough tension to light a fire under your ass but not so much that it stresses you out—the perfect working music.
